verdict.notes: ORIGIN CONFIRMED. stale-lock-file.ts:33-58 isLockOwnerDefinitelyStale with the literal comment 'Timestamp age alone cannot prove the owner stopped writing. Only a mismatched process start time proves PID reuse while the PID is alive' (:39-41), darwin normalization at :46-49 (divide by 1_000_000 when starttime > 10_000_000_000 — the reader called this 'nanoseconds vs microseconds', it is really a magnitude-triggered unit normalization), and :60-82 shouldRemoveDeadOwnerOrExpiredLock falling back to age only when there is no PID. plugin-sdk/file-lock.ts:29 staleRecovery 'fail-closed'|'remove-if-unchanged', :34 reentrantOwner, :97-120 sameFileIdentity dev/ino with the Windows dev===0 case, :157-174 the recovery wiring. KEEP=FALSE on applicability, not on evidence. Halbert does not have the problem this solves: every cross-process lock in the tree is a kernel-advisory fcntl.flock on a macOS-only host — crypto/storage.py:492-498, consent/store.py:245-270, obs/audit.py (LOCK_FILE '.append.lock' at :168), config/being_config.py:539, model/client.py. flock is released by the kernel when the holder dies or the fd closes, so there is no stale owner to reclaim and no owner payload to mis-trust; the '.lock' pathnames are flock targets, not payload sidecars. OC02-infra-rest.summary: Read 29 substantive files out of ~1,100 in this oversized unit, prioritized against the FOCUS text. Strongest findings: (1) a DNS-rebinding-resistant SSRF guard with post-resolution re-checking and cross-origin redirect header stripping — Halbert has zero equivalent despite ~20 outbound HTTP call sites including MCP-proxy and guest-persona paths; (2) filesystem durability/locking (PID+starttime stale-lock reclaim, directory-fsync-after-rename) where Halbert has inconsistent partial coverage (some modules fsync files, none fsync directories, being_config.py fsyncs nothing); (3) host-process supervision (launchd marker detection, subprocess env-var blocklist) confirmed absent, matching the lift master plan's explicit note that the watchdog/daemon workstream was deliberately left un-packeted — this unit's C3/C8 candidates are the concrete shape that packet would take. The unit as literally specified (every src/infra file not in OC01's exclusion grep) is far too large for one reader — it includes a ~150-file outbound/messaging cluster, a ~140-file SQLite migration subsystem, a ~70-file heartbeat cluster already covered elsewhere, and ~80 files of self-update choreography gated on a founder pricing decision (FDR-04). These are called out explicitly in unread_areas rather than skimmed superficially, so follow-up readers can be scheduled against them.

missed_by_reader.title: PATH-hijack-resistant system-binary resolution (strict vs standard trust tiers) — Halbert drives the macOS Keychain through a bare `security` name
missed_by_reader.lines: resolve-system-bin.ts:5-28 (SystemBinTrust doc: strict = 'Only fixed OS-managed directories. Use for security-critical binaries like openssl'; UNIX_BASE_TRUSTED_DIRS = /usr/bin,/bin,/usr/sbin,/sbin; DARWIN_STANDARD_DIRS = /opt/homebrew/bin,/usr/local/bin appended only in 'standard'), :106-136 buildUnixTrustedDirs with the NixOS comment 'Never derive trust from NIX_PROFILES: env-controlled Nix store/profile entries can be attacker-selected', :159-217 resolveSystemBin with the header 'This MUST be used instead of bare binary names in execFile/spawn calls ... to prevent PATH-hijack attacks via user-writable directories'; path-env.ts:195-214 (project-local node_modules/.bin off by default and only ever appended; 'Only immutable OS directories go in prepend so they take priority over user-writable locations'; brew dirs appended and explicitly 'must not be treated as trusted')
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Internal infrastructure binaries are never invoked by bare name. A resolver searches a fixed, non-user-writable directory list and returns an absolute path, with two trust tiers: `strict` (OS dirs only) for anything security-critical, `standard` (OS dirs first, then Homebrew/package-manager dirs) for convenience tools. Separately, the PATH handed to child processes is rebuilt so immutable OS directories are prepended and every user-writable directory is appended, so a planted binary can never shadow a system one.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Add halbert_core/halbert_core/utils/system_bin.py with resolve_system_bin(name, trust='strict'|'standard') searching a fixed list (/usr/bin, /bin, /usr/sbin, /sbin; plus /opt/homebrew/bin, /usr/local/bin only under 'standard') and returning an absolute path or None, and convert the security-critical call sites first: crypto/storage.py:204-205 `_run(argv)` is invoked at :230-231, :249-250, :278, :299 with argv[0] == 'security' (gated only by shutil.which('security') at :227) — a PATH-hijacked `security` receives Halbert's custody key material on stdin and returns whatever it likes on stdout; streaming/sandbox.py:98-100 probes 'bwrap'/'sandbox-exec' by bare name, i.e. the sandbox decision itself is PATH-dependent; crypto/storage.py:271 shutil.which('secret-tool'). Then the ~50 remaining subprocess.run sites that pass bare tool names (utils/ollama.py:49,158; dashboard/__main__.py:66; vision/ocr.py:172; tools/schedule_cron.py:85,94 `crontab`). OpenClaw itself models the endpoint: machine-name.ts:14 calls '/usr/sbin/scutil' and host-account-name.ts:34,39 call '/usr/bin/id' and '/usr/bin/dscl' by absolute path. Halbert already spot-hardcodes absolute paths elsewhere (utils/platform.py:119-125, dashboard/routes/editor.py:182), so the convention exists but is unenforced.

missed_by_reader.title: PID liveness must be paired with process start time (and argv identity) — Halbert's boot-time run-receipt recovery uses a bare os.kill(pid, 0), exactly where PID reuse is most likely
missed_by_reader.lines: gateway-lock.ts:13-14 (imports getFileLockProcessStartTime and isPidAlive from ../shared/pid-alive.js), :36-47 LockPayload carries pid + createdAt + startTime, :203-206 ('process has the same argv shape'), :240-246 which ends `return isGatewayArgv(args, { allowGatewayBinary: true }) ? "alive" : "dead"` — i.e. a live PID whose argv is not a gateway is classified DEAD; gateway-process-argv.ts:18-42 parseProcCmdline/isOpenClawArgv/isGatewayArgv; stale-lock-file.ts:39-52 the start-time comparison already cited in C2
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Owner liveness is a three-part test, not a signal probe: the PID must exist, its recorded process start time must still match, and (for the instance lock) its argv must still look like the program that wrote the record. Any mismatch means the PID was recycled and the record is stale.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Harden scheduler/run_receipts.py. `_default_pid_alive` (:54-66) is `os.kill(pid, 0)` with PermissionError treated as alive, and `recover_on_boot` (:180-197) uses it to decide which `running` receipts become `interrupted`. It runs ON BOOT — the one moment PIDs have been recycled from low numbers — so a stale receipt whose owner_pid now collides with any unrelated live process stays `running` forever and its job is never recovered or re-run (the module's own docstring at :11-13 calls this 'the simplified single-instance rule'). Fix: have `mark_started` (:140-149) record the owner's process start time next to owner_pid (psutil.Process(pid).create_time(), or `ps -o lstart= -p <pid>` to avoid a new hard dependency per the Haloysius subtractive contract), and make the liveness predicate require BOTH pid-exists and start-time-matches, treating an unreadable start time as dead-if-the-receipt-predates-boot. This strengthens an already-lifted mechanism (packet 03 scheduler durability) rather than adding a new one — and it is the site where C2's PID+starttime idea actually applies in Halbert, since the flock-based locks do not need it.

missed_by_reader.title: Machine display name from the OS's human-set computer name (not the DNS hostname), and a host account real name that refuses to fall back to the login name
missed_by_reader.lines: machine-name.ts:10-21 tryScutil calling '/usr/sbin/scutil --get ComputerName|LocalHostName' with a 1s timeout, :23-26 fallbackHostName stripping a trailing '.local', :29-48 getMachineDisplayName preferring ComputerName then LocalHostName then the hostname, cached per process; host-account-name.ts:22-53 readHostAccountName using '/usr/bin/id -F' then dscl RealName on darwin, with normalizeName at :28-33 rejecting any value equal to the login name ('Service accounts often repeat the login in their full-name field') and the export comment at :56 'never seeds a login name'
missed_by_reader.mechanism: The name shown for the machine is the one the human set in the OS (macOS ComputerName), read through a short-timeout system call and cached, with the DNS hostname only as a last resort and its '.local' suffix stripped. The human's name is read from the account's real-name field and explicitly refused when it merely echoes the login shortname.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Two small changes in identity.py / onboarding. (1) identity.py:111-116 resolve_hostname and :123-140 resolve_entity_name end their ladder at `short_hostname(socket.gethostname())` — the raw DNS hostname — which is the one label the founder directive says must never be the name ('No "Sovereign" — use the computer name'). On darwin the computer name is literally `scutil --get ComputerName`, not gethostname(); insert that tier (absolute path /usr/sbin/scutil per M1, short timeout, cached, silently skipped on failure) between being_name() and the hostname fallback, and keep FALLBACK_NAME beneath it. (2) dashboard/routes/settings.py:447-500 update_computer_name stores ai_name/user_name with no OS-derived default; prefill the onboarding user_name from `id -F` / dscl RealName with the 'never the login shortname' rule, so first run proposes a real name instead of an empty field. Both are display-layer only — no model, no security decision — and both make the surface more 'grounded in measured data' per the identity directive.

missed_by_reader.title: Port already in use: name the owning process and say 'that is already me' — Halbert instead silently starts a second instance on the next free port
missed_by_reader.lines: ports.ts:23-29 describePortOwner delegating to inspectPortUsage/formatPortDiagnostics, :33-47 ensurePortAvailable turning EADDRINUSE into a typed PortInUseError, :50-80 handlePortError which prints the listener details and then, when the details match /openclaw|src\/index\.ts|dist\/index\.js/, adds 'It looks like another OpenClaw instance is already running. Stop it or pick a different port.' before exiting 1; ports-probe.ts:24-66 tryListenOnPort (bind, then close immediately 'so the real server can claim the same port'), :69-84 probePortOnHost distinguishing EADDRINUSE/EADDRNOTAVAIL/EAFNOSUPPORT
missed_by_reader.mechanism: A bind conflict is treated as a diagnosis, not an obstacle: the process probes the port, and on EADDRINUSE it inspects who is listening (lsof/netstat backends), prints that, recognises its own signature in the listener's argv, and refuses to start rather than quietly relocating.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: dashboard/__main__.py:47-57 find_available_port loops 8000..8100 and binds the first free port, so launching Halbert twice produces a second live instance on 8001 while the user's bookmark, the Tauri shell and the auth ticket all still point at 8000 — two agents on one machine, each believing it is the host, with no message anywhere. Change the default to: probe the configured port; on EADDRINUSE, identify the listener (lsof -nP -iTCP:<port> -sTCP:LISTEN, resolved via M1's absolute-path helper), and if its command line is Halbert's own, refuse to start with 'I am already running on port <n>' in first person and exit non-zero; only scan for an alternate port under an explicit flag. Pair it with a single-instance advisory flock on a state-dir lock file (the pattern already used at consent/store.py:245-253) so the check does not depend on the port alone. This is squarely in the 'identifies as the host machine' constraint — a steward that silently forks itself is the opposite of that.

OC02-infra-rest.verify_summary: Twelve candidates checked line by line against the origin; all twelve origin claims hold (every cited file exists and the cited mechanism is really there), so no candidate fails on fabrication. Three fail on value or applicability and are dropped: C2 (PID+starttime stale-lock reclaim solves a problem Halbert does not have — every cross-process lock in the tree is a kernel-advisory fcntl.flock on a macOS-only host, released on death, with no owner payload to go stale; the idea is redirected to M2 where it does apply), C9 (SSH argument-injection guard — verified there is no SSH/rsync/scp target construction and no user-supplied hostname reaching argv anywhere in halbert_core, so there is nothing to dispatch), and C11 (CSPRNG jitter — the reader's own text calls it marginal and cosmetic for a single-host system). Three halbert_state verdicts were wrong and are corrected: C1 absent -> partial (dashboard/routes/llm.py:99-129 already has a getaddrinfo-based SSRF check; what is missing is the resolve-then-pin step, redirect re-checking, and closing the provider-label bypass at :105-106 that returns True for any hostname when provider is ollama/lm-studio/apple-foundation — which is why priority goes to high), C7 absent -> partial on a factual error (checked the installed libraries: requests.Session.rebuild_auth and httpx _redirect_headers already strip Authorization cross-origin, and httpx pops Cookie unconditionally; the real gap is that neither strips CUSTOM credential headers, and llm.py:74-89 sends x-api-key to a user-entered base URL with allow_redirects=True while only the first URL is validated), and C10's evidence (Halbert already ships a sliding-window per-IP limiter with LRU eviction at mcp/server.py:1667-1710, applied before auth at :1555-1559 — the task is to reuse it on dashboard/auth.py, not to port OpenClaw's). C5's evidence was also materially wrong in Halbert's favour: scheduler/run_receipts.py:127-132 and monitor_hash.py:152-157 DO fsync the parent directory after the rename, so the reference implementation exists and the finding is inconsistency (being_config.py:861-877 has no fsync at all) rather than absence. C3/C8 both land on the watchdog/daemon workstream the master plan deliberately left un-packeted (line 67 verified verbatim) and are lowered to low as joint design input, not dispatchable work. Four mechanisms the reader missed are added, all with live Halbert call sites: trusted-directory binary resolution (crypto/storage.py drives the macOS Keychain through a bare `security` name resolved off PATH — a hijack there sees custody key material), PID-plus-start-time liveness for scheduler run receipts (recover_on_boot uses a bare os.kill(pid,0) at exactly the moment PIDs recycle, so an interrupted job can be stranded 'running' forever), OS-computer-name-before-DNS-hostname identity (identity.py's last tier is gethostname(), the one label the founder directive forbids, while macOS's computer name is scutil --get ComputerName), and port-conflict diagnosis (dashboard/__main__.py:47-57 silently starts a second Halbert on 8001 instead of saying it is already running). The strongest single dispatch remains the C1+C7 pair as one outbound-egress guard packet. Full JSON written to /private/tmp/claude-501/-Volumes-4TB-BAD-Halbert/b0e3f0dd-594e-4bec-b7ce-4859472b38f8/scratchpad/wf-oss/OC02-infra-rest.verify.json.

candidates.why_solid: This is the load-bearing pattern that every one of the ~250 doctor-*.ts files in this unit follows; it cleanly separates detection from remediation and from rendering, which is exactly the shape a dashboard 'run diagnostics' panel needs.

candidates.title: Tiered repair-mode prompter: safe auto-fix vs force-required vs update-blocked

origin_paths.what: resolveDoctorRepairMode + shouldAutoApproveDoctorFix(requiresForce, blockDuringUpdate)
confirmAutoFix vs confirmAggressiveAutoFix vs confirmRuntimeRepair, each gated differently

candidates.mechanism: Repairs are bucketed into three trust tiers: plain auto-fix (approved by --repair/--yes alone), 'aggressive' auto-fix (needs --repair AND --force), and 'runtime repair' (blocked entirely during an in-progress update even if --repair is set). Non-interactive mode always denies anything not pre-approved by a flag; interactive mode falls back to a real confirm prompt.
candidates.why_solid: Cleanly generalizes 'safe to auto-apply' vs 'needs an explicit stronger confirmation' vs 'never during a conflicting operation' -- exactly the three tiers Halbert's staged-commands/consent model needs for any dashboard-initiated repair action.
candidates.halbert_evidence: halbert_core/halbert_core/persona/permission/ implements a five-axis lattice for agent actions generally, but grep found no repair-mode-specific tiering (safe-fix vs force-fix vs blocked-during-update) anywhere under halbert_core/halbert_core/dashboard or persona/permission.
candidates.task_proposal: When the diagnostics panel (C1) lands, gate its repair actions through three named tiers (auto/force/blocked-in-flight) reusing the existing five-axis permission lattice as the enforcement layer, and block any repair while a self-update or migration is in progress.

missed_by_reader.title: Error and diagnostic text is untrusted content: strip control characters and cap length before it reaches a terminal or a log
missed_by_reader.mechanism: scrubDoctorErrorMessage (7-24) walks the error string character by character, converting tab/CR/LF to spaces (12-14) and DROPPING every other control character and DEL (15-16), collapsing runs of spaces, then truncating to ERR_MESSAGE_MAX_LEN=256 with a UTF-16-safe truncation. The point is that an error message routinely embeds attacker-influenced content -- a filename, a config value, a remote server's response body -- and printing it raw lets ANSI escapes reach the operator's terminal and lets a multi-line error impersonate structure. The same discipline appears as sanitizeForLog around every interpolated config path and binary name in doctor/shared/exec-safe-bins.ts:184-186.

Error strings and exception messages surfaced by tools, dashboard routes and the terminal channel are not sanitized. candidates.title: Run-scoped delegated approval authority bound to exact operational instance, generation-stamped

origin_paths.what: claimAgentRunDelegatedAuthority / getActiveAgentRunDelegatedAuthority / validateAgentRunDelegatedAuthority / releaseAgentRunDelegatedAuthority
AgentRunApprovalLeases: sub-claims dedup by (parent, signal-set), auto-close on abort, close() never revokes whole-run resources
AgentRunDelegatedAuthority shape: {operationalRunInstance, lifecycleGeneration, claimId}

candidates.mechanism: An approval/tool-authority object is minted once per admitted run instance ({instanceId, runId}) and stamped with the registry's current lifecycleGeneration. Every later check re-verifies the exact instance AND generation still match before treating the authority as live; a source-integrity callback is re-run and any throw retires the claim. Sub-scopes for one tool call are 'leases' that dedupe by exact abort-signal set, auto-close when any signal fires, and their closure explicitly does NOT cascade to revoke whole-run resources (e.g. secret egress).
candidates.why_solid: Prevents authority-confusion bugs: a stale approval surviving a run-id recycle or rotated lifecycle generation being replayed against a different execution. The generation stamp + exact-instance compare is a cheap, deterministic check matching Halbert's 'no LLM in any security decision' constraint.

OC01-infra-approvals-devices-backup.summary: Unit OC01 is rich and largely un-packeted for Halbert: the prior OpenClaw review's approvals coverage was conceptual/high-level (two-axis lattice, byte-exact bindings, durable one-shot consents, pairing's challenge-code shape) and did not cite most specific mechanisms read here. The strongest findings are two genuine feature gaps for a single-host assistant holding all its own state with no cloud sync: (1) Halbert has NO self-backup of its own state directory — only third-party backup-tool DISCOVERY exists — while OpenClaw's backup-create/-volatile-filter/-tar-retry/-archive-path-policy cluster is a complete, defensible reference implementation (C5, C6, C17, C18); and (2) Halbert's tool-level file read and command-text shown at approval time both lack the boundary/symlink containment and command-risk-classification machinery OpenClaw applies before either operation (C3, C7, C8) — concrete, evidenced security hardening. The device-identity/pairing cluster contributed several small, high-value, narrowly-scoped patterns (join-code atomic burn, approval-provenance stickiness, halt-and-demand-doctor-fix legacy guard, read-only store variants) that fit Halbert's existing federation/peers.py surface directly. Two clusters are flagged as anti-patterns to NOT port wholesale: the ClawHub marketplace client and the approval-native multi-surface notification router, both solving problems Halbert does not have.

missed_by_reader.title: One approval-presentation builder is the only path to any surface, and every field is sanitized there
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Every approval, of every kind, becomes an ApprovalPresentation through one builder before it can reach any surface, and the builder is where sanitization happens rather than at each renderer. sanitizeOptionalSingleLine (:41-44) wraps every scalar; buildExecApprovalPresentation (:69-97) passes commandText/commandPreview through resolveExecApprovalCommandDisplay, warningText through sanitizeExecApprovalWarningText, scope through sanitizeApprovalScope, and host/nodeId/agentId each through the single-line sanitizer; buildPluginApprovalPresentation (:99-131) does the same for title/description/detail plus an explicit detail truncation. normalizeDecisionList (:28-39) and normalizePluginExternalResolution (:46-58) additionally REJECT (throw) rather than coerce when a plugin offers a malformed decision set -- more than two decisions, a decision other than allow-once/allow-always, or a duplicate. The structural point is that a new surface cannot forget to sanitize, because there is no unsanitized object for it to render.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Add a single approval presentation builder in halbert_core/approval/ that is the only producer of the dict any surface renders, and route dashboard/routes/approvals.py through it. Today dashboard/routes/approvals.py:72-85 (list_pending_approvals) and :200-212 build the response with a raw dict comprehension over ApprovalRequest fields -- task, action, reasoning, risk_level, system_state, affected_resources -- several of which are model-authored (approval/engine.py:38-46; requested_by defaults to 'autonomous_executor'). No redaction, no length cap, no invisible-character handling, no closed set on risk_level. The builder should: run each display string through integrations/observation_text.py's existing structural scrub, then ingestion/redaction.redact_text, then a per-field cap (that order is already pinned and tested at observation_text.py:110-131); refuse rather than coerce when a field is outside its closed vocabulary; and be the only thing routes/approvals.py, the websocket push and any future Tauri surface may emit. This is the concrete dispatchable form of candidate C3 -- C3 supplies the sanitizer, this supplies the guarantee that everything goes through it. Founder fit: 'redaction at the response choke point' already applies to model responses; the approval surface is the second choke point and currently has none.

missed_by_reader.title: The argv-normalization tables that make command-risk detection actually work (interpreter inline-eval + command carriers)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Two data tables plus the matchers that consume them, and they are why candidate C8's detector is not defeated by trivial spelling changes. inline-eval.ts:59-120 FLAG_INTERPRETER_INLINE_EVAL_SPECS enumerates per-interpreter eval flags: python/python2/python3/pypy exact -c PLUS a short-cluster spec listing every option letter that may precede a clustered c (B,E,I,O,P,R,S,b,d,i,q,s,u,v,x) so `python -Ic 'code'` is caught; node/bun/deno -e/--eval/-p/--print; awk/gawk/mawk/nawk -e/--source with an abbreviatedFlags entry recording that pre-4.0 gawk accepted `--s` while modern gawk rejects it as ambiguous, so the older executable sets the floor; ruby and perl with their own cluster letter sets and a numeric-record-separator rule. :309-386 the positional-interpreter specs and a derived INTERPRETER_ALLOWLIST_NAMES used to reject interpreter-like allowlist patterns. :57 + :388-399 strip a version suffix so python3.11 normalizes to python. :439-527 the four matcher shapes -- abbreviated long flag, joined `--source=`, joined raw short `-e'code'`, and clustered short with the prefix-legality walk. command-carriers.ts:8 COMMAND_CARRIER_EXECUTABLES = sudo, doas, env, command, builtin; :16-31 the env option-arity tables including ENV_SPLIT_STRING_OPTIONS (-S/-s/--split-string, whose payload is re-split, bounded at MAX_ENV_SPLIT_PAYLOAD_DEPTH = 32); :32-70 the sudo option tables distinguishing value-taking from standalone flags so the carried argv starts at the right index; :400-420 resolveCarrierCommandArgv dispatching per executable with exec behind an opt-in.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Port the two tables (and only the tables plus a small matcher) into a new halbert_core/shell/command_argv.py, then make streaming/injection_check.py:86-97 check_injection run its existing pattern list against every normalized argv candidate rather than only the raw string. Halbert today has no argv normalization at all: injection_check.py:49-79 is a regex list over the command text and dashboard/routes/terminal.py:131-212 is substring matching over command.lower(), so `env FOO=1 python3.11 -Ic '<code>'`, `sudo -u x --preserve-env node -e '<code>'`, `env -S 'python -c ...'`, and xargs/find -exec carriers all read as ordinary text and land in SafetyTier.SAFE. Scope: sudo/doas/env/command/builtin/exec carriers with their option arities; python/node/ruby/perl/awk/sh inline-eval flags with clustered-short and joined forms; version-suffix normalization; a cycle guard on the argv-join key exactly as risks.ts:34-36/52-56 does. Deterministic and table-driven, so it satisfies the no-LLM-in-security-decisions directive by construction. This is the payload C8 needs; dispatch them as one packet.

missed_by_reader.title: Durable publish as a commit boundary: exclusive create, fd-identity verification, and a fail-closed directory fsync
missed_by_reader.lines: directory-durability.ts:30-47, 95-123; backup-archive-publication.ts:42-52, 54-78, 198-208; backup-create-stream.ts:131-157, 158-188
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Producing a file and then making it visible is treated as a commit with three named obligations. (1) Exclusive creation: backup-create-stream.ts:131-135 opens the output with flags 'wx' and mode 0o600 -- refusing a pre-existing path instead of following a symlink -- and backup-archive-publication.ts:42-52 assertTargetAbsent lstats the final target and throws 'Refusing to overwrite existing backup archive'. (2) Identity verification: backup-create-stream.ts:136-142 fstats the descriptor at open, :149-157 re-lstats the path after the pipeline and throws 'Backup archive path changed while writing' unless sameFileIdentity holds; removePreparedBackupArchive (:53-69) and removeDirectoryIfOwned (backup-archive-publication.ts:54-74) only unlink/rmdir when the current inode still matches the recorded one, so cleanup can never delete a replacement. (3) Durability as policy, not best effort: directory-durability.ts:41-47 requireDirectorySync THROWS when the filesystem reports the parent-directory sync as unsupported, and :95-123 publishFileNoClobber takes an explicit durability: 'fail-closed' | 'degrade' knob and wraps the failure with a typed phase ('directory-sync'), so 'we renamed but never fsynced the directory' is a stated outcome rather than an accident. isUnsupportedDirectorySyncError (:30-38) is the narrow errno list that earns the degrade.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Extract Halbert's atomic-write pattern into one helper in halbert_core/utils/ and use it everywhere, because the tree currently disagrees with itself about the last step. Two sites do it correctly: scheduler/run_receipts.py:103-133 (mkstemp, fsync file, os.replace, then open the parent directory and fsync it, with the comment 'fsync the directory so the rename itself is durable') and scheduler/monitor_hash.py:145-157. Three sites stop one syscall early and can lose the rename on a crash: scheduler/engine.py:50-58 (job persistence), scheduler/executor.py:305-320 (the restart ledger, whose entire purpose is surviving a reboot), and mcp/config.py:788-800 (the MCP config writer). The helper should take the durability decision explicitly (fail-closed by default) and should record the temp file's identity so the error-path unlink cannot remove a file it did not create; today all five sites do a bare os.unlink(tmp) by path. Small, mechanical, and it closes a real crash-durability inconsistency rather than adding a feature.

missed_by_reader.title: An automation's identity is declared by its runner, never inferred from a run id or session key
missed_by_reader.mechanism: A 48-line module whose header states the whole rule: the cron runner records {agentId, jobId, jobConfigRevision, jobName} against the active run at start and clears it at end, and 'exec-approval creation and gateway allowlist evaluation read it so cron standing grants never infer job identity from session keys or run ids.' Three details make it more than a map: jobName is annotated at :10-11 as 'Display name for operator surfaces (approval cards); not identity' -- the human-readable string is structurally separated from the authority key; jobConfigRevision is part of the identity, so a standing grant pinned to a job stops matching the moment the job's config changes; and the returned cleanup closure (:35-39) compares the stored value by reference before deleting, so a late unregister cannot clear a successor's entry. missed_by_reader.title: Display compaction at an approval surface must never hide a segment that changes what is being approved

missed_by_reader.title: Progress-idle watchdog with a diagnostic stall message, instead of a wall-clock timeout
missed_by_reader.mechanism: A long-running produce-to-file operation is bounded by absence of progress, not by elapsed time. reportProgress (:91-123) refreshes a single 5-minute timer (BACKUP_ARCHIVE_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS, :8) on every observed byte, and when it fires it destroys the producer stream AND aborts the consumer via an AbortController, so both halves of the pipeline unwind. Two details worth copying: the timeout ERROR NAMES WHERE IT STALLED -- phase (entry/output/raw/traversal), the last entry path truncated safely to its last 512 UTF-16 units, and separate raw-producer and output byte counters, so 'the backup hung' becomes 'it hung reading this file after N bytes'; and a `settled` flag (:92-96) makes late producer callbacks unable to refresh the timer after cleanup, the same stale-callback discipline candidate C2 describes. observeBackupTarEntryProgress (:35-48) additionally pauses a stream it had to touch to observe, so instrumenting progress does not itself start flow.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Adopt progress-idle (not elapsed-time) bounding, with a stall message that names the phase and the last unit of work, for Halbert's long-running operations -- the self-backup from candidate C5 first, then RAG corpus builds and any watched-terminal command with a no-output rule. Note: OSS-REVIEW-OPENCLAW-2026-09-07.md:99 already names 'typed timeout causes (task-budget | owner-deadline | progress-idle | abort-grace)' as part of the un-packeted command-lanes item, so this is evidence for that item rather than a new one; the specific contribution here is the diagnostic payload (phase + last entry + two byte counters) and the settled-flag guard against a late callback rearming a cancelled watchdog. missed_by_reader.title: A backup manifest declares its assets, and the symlink policy is enforced against that declaration on both create and verify
missed_by_reader.mechanism: The reader cited assertArchiveSymbolicLinkTarget for its zip-slip check but not the stronger half. The file's second line states the invariant -- 'Creation and verification must agree on which archive paths can be restored' -- and the enforcement is two-sided: :70-74 requires the resolved link target to stay inside the declared archiveRoot (the classic containment check), and then :75-83 separately requires BOTH the link entry itself AND its target to fall inside some entry of the manifest's declared `assets` list. A link that stays inside the archive root but points at a path the manifest never declared is rejected. normalizeArchiveRoot (:39-45) additionally forces the root to be a single path segment, and assertPortableRelativePathSyntax (:5-16) rejects absolute paths, Windows drive paths and backslashes with a label naming which field failed. The effect is that the manifest, not the tar stream, is the authority on what a restore may write.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: When the self-backup from C5 is designed, make the manifest the authority rather than an inventory: the backup writer declares the asset roots up front, and both the writer and any future restorer validate every entry (and every symlink target) against that declaration, not merely against 'inside the archive'. Halbert has no manifest concept for its own state today -- persona/memory_purge.py:293-300 is a bare tar.add of a directory -- so this is a design constraint to bake in rather than a retrofit. It matters more for Halbert than for OpenClaw: a Halbert backup contains the consent ledger, the conversation store and the persona files, so a restore that can be steered to write outside the declared set is a permission-system bypass, not just a file-overwrite bug.

candidates.title: File-lock hardening: reentrant-owner key, two staleness-recovery modes, pid+starttime identity, doctor-time definite-stale reclaim

origin_paths.what: FileLockOptions.staleRecovery: 'fail-closed' | 'remove-if-unchanged' -- security-sensitive state can require fail-closed, generic locks default to reclaiming a dead-owner's lock only if the sidecar's identity is unchanged since staleness was first observed
createCurrentProcessLockPayload embeds both pid AND process start time; staleness is judged by comparing both, defeating PID-reuse false negatives
reclaimDefinitelyStaleFileLock re-verifies the lock file's (dev,ino) identity plus staleness immediately before removing the path

candidates.mechanism: Stale-lock reclamation closes two opposite bugs: PID-reuse false-negatives via a process-start-time cross-check, and reclaim-race false-positives via file-identity re-verification immediately before deletion, with an explicit fail-closed mode.
candidates.why_solid: Read the full 250-line file including both staleness code paths and the doctor reclaim function.
candidates.halbert_evidence: halbert_core/halbert_core/scheduler/run_receipts.py:56-67 _default_pid_alive uses os.kill(pid, 0) with NO process-start-time cross-check, vulnerable to the exact PID-reuse false-negative this file guards against. Halbert's consent store instead uses kernel fcntl flock (released automatically on process death), sidestepping the whole staleness-heuristic bug class for that one subsystem, but run_receipts.py does not.
candidates.task_proposal: Harden scheduler/run_receipts.py's _default_pid_alive to also compare process start-time against a starttime recorded in the receipt at claim time, not just os.kill(pid, 0) -- closing the PID-reuse window where a run receipt could be mistaken for still-owned by a process whose pid was reassigned.

verdict.notes: Best candidate in the set; origin verified exactly. file-lock.ts:28-29 staleRecovery 'fail-closed' | 'remove-if-unchanged'; :77-87 createCurrentProcessLockPayload embeds pid AND starttime; :193-235 reclaimDefinitelyStaleFileLock lstats the sidecar for its (dev,ino) identity first and re-verifies that same identity plus the payload immediately before removal (:210-213, :223-224). The staleness rule itself is infra/stale-lock-file.ts:33-59, whose comment is the point: 'Only a mismatched process start time proves PID reuse while the PID is alive.' Halbert defect confirmed, one line off the reader's citation: scheduler/run_receipts.py:57-68 (not 56-67) _default_pid_alive is a bare os.kill(pid, 0) — and note its PermissionError branch returns True, i.e. it fails OPEN toward 'alive'. Consumed by recover_on_boot at :192. Priority raised to high, because the reader understated the likelihood: recover_on_boot compares an owner_pid recorded in a PREVIOUS boot session against the current boot's pid namespace, where low pids are reassigned from scratch — collision is ordinary, not exotic, and the consequence is a receipt stuck in 'running' forever so that job's interrupted run is never recovered. See missed item M1 for the cheaper fix the same unit already ships (a per-process incarnation token), which is platform-independent and does not need /proc or proc_pidinfo parsing.

missed_by_reader.title: Per-process incarnation token: liveness that fails closed instead of trusting a PID probe
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Every cross-process record carries an envelope of {processId, processToken, processStartTime, failedAtMs}. processToken is one randomUUID minted per process lifetime (:20, comment: 'a restarted process (even with a recycled PID) can never match records written by its predecessor'). processLooksLive (:83-89) then decides by identity, never by a liveness syscall: for the CURRENT pid the token must match; for a sibling pid the /proc starttime must match; and where starttime is unavailable the record is HIDDEN rather than trusted — the comment at :76-82 is explicit that 'sibling visibility is sacrificed instead of trusting a bare kill(0) liveness probe'. Unverifiable identity fails closed in both directions, so a recycled PID can neither keep a dead process's records alive nor let them be misattributed.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Close the run-receipt PID-reuse hole with an incarnation token rather than a starttime parser. Halbert is single-instance, so the whole problem collapses: mint one uuid4 at process start, write it into the receipt alongside owner_pid in RunReceiptStore.mark_started (halbert_core/halbert_core/scheduler/run_receipts.py:137-150), and have recover_on_boot (:180-198) mark a running receipt interrupted whenever its token is not this process's token — no os.kill probe at all, so PID reuse across boots becomes unrepresentable rather than merely unlikely. While there, fix the fail-open direction in _default_pid_alive (:65-68), where PermissionError currently returns True; if a pid probe survives at all it should treat an unverifiable owner as dead-and-recoverable, matching the origin's rule. This is the same defect C13 names, with a cheaper and platform-independent fix.

missed_by_reader.title: Failure direction and time budget declared per extension point in one table, not decided inside each seam
missed_by_reader.lines: 43-49 (plus src/plugins/hooks.ts:130-183)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: The global hook runner is constructed once with `failurePolicyByHook` naming exactly three fail-CLOSED hooks — before_agent_run, before_install, before_tool_call — while every other hook defaults to fail-open (hooks.ts:128-132). Alongside it, hooks.ts:145-183 declares two timeout tables keyed by hook name, and each entry's comment states which way a timeout resolves and why: policy hooks get 15s because 'a bounded timeout turns a stalled policy process into a denial instead of freezing the operation' (:168-171), observation hooks get 30s and fail open (before_compaction/after_compaction :157-164), gateway_stop gets the Gateway's own 5s teardown budget 'so one plugin cannot consume the process watchdog' (:163-164). The design point is that whether a seam fails open or closed, and how long it may take, is data in one place rather than a judgement re-made inside every try/except.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert has the opposite shape: 101 sites across halbert_core carry a hand-written 'non-fatal' swallow, each with its own prose justification, and one of them is wrong. agents/turn_event_tee.py:82-85 (_scrub_text) catches every exception from the echo guard and redaction registry and returns the ORIGINAL, unredacted text, then fans it out to every subscriber. That fail-open was inherited from state_machine.py::_echo_guard_egress, where it is defensible ('a guard failure must never cost the user their answer' — the user already saw the material), but the tee's audience is explicitly different: its own docstring says a second screen in the room and the voice HUD. Task: make the tee's redaction seam fail closed (drop or blank the payload when the guard or registry is unavailable) and record the fail-open/fail-closed direction of each observation-vs-policy seam in one table rather than per call site, so the choice is reviewable.

missed_by_reader.title: Untrusted consumers get an isolated copy, and a value that cannot be isolated is refused
missed_by_reader.lines: 5-76 (plus src/plugins/hooks.ts:184 deepFreezeHookValue)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: cloneHookIsolationValue (:63-76) structuredClones every mutable input before handing it to hook code, so one consumer cannot mutate what the next consumer or the caller sees. The interesting half is the refusal: containsSharedMemory (:5-61) walks the value (Maps, Sets, typed-array views, WebAssembly.Memory, all own keys, cycle-guarded) and throws HookIsolationError if it finds SharedArrayBuffer-backed memory — both before AND after the clone (:65-71) — because cloning a handle to shared memory produces a new object over the same bytes and isolation would be a lie. Values that cannot be isolated are rejected rather than passed along with a false guarantee.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: agents/turn_event_tee.py:116-133 builds one `cleaned` dict and passes that same object to every subscriber in the list. 'Observe-only' is currently enforced only by 'the callback gets no handle that acts on the turn' (:97-107) — not by input immutability: a subscriber can mutate the shared dict and change what later subscribers see. Two latent defects in the same six lines: the dict comprehension at :125-128 scrubs only TOP-LEVEL string values, so any nested dict or list of strings would bypass the echo-guard seam entirely (today's publishers, state_machine.py::_tee_publish, send flat scalars, so this is latent rather than live). Task: hand each subscriber its own copy (copy.deepcopy or an immutable mapping) and make the scrub recursive, so 'observe-only' is a property of the data handed out rather than of the API surface.

missed_by_reader.title: The same policy key, opposite defaults by origin: first-party defaults open, everything else defaults closed
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Seventeen lines that state a trust asymmetry once. resolveConversationAccessAllowed(origin, policy) (:10-17) returns `policy?.allowConversationAccess !== false` when origin === 'bundled' (first-party: opt-OUT) and `policy?.allowConversationAccess === true` for every other origin (third-party: opt-IN). Same config key, same call site, inverted default keyed on provenance — so an unconfigured third-party plugin cannot read the conversation, while an unconfigured bundled one can, without either case needing a special branch at the consumer. resolvePromptInjectionAllowed (:6-8) is the opt-out companion for the injection surface.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert's skill trust is location-based only: skills/loader.py:43-51 lists four roots and :54-68 daemon_skill_dirs deliberately narrows the daemon to builtin + ~/.config/halbert/skills (the docstring records that the wider set had loaded twelve unrelated Claude Code skills from $HOME). But once parsed, provenance stops mattering: parser.py:320-323 defaults `state = 'trusted'` for any file without a sidecar, and the only gate on it is catalog listing (catalog.py:123-124). Skill text reaches the model as its own directive (loader.py:56-58). Task: carry an origin on the parsed Skill (builtin | operator-config | project-local | compat) and key the defaults that matter — whether its prompt may be injected into the system prompt at all, and whether it may widen allowed_tools — to that origin, stated once the way the origin states it, so a non-builtin file has to opt IN rather than inherit 'trusted' from the absence of a sidecar.

missed_by_reader.title: A review that cannot be shown in full cannot be approved
missed_by_reader.mechanism: MAX_INSTALL_POLICY_NOTICE_CHARS is 4,000 (:36). failOversizedInstallPolicyWarning (:99-126) formats the notice the operator would have to approve and, if it exceeds that budget, returns `blocked: { code: 'security_scan_failed', reason: 'install policy failed closed: policy review exceeds the 4,000-character display limit...' }` — an approvable warning that cannot be displayed whole is converted into a refusal rather than shown truncated. The BLOCK path (:127-176) is deliberately different: a block needs no consent, so it degrades by omitting findings and saying so. The asymmetry is the mechanism: truncation is acceptable when nobody is being asked to agree, and unacceptable when they are.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert's consent evidence is stronger on authorship and weaker on display. consent/copy.py:366-416 serves fixed shipped copy with a committed digest manifest, and store.py:411-418 refuses a grant without text_shown_sha256, so the digest is provably of the intended wording. Nothing, however, verifies the surface actually rendered that wording in full — the record can carry the digest of a full review screen the operator only saw the top of. Task: give the review-screen path a display invariant (a max length in the copy manifest matched to the review surface's capacity, and/or a render-side assertion that the whole text was laid out) and treat a review that cannot be displayed whole as a refusal to record the grant, matching the origin's rule and Halbert's own 'a boolean anyone could have asserted' reasoning.

missed_by_reader.title: Reopening a store namespace with different quotas is refused, not silently resolved
missed_by_reader.lines: 23-58 (call sites: plugin-blob-store.ts:180-186, plugin-state-store.ts:197, 423-428, 481)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: createPluginStoreOptionPolicy keeps a Map from `${pluginId}\0${namespace}` to the option signature the namespace was first opened with; assertConsistent (:39-54) compares every field both ways and throws 'namespace ... was reopened with incompatible options' on any disagreement. Quotas, TTL and overflow policy are thus properties of the namespace rather than of whichever call site happened to open it first — two callers cannot silently disagree about the cap on shared rows. plugin-blob-store.ts:174-176 adds the related invariant that maxBytesPerEntry may not exceed maxBytesPerNamespace.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert has roughly a dozen independently hand-rolled SQLite/JSON stores (continuity/state_store.py, continuity/promotion.py, continuity/timeline.py, attunement/store.py, findings/store.py, model/outcome_store.py, somatic/store.py, audio/storage/speaker_store.py, agents/conversation_sqlite.py, home/behavior.py) plus caches whose caps are constructor arguments (vision/cache.py:33-45 takes ttl_days and max_bytes per instance; watcher.py:288 is currently the only construction site). No shared discipline says the cap belongs to the store rather than the caller. Low priority and cheap: when a store's limits are constructor arguments, assert on open that a second opener of the same path/namespace passes the same limits, so a future second call site cannot silently halve a retention window.

verdict.notes: Origin read in full (42 lines); mechanism real but the verification is described wrongly. replaceSensitiveValuesInRaw 7-23 sorts longest-first and skips the empty string (comment 12-13: replaceAll('') corrupts the whole snapshot). shouldFallbackToStructuredRawRedaction 26-42 does NOT 'deep-equal the expected redacted structure' — it JSON5-parses the redacted text, runs the caller's restoreParsed to put the real values BACK, and returns true unless isDeepStrictEqual(restored.result, originalConfig); a restore-round-trip against the ORIGINAL, stronger than stated. KEEP=FALSE on three grounds: (1) the reader itself did not verify the Halbert side ('was not directly confirmed in this session') and the rule is default keep=false; (2) I checked — Halbert has no raw-text config redaction surface: security/result_redaction.py:105-190 is purely structural (_redact_value/_redact_dict walk parsed structures substituting _SECRET_MARKER), i.e. already the origin's safe fallback path, and the nearest raw substitution, mcp/config.py:343-347 _scrub, produces log/error text that is never re-parsed as config; (3) the proposal is conditional on a surface that does not exist. Record the round-trip-restore idea in the config docs if such a surface is ever built.

anti_patterns.title: Monolithic single-function write orchestrator
anti_patterns.evidence: src/config/io.write.ts is a single 578-line exported function (writeConfigFileFromContext) threading ~15 concerns — snapshot re-validation, include resolution, env-ref preservation, cron-owner refusal, tilde restoration, merge-patch computation, stat/size comparison, suspicious-write detection, audit-record creation, snapshot-journal bookkeeping, post-commit rollback closures — through one deeply nested function body.
anti_patterns.why_not: Halbert already favors small, single-purpose, well-documented modules (write_guard.py, provenance.py); each mechanism lifted from this unit should land as its own small function/module in that style, not be assembled into one do-everything write function.

anti_patterns.title: Full SQL schema + ORM for a single small JSON fingerprint
anti_patterns.evidence: src/config/io.health-state.ts:1-168 stands up a dedicated Kysely-typed SQLite table (config_health_entries) with onConflict upsert logic just to persist a ~10-field JSON blob per config path.
anti_patterns.why_not: Halbert already has a lightweight SQLite-backed ledger (continuity/state_store.py) that is the natural place for an equivalent fingerprint; adding a second parallel table+ORM surface to mirror the origin's own module boundaries is needless infrastructure duplication for a single-user, single-host system.

anti_patterns.title: Near-one-file-per-micro-concern fragmentation
anti_patterns.evidence: The unit is 819 files, many under 50 lines (byte-size.ts: 32 lines, model-cost.ts: 16 lines, io.state.ts: 27 lines, io.ownership-write-guard.ts: 16 lines), reflecting OpenClaw's large multi-channel/multi-plugin team conventions.
anti_patterns.why_not: That granularity serves a codebase with dozens of channel integrations and many contributors coordinating merge conflicts; it is not a structure to imitate for Halbert's much smaller, single-maintainer config surface — group lifted mechanisms into a small number of cohesive modules instead.

OC05-config.summary: src/config in OpenClaw is an unusually rich, security-conscious config subsystem built around one core idea: config is a durable, auditable artifact that must survive both external tampering and the software's own mistakes. Read in depth: the full write path (io.write.ts + io.write-safety.ts + io.ownership-write-guard.ts), the clobber-snapshot and observe/recovery machinery (io.clobber-snapshot.ts, io.observe-recovery.ts, io.observe-suspicious.ts, io.health-state.ts, recovery-policy.ts), the audit journal (io.audit.ts), backup rotation, env-var substitution, future-version-guard, dangerous-name-matching, byte-size parsing, context-visibility precedence, model-cost merging, legacy-key detection, issue-location/issue-format (line-mapped, redaction-aware validation errors), includes.ts's CWE-22 boundary hardening, and the redact-snapshot/sensitive-paths subsystem. Cross-checked against Halbert's actual config code (config/being_config.py, config/sensitivity.py, tools/write_config.py, continuity/write_guard.py + provenance.py, model/llm_config.py, model/config_layers.py, obs/audit.py, utils/platform.py). Verdict: Halbert's core internal config writers already use atomic temp-file+rename, a genuinely more sophisticated content-based+key-based sensitivity classifier than OpenClaw's regex-only isSensitiveConfigPath, a ledger-based CAS write guard philosophically equivalent to OpenClaw's snapshot-hash clobber check, and a mature signed audit log arguably richer than OpenClaw's SQLite audit rows. The gaps are concrete and specific rather than wholesale: (1) the general-purpose, agent/MCP-exposed write_config.py tool is the one writer NOT using Halbert's own atomic-write idiom, and keeps only a single overwritten backup slot; (2) nothing distinguishes 'someone else changed this file' (already caught) from 'the payload I'm about to write is itself suspiciously destructive', so a hallucinated/truncated LLM-generated edit has no dedicated backstop; (3) nothing runs a health check purely on config load (only on write); (4) nothing detects a masked/redacted display value being saved back over a real secret, despite Halbert's redaction machinery being exactly the system that could produce that failure; (5) API keys are stored as raw plaintext with no env-var/secret-ref indirection; (6) no version-skew guard across Halbert's several independently-updatable processes; (7) no strict unknown-key rejection or dead-key regression test, despite the founder's explicit no-legacy-shims directive being exactly what that pattern enforces. Twelve candidates were written, prioritized toward cheap, high-alignment fixes (C1, C3, C5, C8) over larger product decisions (C6, medium priority). Anti-patterns flagged: the origin's single 578-line write-orchestrator function, its dedicated SQL/ORM table for a tiny fingerprint blob, and its very fine-grained one-file-per-concern module structure — none of these shapes should be imitated even while the individual mechanisms are worth lifting.

missed_by_reader.title: Optimistic snapshot-race guard (config CAS) — models.yml read-modify-write has no lock and no conflict detection
missed_by_reader.lines: io.write-safety.ts:13-44 (assertBaseSnapshotStillCurrent); mutation-conflict.ts:1-12 (ConfigMutationConflictError with a retryable flag); io.write.ts:441-450 (the same check re-run INSIDE the rename hook)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Every config write carries the snapshot it was computed from. assertBaseSnapshotStillCurrent (io.write-safety.ts:13-44) re-reads the file, re-hashes it and throws ConfigMutationConflictError('config changed since last load') when existence or hash differs, and throws non-retryably when the config PATH itself changed. The detail the reader missed: io.write.ts:441-450 wraps fs.promises.rename so the base-snapshot check runs again immediately before the atomic publish, inside the same rename call, closing the validate->commit window. Read-then-write races become a typed retryable error instead of a silent lost update.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert has this for one of its two config files and not the other. config/being_config.py:506-580 implements being_config_lock — an advisory fcntl.flock on a lock file beside being.yml held for the whole load-modify-save cycle, with a per-path threading.RLock and depth counter (523-525) so re-entry does not touch the flock. model/llm_config.py has NO equivalent: save() at 765-778 does _read_for_write -> mutate -> _write_raw and update() at 816-835 does load -> _deep_merge -> save, both unlocked; llm_advisory_lock (model/client.py:102-125) is a different lock that serialises LLM CALLS and is never called from llm_config.py. The write itself is atomic (llm_config.py:413-434 mkstemp+os.replace) so there is no torn file — the failure is a clean lost update, and the payload is the API-key store. Concrete because the founder runs concurrent sessions against this repo and dashboard/routes/llm.py serves a read-modify-write settings drawer over HTTP. Task: give model/llm_config.py the same advisory-lock treatment being_config.py already has (reuse the pattern, keyed on models.yml), and complementarily have _write_raw take the digest of what was read and refuse the replace if the on-disk digest no longer matches, raising a typed retryable ConfigConflictError. The digest half degenerates cleanly to a single user: with no contention it never fires.

missed_by_reader.title: Config content reaches the model unredacted — write_config returns a raw unified diff of any host config file
missed_by_reader.lines: commands-config.ts:103-123 (snapshot redacted BEFORE it is rendered into a chat reply); redact-snapshot.ts:284 (redactConfigSnapshot); io.audit.ts:90-127 (config-set argv VALUE positional replaced with '***' when the PATH positional matches isSensitiveConfigPath; --batch-json blanked); redact-argv.ts:43-80 (SECRET_FLAG_SUFFIX_PATTERN + redactSensitiveArgv)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: The origin's invariant across this unit is that config VALUES never appear in derived text. Anything that renders config to a human or a log passes through redaction first: /config show builds parsedBase from redactConfigSnapshot(snapshot, schema.uiHints) at commands-config.ts:108 before it can render either a single path or the whole file into a reply; the audit journal redacts argv by flag-name shape and additionally blanks the value of `config set` when the path is sensitive (io.audit.ts:123-126); validation errors omit the received value for sensitive paths (issue-location.ts:285-297). Redaction is attached to the rendering seam, not to any one caller.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert has the opposite arrangement on its internal tool path. tools/write_config.py returns outputs={'diff': diff} where diff is a difflib unified diff of the real file contents (write_config.py:198-206 YAML, 220-230 JSON, 256-266 INI, 87-88 rollback). That ToolResponse goes straight to the model: agents/react_agent.py:318-322 does result_content = json.dumps(step.tool_result or {'error': step.error}) and appends it as a message. The only redaction choke point in the codebase is the MCP one — grep -rn 'redact_result' finds it solely in security/result_redaction.py, mcp/response.py:43 and mcp/response.py:71 — and agents/state_machine.py:3767-3803's echo guard redacts the OUTBOUND reply through the variant registry (acked-egress values only), not tool results flowing INBOUND. So write_config(path='~/.config/halbert/models.yml', ...) hands the model diff hunks of the API-key store, likewise any /etc config carrying a password. This is the concrete instance of the question already parked as 05-C in OPENCLAW-LIFT-MASTER-PLAN-2026-09-07.md:45 ('whether internal (non-MCP) tool results route through the shared redaction core') — reopen it with this payload named, because it is the strongest argument in the set. Task: route write_config's diff through security/result_redaction.redact_result at minimum, better at the tool-result seam in react_agent.py so every internal tool inherits it, exactly as the origin attaches redaction to the rendering seam.

missed_by_reader.title: The policy gate is skipped on dry runs, so write_config's preview is an unpoliced read of any file on the host
missed_by_reader.lines: io.observe-recovery.ts:190-213 (createBackupRestoreAuditAppendParams / createConfigObserveAuditAppendParams — READ-side observations get audit records, not just writes); io.write.ts:388-407 (the rejected-write path audits BEFORE throwing, so a refused attempt is still recorded)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: In the origin, observing a config is itself an audited, policy-relevant event: the read path emits audit records through createConfigObserveAuditAppendParams (io.observe-recovery.ts:190-213), and a write that is refused is audited at the moment of refusal (io.write.ts:398-406, appendWriteAudit('rejected', error)) rather than dropped. Read and write are separately gated; 'I was only looking' is not an exemption.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: In Halbert the policy gate is explicitly write-only. tools/base.py:40-59 _policy_check begins `is_apply = self.side_effects and not (req.dry_run or not req.confirm)` and returns (True, None) immediately when is_apply is false — so a dry_run/unconfirmed write_config call never reaches load_policy()/decide(). tools/write_config.py:67-68 calls it and then, regardless of outcome, reads the target file (write_config.py:190-192, 209-211, 237-240) and returns a unified diff of it (see the previous item for where that diff goes). The result is a general file-read primitive reachable with no path policy and no confirmation, on a tool whose declared purpose is writing: naming a key in `changes` returns that key's neighbourhood from the real file, so an agent can walk a config file it was never allowed to read. Task: apply the path policy to write_config's read as well as its apply — either move the gate above the dry-run branch for tools that return file content, or add an explicit read-scope decision (decide(pol, self.name, is_apply=False, ...)) whose denial suppresses the diff rather than the write. Pair with the redaction item above; either fix alone leaves half the hole. Deterministic policy only, no model in the decision.

missed_by_reader.title: HMAC-fingerprinted per-leaf config diff baseline — field-level change attribution with no value ever stored
missed_by_reader.lines: 32-75 (loadConfigJournalFingerprintKey: 32 random bytes at <stateDir>/config-journal-fingerprint.key, created with openSync(keyPath,'wx',0o600), EEXIST-tolerant, chmod 0600, cached per path); 77-89 (fingerprintConfigSnapshotValue: HMAC-SHA256 of the JSON-encoded leaf truncated to 12 hex chars, prefixed 'fp:'); 91-112 (fingerprintConfigSnapshotLeaves + fingerprintConfigSnapshotAuthoredConfig, structuredClone then every leaf replaced)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: The config change journal keeps a diff baseline in which every leaf value is replaced by a keyed HMAC fingerprint rather than the value or a redaction marker. That preserves the one property a diff needs — same value fingerprints the same, different value fingerprints differently — while storing nothing recoverable, and the key is machine-local so the fingerprints are useless off the host. Two details show the care: leaves are JSON-encoded before hashing (comment at 84-85) so the number 1 and the string "1" fingerprint differently and a type-only edit is not read as opaque; and when the key store is unavailable it degrades to the plain '***' marker (78-81) so a write is never blocked by the journal.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert's provenance plane is value-safe but coarse. continuity/provenance.py:131-191 record_file_change takes before_text/after_text and — per its own docstring at 158-159 — uses them 'only to compute digests', writing before_sha256/after_sha256 into obs.audit.write_audit. So Halbert can say 'being.yml changed' but never 'your secret_tier changed and your cloud_ok_keys did not' — precisely the question a host steward that speaks in first person about its own state should answer without an LLM and without holding a secret. Task: add an optional per-leaf fingerprint baseline for the two config files Halbert owns (being.yml, models.yml), keyed by a 32-byte machine-local key created once at 0600 beside the config (Halbert already has the 0600-exclusive-create idiom at integrations/frigate/frigate_config.py:135-139 and the 0700 dir idiom at crypto/storage.py:185), stored alongside the existing digest in the continuity ledger rather than in a new table (the reader's own anti-pattern note applies), and used to render 'which fields changed' in the audit/observation surface. Degrades cleanly: no key, no fingerprints, existing whole-file digest behaviour unchanged.

missed_by_reader.title: Dangerous-env-var denylist before materialising or inheriting an environment
missed_by_reader.lines: state-dir-dotenv.ts:17-27 (1 MiB read cap; isBlockedServiceEnvVar rejecting the downgrade-override var plus isDangerousHostEnvVarName/isDangerousHostEnvOverrideVarName); 41-54 (isUnresolvedShellReference: drops a value that is ENTIRELY $VAR / ${VAR} / $(cmd) while deliberately keeping a real credential that merely contains a '$', e.g. "abc$2!"); 68-90 (the parse loop applying both filters); host-env-security.ts:7-52 (key-shape regexes and the four blocked sets, plus the TERM/LANG/LC_* cosmetic-override allowlist at 28-40); host-env-security-policy.json:2-115 (the curated blockedEverywhereKeys list: NODE_OPTIONS, PYTHONPATH/PYTHONHOME, BASH_ENV, ENV, GLIBC_TUNABLES, GCONV_PATH, IFS, PS4, RUSTC_WRAPPER, JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, VIMINIT, LUA_INIT, GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF, SUDO_ASKPASS, ...)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Before an environment is either persisted into a managed service env file or inherited by a spawned runtime, keys are filtered against a curated denylist of variables that turn an innocuous command into arbitrary code execution — split into blocked-everywhere, blocked-when-inherited and blocked-as-override sets, with a narrow allowlist for cosmetic overrides. The policy is DATA in a JSON file, not code, so the list can be reviewed as a list. The dotenv loader additionally refuses to persist a value that is only an unexpanded shell reference, because dotenv does not expand it and a single-quoted LaunchAgent/systemd env file would store the literal $VAR string where a credential was meant.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert spawns shells with the full ambient environment and no filter: streaming/pty.py:289-293 does child_env = dict(os.environ), applies caller overrides, then os.execvpe('/bin/sh', ['/bin/sh','-c', self._command], child_env); the only caller supplying an env is streaming/session_manager.py:75/99. grep -rn 'LD_PRELOAD|DYLD_INSERT|PYTHONPATH|BASH_ENV|NODE_OPTIONS' --include=*.py over halbert_core returns nothing — none of these names is known to the codebase. Partial rather than absent because streaming/sandbox.py already wraps agent-emitted commands in bwrap (Linux) or sandbox-exec (macOS) and constrains WRITES, and streaming/injection_check.py exists — but neither touches the environment, and the sandbox is skipped where the wrapper is unavailable (sandbox.py:94-106 is_available). The realistic Halbert threat is not a hostile local user; it is that a prompt-injected turn, a skill, or a watched user shell sets BASH_ENV or PYTHONPATH and a later agent-run command executes attacker-chosen code inside the sandbox's own allowances. Task: lift host-env-security-policy.json as DATA into halbert_core (it is a reviewable list, and lifting the list is the value), add a deterministic sanitize_child_env() applied at streaming/pty.py:289 and at every subprocess.run in tools/ (system_tools.py:157, accelerator_tools.py:35, gpu_tools.py:103, schedule_cron.py:85/94), and note the licence/provenance of the lifted list. Prerequisite for candidate C6 if api-key-via-env is adopted.

missed_by_reader.title: Config-load happens on a write path: being.yml is rewritten during load, with no snapshot of what was overwritten
missed_by_reader.lines: 7-18 (CONFIG_CLOBBER_SNAPSHOT_LIMIT 32; CONFIG_CLOBBER_LOCK_STALE_MS 30s / RETRY 10ms / TIMEOUT 2s; a KeyedAsyncQueue so local writers queue before contending on the filesystem lock, with the comment at 12-13 explaining the ordering); 20-47 (the sync+async fs surface the lock directory needs)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Whenever the origin's recovery machinery is about to overwrite a config file it first preserves the bytes it is about to destroy into a capped ring of clobber snapshots (32 per config path), coordinated by a stale-tolerant cross-process filesystem lock with a local async queue in front so sibling tasks in one process do not burn the lock timeout on each other. This is distinct from candidate C2's backup ring: the .bak ring preserves state before an intentional edit, the clobber ring preserves state before an automatic, non-user-initiated overwrite.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert has an automatic, non-user-initiated config overwrite on the LOAD path with no snapshot of it. config/being_config.py:663-688 _apply_runtime_relocks mutates the config in place (volatile-unlock reset on the first load of each process, and secret_tier expiry relock) and config/being_config.py:690-696 _persist_relock then calls _save_being_config_unlocked, warning rather than raising on failure. So every process start can rewrite being.yml without a user asking, and that write keeps no copy of what was there — the atomic replace at being_config.py:863-870 leaves no .bak, unlike write_config.py which at least does copy2. The flock at being_config.py:543-580 makes this safe against concurrent Halbert processes, so this is not a race; it is that an automatic write has no undo. Task: before _persist_relock's save, copy the current being.yml into a small capped ring (2-3 slots is enough for a single host; reuse whatever helper C2 lands for write_config), and record the relock in the audit plane via continuity.provenance.record_file_change with reason='volatile unlock relock' / actor=ACTOR_SYSTEM so the rewrite is attributable rather than silent. Do NOT lift the origin's lock machinery — Halbert's flock already covers that half.

OC05-config.verify_summary: Twelve candidates verified against the origin at the cited lines and against Halbert by grep. Ten origin claims hold; one (C1) has the right mechanism at the wrong lines — replaceFileAtomic is io.write.ts:425-450, not 246-262, and src/infra/replace-file.js does not exist (the file is replace-file.ts, an 8-line re-export of a vendored package), so the reader's description of the helper's internals was never read. C5's origin functions exist as cited but its MECHANISM framing is wrong: collectPollutedSecretPlaceholders gates last-known-good promotion (io.observe-recovery.ts:510) and restore (:597), never a write, so the reader's proposal is an extension rather than a lift. Two halbert_state claims are wrong and both understate what Halbert has: C5 (integrations/frigate/frigate_config.py:143-147 _is_masked_credential already exists and is applied at dashboard/routes/frigate.py:93/96; the llm_config surface closes the same hole differently via never-send + _carry_forward_api_keys, with the frontend cooperating at modelPickerTransport.ts:79 and 84-87) and C6 (mcp/config.py:180-209 token_env is exactly the env-var secret indirection the reader called absent — turning C6 from 'propose a new syntax' into the cheaper 'extend the existing idiom'). Ten kept, two dropped: C11 (a 25-line utility with no caller) and C12 (Halbert has no raw-text config redaction surface — security/result_redaction.py:105-190 is purely structural, already the origin's safe fallback — and the reader itself did not verify it). C7 is correct but keep=false on value: a downgrade guard buys a single-user single-host install with no users almost nothing and cuts against the no-back-compat directive. Priorities corrected: C4 medium->low (heaviest mechanism in the unit; auto-restoring config on read is an autonomous destructive act on a machine whose operator is present), C5 high->medium (primary vector already closed; value is unification), C9 medium->low, C10 low->medium (Halbert's own detector, findings/detectors/permissions_hygiene.py:56-90, audits ~/.ssh but not Halbert's config dir, which for a root-run install is /etc/halbert holding the API-key store). missed_by_reader.mechanism: An active repair path for an agent session wedged in a processing/waiting state: after a no-forward-progress age the run handle is treated as leaked and its lane reclaimed. The load-bearing part is the refusal ladder — DiagnosticSessionRecoverySkipReason is a closed union of eleven named reasons recovery must NOT fire ('active_embedded_run', 'active_reply_work', 'human_input_wait', 'runtime_owned_wait', 'deferred_maintenance_wait', 'terminal_outcome_committed', 'global_lane_wait', 'active_lane_task', 'already_in_flight', 'missing_session_ref', 'stale_session_state'), so a session legitimately waiting on a person, or one that has already committed a terminal outcome, is never reclaimed. Outcomes are typed per action rather than free text, and in-flight recoveries dedupe by logical session key, not by generation.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert has the wedge but not the repair. agents/state_machine.py:512-519 and :1477-1482 bound only the ACQUIRE side — _acquire_turn_lock with TURN_LOCK_TIMEOUT_S, whose comment says 'a wedged turn surfaces as an error the user can retry instead of queueing every later message behind a badge that never changes'. That fails the NEW turn; the wedged turn keeps the lock, so the session stays wedged for the life of the process and every later turn on it fails identically. Task: add a turn-reclamation path in agents/state_machine.py that, after a no-forward-progress age on the held turn lock, cancels the owning turn task and releases the lock — gated by a closed, named skip-reason enum modelled on diagnostic-session-recovery.ts:7-19 with Halbert's own reasons (awaiting_confirm — the paused /confirm turn at :1477 is precisely a legitimate human wait and must never be reclaimed; approval_pending; guest_handback_pending; tool_running_with_live_output; already_reclaiming). Emit one typed receipt per reclamation to obs/audit.py and surface it on the existing status surface. Deterministic thresholds only, no model in the decision.

missed_by_reader.title: The daemon writes no log file, and the log line it does emit is hand-built JSON that breaks on any quote or newline
missed_by_reader.lines: logger-file-transport.ts:10-15 (DEFAULT_MAX_QUEUED_RECORDS 4096, MAX_APPEND_BATCH_BYTES 64KB, MAX_ROTATED_LOG_FILES 5, MAX_TRACKED_APPEND_FAILURE_FILES 64), :47-64 (rotatedLogPath/rotateLogFile: rm the oldest, shift .1..5, rename the live file), :29-45 (bounded queue with droppedCount/droppedTarget accounting), :7 and :184 (redactSensitiveText imported and applied at the transport; rotation attempted inline on size, failure degrades to continued writes at :131); json-console-line.ts:9-28 (formatJsonConsoleLine builds an envelope OBJECT and serializes with JSON.stringify plus a redacting replacer that skips only the structural time/level fields, then redacts the serialized string again), :2 (stripVTControlCharacters)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: The process log is a real JSONL file transport: records queue with a hard cap and drops are counted rather than silently lost, appends batch under a byte ceiling, the file rotates through five generations at maxFileBytes, a rotation failure degrades to continued writes with a warning instead of losing the log, and redaction is applied inside the transport. The envelope is produced by JSON.stringify over an object with a redacting replacer — never by interpolating a message into a JSON-shaped template string.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Two concrete defects in one file. dashboard/__main__.py:22-26 is the only logging configuration the running backend has: logging.basicConfig(level=INFO, format='{"ts": "%(asctime)s", "level": "%(levelname)s", "logger": "%(name)s", "msg": "%(message)s"}') — a JSON document assembled by %-interpolation. Any message containing a double quote, a backslash or a newline produces an invalid JSON line, and a message carrying '", "level": "error' forges a whole record: a log-injection primitive reachable from any %s-formatted tool/user string (executor command echoes, mcp.py redacted error details). obs/logging.py:9-21 already has a correct JsonFormatter using json.dumps — it is simply not the one the daemon installs. Second, no FileHandler exists anywhere in the daemon (grep FileHandler|RotatingFileHandler|TimedRotating over halbert_core/halbert_core hits only rag/ and tools/ CLI basicConfig calls), so the backend writes to stdout only — which is why C6 (tail your own log) and C7 (support bundle) have no input. Task: in dashboard/__main__.py install obs.logging.JsonFormatter on a RotatingFileHandler under utils.paths.log_subdir(), keep the stdout handler, cap and rotate (5 generations), and attach the C8 redaction filter to the handler so it covers both sinks. Prerequisite for C6, C7 and restart diagnostics (C3).

missed_by_reader.title: Bounded fire-and-forget background work: concurrency cap, queue cap, per-job timeout, control-character-stripped single-line error logs
missed_by_reader.lines: 8-11 (DEFAULT_MAX_CONCURRENT_FIRE_AND_FORGET_HOOKS 16, DEFAULT_MAX_QUEUED_FIRE_AND_FORGET_HOOKS 256, DEFAULT_FIRE_AND_FORGET_HOOK_TIMEOUT_MS 2000, MAX_HOOK_LOG_MESSAGE_LENGTH 500), 52-69 (replaceLogControlCharacters maps every codepoint <=0x1f, 0x7f, U+2028 and U+2029 to a space), 71-77 (formatHookErrorForLog collapses whitespace and truncates UTF-16-safely), 89-121 (runFireAndForgetHookJob: an informational per-job timeout log that deliberately does not double-report a later rejection, active-count bookkeeping in finally, queue drain)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Background work fired off a hot path is never unbounded: shared state caps in-flight and queued jobs, each job gets an informational timeout log so a hook that never settles is visible without being killed mid-flight, and every error message written to the log is first stripped of control characters — including the line-separator codepoints U+2028/U+2029 — and truncated, so a hook error can neither forge a log line nor blow the log up.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert fires background work off turn hot paths with no ceiling. skills/telemetry.py:24-27 states the right failure posture ('Telemetry is a reportability feature, never a gate ... every function here fails soft') but there is no concurrency or queue bound and no per-job timeout; the same shape recurs at the turn-event tee and the continuity journal write points.
