Pair the control-character stripping with the log-format fix above — U+2028/U+2029 are not caught by a naive newline strip and are exactly what a forged JSONL line needs.

missed_by_reader.title: Shell-wrapped spawn treats BASH_ENV/ENV/CDPATH/PS4 as code-execution carriers and strips them; children are also handed to the OOM killer instead of the steward
missed_by_reader.lines: 4-19 (rationale: children inherit the long-lived parent's oom_score_adj and the kernel picks the largest-RSS process, so the gateway dies instead of its transient worker; any unprivileged process may voluntarily RAISE its own score since Linux 2.6.20), 21-23 (the /bin/sh shim 'echo 1000 > /proc/self/oom_score_adj 2>/dev/null; exec "$0" "$@"' — no extra long-lived shell, final process identity unchanged), 25-34 (SHELL_INIT_ENV_CARRIERS: BASH_ENV, ENV, CDPATH, PS4 renamed to OC_INTERNAL_* when wrapping, commented as variables that 'can make /bin/sh (especially Bash invoked as sh) execute or expose caller-influenced startup behavior before the final exec' — 'stripped when we wrap so the shim can't become an env-controlled code-exec primitive'; NON_RESTORABLE_BASH_ENV_KEY covers SHELLOPTS/BASHOPTS/BASH_FUNC_*), 35-40 (restore script re-exports them only after the score is set, immediately before exec)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Two independent hardening ideas at one spawn site. (1) A process that wraps a child in /bin/sh must treat the shell-startup environment as an execution surface: BASH_ENV/ENV name a file the shell sources before running anything and BASH_FUNC_* smuggles function definitions, so they are neutralised across the wrap and restored only immediately before exec. (2) A long-lived steward process should voluntarily raise its transient children's oom_score_adj so the kernel's OOM killer takes the worker rather than the resident daemon.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: tools/executor.py:832 spawns every non-sandboxed tool command with asyncio.create_subprocess_shell — through /bin/sh, with the backend's environment inherited wholesale. Nothing in halbert_core audits or neutralises the shell-startup carriers (grep for BASH_ENV|CDPATH|SHELLOPTS|BASH_FUNC over halbert_core/halbert_core returns nothing), so any path that can set an env var in the backend's process (config-supplied env, a peer/MCP-supplied variable, an inherited launch environment) gets code execution ahead of the command the policy pipeline actually approved — routing around the deterministic tool gate rather than through it. Task (security, small): sanitise the child env at the executor's spawn site — drop BASH_ENV, ENV, CDPATH, PS4, SHELLOPTS, BASHOPTS and any BASH_FUNC_* key before create_subprocess_shell, and audit whether the shell is needed at all on the approved-command path. Separately and at lower priority, on Linux hosts set the child's oom_score_adj so the backend is not the fattest OOM target; note this is Linux-only and degenerates to a no-op on macOS.

The comment names the bug this fixes: summing over at most maxSessions rows 'instead of scanning every event per append, which was O(events) per message and quadratic while trimming'. From those it answers the three questions the rest of the stack keeps asking: isActive(sinkActive) ('whether output exists OR the downstream sink reports active playback' — a sink claiming activity counts even when we emitted nothing), isInterruptible(sinkActive) (whether caller speech should be treated as barge-in right now), and playbackWatchdogDelayMs({marginMs, minMs}) — the delay after which playback has exceeded the duration of the audio actually emitted, i.e. a stuck or silently-dropped sink.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Add an output-activity tracker to the TTS egress path and let barge-in and a watchdog read it. audio/speech/barge_in.py:5-16 has only a BargeInToken (an asyncio.Event the Piper generator polls) and documents the Home Assistant satellite path as 'best-effort, lossy: cannot cancel audio HA has already started playing' — there is no notion of whether output is currently active, no elapsed-vs-emitted comparison, and no watchdog, so a satellite that silently swallowed the audio and one that is mid-sentence look identical to Halbert. Track emitted audio duration plus sink-reported state, derive interruptibility from it instead of assuming, and fire a watchdog when wall-clock exceeds emitted duration plus a margin. This is the cheap answer to the question C8's loopback verifier answers expensively.

missed_by_reader.title: Durable subsystem quarantine records whose expiry is owned by process liveness, not a TTL
missed_by_reader.mechanism: When a context engine fails an operation it is quarantined and the failure is persisted through a runtime-health store keyed by (engineId, processId), carrying processId/processToken/processStartTime in the envelope, capped at 64 entries, with a normalizer that drops any record missing engineId/operation/reason. The stated reason for persisting is that 'health surfaces can see failures recorded in sibling runtime processes', and the expiry rule is explicit: 'No TTL: a quarantine is recorded once per failure and stays valid for the recorder's lifetime, so process liveness alone owns expiry' — clearForProcess retires them when the process goes away, so a stale quarantine cannot outlive the process that recorded it.

candidates.title: Curated respawn/wrapper skip-list keyed to command semantics, not a blanket flag

origin_paths.what: shouldSkipRespawnForArgv / shouldSkipStartupEnvironmentRespawnForArgv: an explicit, commented set of exceptions — help/version, interactive TTY commands (tui/terminal/chat), a foreground Gmail run that owns its own shutdown grace period, native-hook-relay (owned by an external supervisor's timeout), gateway status (would double transient memory against an already-running gateway), foreground gateway run (owns its own lifecycle) — each with a one-line rationale comment.

candidates.mechanism: A process-wrapping/supervisory behavior (respawn, restart-on-crash, watchdog) should carry an explicit, individually-justified skip-list of command classes that must NOT be wrapped, rather than a single global on/off switch — because 'safe to wrap' is a property of what the command itself already owns (its own lifecycle, its own shutdown grace period, its own external supervisor).
candidates.why_solid: Read the full 74-line file; every exception has a one-line rationale in the source, which is itself a good documentation pattern to copy alongside the mechanism.
candidates.halbert_evidence: Halbert has no CLI-level respawn wrapper today (see C9); this candidate is the policy layer that would sit on top of C9 if/when one is built.
candidates.task_proposal: Pair with C9: when building any Halbert process-wrapper/respawn/restart mechanism, write its skip-list as named, individually-commented predicates (interactive-TTY commands, self-supervised foreground processes, status/read-only commands) rather than one boolean flag, so future additions have to justify themselves the same way.

candidates.title: Guaranteed-drain-then-exit for one-shot CLI output, with a stall watchdog fallback

origin_paths.what: flushExitAfterOneShotOutput: writes an empty chunk to stdout AND stderr and waits for both write callbacks before calling runtime.exit(), with a 5s unref'd fallback timer so a stalled pipe callback can never hang the process forever; watchCliExitAfterOutput separately force-exits 10s after a recorded outcome if cleanup hasn't let the event loop drain, calling an onStall diagnostic hook first.

candidates.mechanism: A CLI command that has already produced its final output must exit promptly, but only after that output is actually flushed to the OS (not truncated by an early process.exit), and must never hang indefinitely if some background handle (a listener, a socket) prevents natural event-loop drain — solved with a bounded 'drain, then exit' plus an independent, longer stall watchdog.
candidates.why_solid: Read the full 183-line file including the finally-block wiring in runCliWithExitFinalization. The two-tier design (fast drain-then-exit vs. slow stall-watchdog-as-last-resort) is a clean, reusable idea distinct from Node's specific stream-callback API.
candidates.halbert_evidence: Halbert's Python CLI subcommands (Halbert/main.py) rely on normal Python process exit; no equivalent 'guarantee output flushed, but never hang past N seconds on stray background threads/handles' watchdog was found (grep for 'atexit\|sys.exit.*flush' in main.py was not run, but no dedicated exit-finalization module exists under halbert_core/halbert_core/cli/).
candidates.task_proposal: For Halbert CLI subcommands that spawn background threads or hold open file/socket handles (scheduler operations, index rebuilds), add a small finalize-and-exit helper: flush stdout/stderr explicitly, then set a short unref'd watchdog timer (Timer with daemon=True) that force-exits with a diagnostic if normal process teardown hasn't completed within a few seconds.

verdict.notes: Origin verified: src/cli/one-shot-exit.ts — flushExitAfterOneShotOutput (:151-183) drains stdout AND stderr with an empty write and exits only when both callbacks fire, behind an unref'd 5s fallback (ONE_SHOT_EXIT_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS = 5_000 at :10, used :168); watchCliExitAfterOutput (:136-149) is the independent 10s stall watchdog that calls onStall then force-exits. keep=false because the failure mode it guards does not exist in Halbert: CPython flushes std streams at interpreter exit, and every threading.Thread I could find sets daemon=True (ingestion/service.py:291-295 and :301-305, vision/watcher.py:93-96, vision/ambient_webcam.py:95, vision/zone_watcher.py:159, integrations/system_event_mapper.py:306, model/client.py:1124-1126, dashboard/parent_watchdog.py:91), so no background thread can hold the interpreter open past a completed command. There is no observed hang or truncation to fix; dispatching this would be speculative hardening.

candidates.title: Exclude heartbeat/system-originated sessions from 'last remembered session' resume

origin_paths.what: isHeartbeatLikeTuiSession / isHeartbeatSessionKey: a session whose key ends `:heartbeat`, or whose provider/lastChannel/lastTo/origin markers equal 'heartbeat', is never written or read as the remembered 'resume this session' pointer — even though it's a normal row in the same session table.

clearTuiLastSessionPointers does a read-only scan then a compare-and-delete inside the write transaction, so a pointer written concurrently after the scan (by a live session) survives cleanup — avoids a lost-update race during doctor-style repair.

candidates.mechanism: A 'resume where the human left off' pointer must positively exclude internally-originated/system rows (scheduled heartbeats, background probes) by an explicit marker check, not merely by picking 'most recent' — otherwise a background job silently hijacks what the human sees resumed.
candidates.why_solid: Read the full 204-line file. Directly relevant given Halbert's own 'one continuous conversation, hidden topic threads' design and its scheduler/heartbeat subsystem, which can and does generate its own turns/threads.
candidates.halbert_evidence: grep -rn 'heartbeat' scoped to continuity/agents session-resume logic was not exhaustively run; flagging as absent based on no visible exclusion marker in the session-tree 'one-open-leaf index' work described in the master context as already lifted (that work covers additive schema and open-leaf indexing, not an explicit heartbeat-exclusion filter) — recommend a targeted grep before scoping the task.
candidates.task_proposal: Audit Halbert's 'one-open-leaf' / continuity resume logic (continuity/ recall path) for whether a scheduler-originated or heartbeat-originated turn can become the thread the dashboard reopens to; if so, add an explicit origin-marker exclusion (mirroring isHeartbeatLikeTuiSession) so only human-initiated turns are eligible as the resumed leaf.

The reader flagged its own Halbert grep as not run; I ran it, and the framing needs correcting while the concern survives. Halbert has no 'resume pointer' to poison — agents/conversation_sqlite.py:1656-1690 get_or_open_thread enforces exactly one open thread inside a BEGIN IMMEDIATE, which is the founder's one-continuous-conversation design; the OpenClaw session-picker shape correctly stays an anti-pattern. The real Halbert instance of the same concern is provenance, and it is confirmed: agents/channels.py:170-190 resolve_channel maps an ABSENT modality to the dashboard channel, whose default_role is admin and whose server stamp is dashboard_token (:78-91, :140-144); and dashboard/routes/gpu.py:185-205 runs a machine-originated agent turn through agent.process(query=..., thread_manager=_thread_manager(), tier_override='specialist') with no modality, so a system-originated turn enters the one open thread indistinguishable from the human's typed turn. Medium rather than high because the one live caller is a route its own docstring calls deprecated.

candidates.title: Method-scoped retry-with-deadline for a not-yet-ready backend on first connect

origin_paths.what: isRetryableStartupUnavailable only retries a caught error if it's specifically an UNAVAILABLE/retryable GatewayClientRequestError AND (when the server attached method details) the failed method matches the one being retried; resolveStartupRetryDelayMs clamps the server's suggested retry-after between 100ms-5s; the retry loop itself runs against a hard 60s deadline (Date.now()+STARTUP_CHAT_HISTORY_RETRY_TIMEOUT_MS) after which it gives up rather than retrying forever.

candidates.mechanism: A first-connect retry loop for 'backend still warming up' must be scoped to the specific RPC method that failed (so it doesn't silently swallow an unrelated concurrent error under the same catch), clamp its backoff to a sane range even if the server suggests something extreme, and give up loudly after a bounded deadline rather than retrying forever.
candidates.why_solid: Read the relevant ~50 lines plus grepped the calling site's deadline math directly (lines 364-378). The three-part discipline (method-scoped retryability check, clamped backoff, hard deadline) is more careful than a naive 'retry on any error' loop.
candidates.halbert_evidence: /Volumes/4TB-BAD/Halbert/halbert_core/halbert_core/dashboard/frontend/src/hooks/useAgentStream.ts:1085,1103 explicitly defers retry/timeout policy to the backend httpx client (comment: 'retry policy lives on the backend'); this is a reasonable design choice already made, but no method-scoped retryable-error check or hard deadline was located in the frontend's own connection-retry code — flagging partial rather than absent since the design intentionally centralizes retry server-side.
candidates.task_proposal: If Halbert's dashboard frontend ever needs its own first-connect retry loop (e.g. waiting for the FastAPI backend or a local model server to finish booting before the first useAgentStream/useBeingEvents call), apply the three-part discipline: check the specific failed call, not any-error; clamp backoff; give up after a bounded deadline with a visible error rather than spinning forever.

verdict.notes: Origin verified: src/tui/gateway-chat.ts:101-118 isRetryableStartupUnavailable (requires GatewayClientRequestError with gatewayCode 'UNAVAILABLE' AND retryable, and when the server attached details.method it must equal the method being retried), :120-125 resolveStartupRetryDelayMs clamping the server's retryAfterMs to [100ms, 5s], :363-379 loadHistory looping against `Date.now() + STARTUP_CHAT_HISTORY_RETRY_TIMEOUT_MS` (60_000 at :78) and rethrowing past the deadline. Halbert 'partial' holds and the reader's citation is right in substance: hooks/useAgentStream.ts:1083-1108 documents the deliberate choice ('httpx on the backend handles retry/timeout policy') and already implements the transferable half — a fixed 5-minute deadline that aborts and surfaces a written, actionable error rather than spinning. keep=false: the task_proposal is explicitly conditional ('if Halbert's frontend ever needs its own first-connect retry loop'), and the deliberate server-side centralization is a design decision already made, not a gap.

candidates.title: isMainModule guard against a bundler accidentally re-running entry side effects

origin_paths.what: Explicit comment + guard: the bundler may import entry.js as a shared dependency when dist/index.js is the real entry point; without the isMainModule check the top-level side effects (starting the gateway) would run a second time and crash on the port/lock already held by the first.

candidates.mechanism: Any module with top-level side effects that is also importable as a library dependency needs an explicit 'am I actually the process entry point' guard, because a bundler or re-export chain can cause it to be imported (and its top-level code executed) without being the intended entry.
candidates.why_solid: Small, precisely-commented 12-line guard read in full; the comment itself documents the exact failure mode it prevents (duplicate gateway start, port/lock crash).
candidates.halbert_evidence: Python's own `if __name__ == "__main__"` idiom is the direct language-level equivalent and is presumably already used by Halbert's entry point, so this is largely N/A as a distinct gap — noting as low-value rather than a real gap; worth confirming the heavy import block noted in C1 does not run its side effects when main.py is imported as a library rather than executed directly.
candidates.task_proposal: No dedicated task needed beyond confirming (as part of C1's work) that Halbert/main.py's top-level heavy-import block does not execute unwanted side effects when the module is imported rather than run directly — Python's __name__ == '__main__' idiom already covers the OC07 guard's intent.

verdict.notes: Origin verified: src/entry.ts:107-121, comment and guard, with the documented failure mode ('the bundler may import entry.js as a shared dependency... would call runCli a second time, starting a duplicate gateway that fails on the lock / port'). The reader then talked itself out of the candidate ('largely N/A for Halbert, the __name__ idiom solves this') — that is wrong, and the correction is the point. Halbert/main.py does have `if __name__ == '__main__'` at :2670, but the guard is in the wrong place: dashboard/app.py:1744 executes `app = create_app()` at MODULE scope, so every importer of that module constructs the whole FastAPI app. Proven, not inferred: running `Halbert/main.py --version` (whose import block reaches dashboard.app at main.py:50) emits 'Turn-event tee bridged to the /ws fan-out' (app.py:1035), 'Indexing state initialized (fresh start)' and 'Halbert Dashboard API created' before printing the version. The module-scope instance exists for the `uvicorn ...dashboard.app:app` convention, so the fix is the lazy form (uvicorn --factory, or a module-level __getattr__ that builds on first attribute access), not deleting it. Keep as the general guard; it and C1 are the same defect from two directions and should be dispatched as one task.

anti_patterns.title: Node-specific fast-path/respawn mechanisms (compile-cache respawn, ESM resolve hook, Windows stack-size respawn) as literal code to port

candidates.title: Secret sentinels: seal resolved secrets into opaque AES-256-GCM tokens instead of ever holding plaintext in prompts/env

origin_paths.what: mintSecretSentinel/sealSecretSentinel/resolveSecretSentinel: a resolved secret is sealed with AES-256-GCM under a process-global key, keyed-HMAC nonce (deterministic per label+value so re-resolution is stable without a plaintext reverse map), and substituted back only by the process that minted it. looksLikeSecretSentinel/containsSecretSentinel/swapSecretSentinelsInText let callers detect and swap sentinels flowing through arbitrary text.

createSecretEgressBodyTransform rewrites sentinel substrings across chunk boundaries in an HTTP body stream; an unresolved or malformed sentinel reaching this point throws SecretEgressSubstitutionError('unresolved-sentinel') rather than silently forwarding it.

candidates.mechanism: Whenever a secret is resolved for use (env var, header, tool arg), it is immediately sealed into an opaque `oc-sent-v2.<ciphertext>.end` token; the token, not the plaintext, is what gets logged, put in a subprocess's env, or stored in an assistant/tool transcript. Only a narrow, trusted choke point (the egress proxy, or a direct in-process call) resolves the sentinel back to plaintext at the last possible moment. missed_by_reader.mechanism: Every path that touches a secret value — minting a sentinel, sealing one, and resolving one back to plaintext — unconditionally calls registerSecretValueForRedaction(value). The registry is bounded, so re-registering on every USE (not only at discovery) is what keeps a long-lived credential from being evicted by newer entries and silently dropping out of the redaction set.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert has the registry (ingestion/redaction_registry.py:32-92) and it already refreshes recency on re-register (move_to_end at :57) and evicts FIFO past max_entries=512 (:59-62) — that half is lifted and correct. Halbert's own operator-supplied cloud credentials are never registered at all — model/llm_config.py:465 stores the api_key verbatim, :898-906 resolve() hands it out inside ResolvedModel, :977-983 api_key_for(url) returns it, and dashboard/routes/llm.py:74-89 puts it into an x-api-key / Authorization header. Fix: call get_global_registry().register(key) (and get_global_echo_guard().note_injected(key)) at the two resolution choke points in model/llm_config.py (resolve() and api_key_for()) — exactly where the origin puts it. Small, deterministic, no new subsystem, and it makes the already-lifted registry actually cover the credentials Halbert holds.

missed_by_reader.mechanism: Any string that will be rendered into a terminal or a log line is either rejected outright when it carries C0/C1 control characters, or normalised by stripping ANSI escapes before escaping the remaining controls — with the ordering made explicit so that removing bytes cannot synthesise a new escape sequence.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert watches user shells and turns their output into prompt material. streaming/shell_integration.py:1-12 states the parser 'passes all bytes through to xterm.js unchanged — boundaries are metadata, not filtering', and :183-205 parses OSC 133 A/B/C/D and OSC 7 out of the raw PTY byte stream; the agent's own blocks are wrapped in printf'd markers at streaming/agent_pool.py:238-240. streaming/redact.py redacts credentials from block output_head/output_tail before persistence, but nothing strips ANSI/C0/C1. Consequence: a command whose OUTPUT contains an OSC 133 D sequence (a `cat` of an attacker-authored file, or a remote host banner) is parsed as a real block boundary with an attacker-chosen block id and exit code, and streaming/watched_shell.py then hands that forged block to the AI as 'what the user ran'. Two asks: (1) accept a D/C marker only when its id matches a block id this host minted this session, dropping unmatched markers as data; (2) run a sanitizeTerminalText-equivalent (strip ANSI, then escape remaining C0/C1) over block text on the path into persistence and into the prompt, in that order.

missed_by_reader.title: Pasted credentials are normalised before they can be pushed into an HTTP header
missed_by_reader.mechanism: One shared normalizeSecretInput() sits at every boundary where a credential arrives from config, env, a setup prompt or a plugin SDK caller: it removes CR/LF/LS/PS anywhere in the value (:25), drops every non-Latin1 code point and every C0/C1 control (:26-37) — the docstring names the exact failure it prevents, 'break HTTP header construction (ByteString violations)', so a smart-quote-contaminated paste fails as an auth error instead of crashing request setup — and trims the ends while deliberately preserving interior spaces so 'Bearer <token>' is not silently altered. normalizeOptionalSecretInput (:43-46) maps empty to undefined so 'not configured' stays distinguishable from 'empty string'.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert takes api_key straight from the dashboard PUT and stores it verbatim — model/llm_config.py:465 `"api_key": str(ep.get("api_key") or "")` inside the endpoint coercion, with no whitespace/control handling — and dashboard/routes/llm.py:82-89 puts that exact string into `x-api-key` or `Authorization: Bearer ...`. A key pasted with a trailing newline or a smart quote (routine when copying from a provider console or a PDF) surfaces as an opaque request-construction failure rather than 'that key is not valid'. Add a normalize_secret_input() helper applied at the one coercion point (llm_config.py:460-466) so every reader inherits it: strip \r\n   and C0/C1 anywhere, drop non-Latin1 code points, strip the ends, keep interior spaces. ~15 lines plus a test, and it removes a class of confusing failure before Halbert has users.

candidates.title: Pinned-DNS SSRF-guarded fetch (resolve once, dispatch to the resolved IP, re-check every redirect)

origin_paths.what: fetchGuardedMediaResponse routes every attempt through fetchWithSsrFGuard with a dispatcherPolicy/lookupFn pair, retries alternate dispatcher attempts, and pre-checks Content-Length before ever streaming a byte (assertMediaContentLength).
fetchLinkContent reuses the same fetchWithSsrFGuard + GUARDED_FETCH_MODE.STRICT for a completely different feature, proving the guard is a shared choke point, not per-caller reimplemented.

candidates.mechanism: One guarded-fetch primitive owns: protocol/scheme allowlist, hostname/IP blocklist (private/loopback/link-local/metadata), DNS resolved once and the actual TCP connection pinned to that resolved address (via a custom dispatcher/lookupFn), redirect targets re-validated against the same policy on every hop, and a Content-Length pre-check that cancels the body before reading a single byte if it already exceeds the cap. Every media/link consumer in the repo calls through this one function instead of rolling its own urllib/requests call.
candidates.why_solid: Directly closes a TOCTOU class of SSRF: resolve-hostname-then-separately-connect (DNS rebinding between check and use) is exactly the pattern Halbert's own code has today.
candidates.halbert_evidence: halbert_core/halbert_core/dashboard/routes/llm.py:96-127 `is_safe_url()` does `socket.getaddrinfo` once to validate, then a *separate* `requests`/httpx call is made later with no pinning to the validated address and no re-check on redirect targets — classic TOCTOU. halbert_core/halbert_core/dashboard/routes/compute.py:37,218 reuses the same `is_safe_url` with the same gap. `grep -rn 'is_safe_url\|resolve_pinned' halbert_core/halbert_core` found only these two call sites; no shared `infra/net/ssrf.py`-equivalent module exists.
candidates.task_proposal: Build one `halbert_core/halbert_core/net/ssrf_guard.py`: resolve the hostname once, validate the resolved IP (not just the hostname string) against the private/loopback/link-local/metadata blocklist, then make the actual HTTP call pinned to that resolved IP (e.g. via a custom Transport/connect override), re-validating on every redirect hop before following it. Replace `is_safe_url()` call sites in llm.py and compute.py with calls through the new guarded-fetch wrapper instead of the current validate-then-fetch-separately pattern.

verdict.notes: ORIGIN CONFIRMED, line ranges corrected. fetchGuardedMediaResponse is src/media/fetch.ts:297-395 (not 247-300): builds `attempts` from dispatcherAttempts (321-324), runs each through fetchWithSsrFGuard with `lookupFn: attempt.lookupFn ?? lookupFn, dispatcherPolicy: attempt.dispatcherPolicy` (331-345), falls through to a second dispatcher only when shouldRetryFetchError says so (351-378). The Content-Length pre-check is assertMediaContentLength, DEFINED at fetch.ts:432 and called at :554/:719 -- NOT inside 247-400 as the reader wrote. The pinning itself lives one directory outside the unit: src/infra/net/ssrf.ts:1 ('build pinned DNS lookups'), :236 ('redirects must re-evaluate against their own URL'), :595-706. Second path exact: src/link-understanding/runner.ts:72-83, fetchWithSsrFGuard with GUARDED_FETCH_MODE.STRICT. candidates.title: Reconnecting realtime-transcription WebSocket transport: exponential backoff with a stability-reset window, bounded drop-oldest audio queue, and send-side backpressure via bufferedAmount

origin_paths.what: REALTIME_TRANSCRIPTION_WS_MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES=16MB (inbound), REALTIME_TRANSCRIPTION_WS_MAX_BUFFERED_BYTES=1MB (outbound backpressure ceiling), DEFAULT_MAX_QUEUED_BYTES=2MB (local audio queue while disconnected), RECONNECT_STABLE_RESET_MS=30_000 — a reconnect only earns a fresh retry budget once the connection has stayed provider-ready for 30s, so a flapping connection can't infinitely retry at full speed.

sendAudio grep confirms: audio queued while reconnecting is capped by byte budget with oldest-dropped-first eviction, and the socket's own `bufferedAmount` is checked against the buffered-bytes ceiling before each send so a stalled remote provider cannot grow process heap unbounded.

OC10-media-pipelines.summary: This unit is a large (~185-file) media subsystem spanning ingestion/normalization (src/media), understanding pipelines for image/audio/video (src/media-understanding), link unfurling with SSRF safety (src/link-understanding), three generation-provider families (image/video/music-generation + shared media-generation), meeting-transcript persistence (src/transcripts), realtime STT websocket transport (src/realtime-transcription), and an agent-authored HTML/widget rendering surface (src/canvas). None of it was mentioned in the prior OSS review docs or master plan (grep of all three found zero references to any of these directory names), so this is genuinely unmined territory for Halbert. The strongest lifts are security-shaped: a pinned-DNS SSRF-guarded fetch primitive (C1) that closes a real TOCTOU gap Halbert's own llm.py/compute.py have today, and a deterministic link-detection safety pipeline (C2) Halbert has zero equivalent of. The second strongest cluster is the canvas/widget system (C6-C8) — Halbert's dashboard has no mechanism at all for the agent to render a rich HTML panel, and if that capability is ever wanted, this repo's isolation contract (frozen primitives, ticketed RPC, trusted-click-only navigation, path-escape-proof document store, flat size/count caps) is a complete, battle-tested reference to build from minus its multi-tab 'board' UI metaphor, which conflicts with Halbert's one-conversation philosophy. Media-understanding's per-capability defaults table (C3) and its transcribe-before-mention-check/echo pattern (C5) are smaller, concrete wins for Halbert's existing voice pipeline. Three areas were deliberately weighed and rejected for wholesale lifting (see anti_patterns): the generation-provider model catalogs (conflicts with the never-name-models directive), the transcripts/ meeting-bot plugin architecture (wrong product shape for a single-user host), and widget-tool's persistent multi-tab dashboard-board metaphor.

candidates.mechanism: Every tool-calling provider requires one tool_result per tool_use before the next assistant turn or the request is rejected. This walks history, pairs each tool-call occurrence with its result (handling duplicates/orphans/displaced results), and synthesizes a placeholder error result for anything unpaired so an interrupted transcript can still be replayed.
candidates.why_solid: Halbert's interrupt algebra and turn-lock/abandon path mean a turn can be cut off after a tool call was dispatched but before its result was recorded; replaying that partial state to a tool-calling model would otherwise fail.
candidates.halbert_evidence: tool_calls are tracked as an in-turn ctx.tool_calls list (state_machine.py:878,1219,1286) assembled into provider blocks at end_turn; grep for tool_call_id|tool_use|pair in context/assembler.py returns nothing — no pairing/repair pass exists where history is assembled for replay. Risk is narrower than a raw-message-list architecture since Halbert persists whole turns, but mid-turn multi-round-trip abandonment is unverified as unreachable.
candidates.task_proposal: Add a pairing-check pass to context/assembler.py that synthesizes an isError placeholder for any tool_call lacking a result before that history is sent back to a tool-calling model, mirroring makeMissingToolResult's shape/tag.
candidates.prerequisites: Confirm empirically whether ctx.tool_calls can reach a second model round-trip within one turn with an unresolved call before investing full effort.
candidates.risks: Speculative failure mode; low cost if the path turns out unreachable (defensive no-op), high value if real.

verdict.notes: ORIGIN CONFIRMED: tool-result-pairing.ts SYNTHETIC_MISSING_TOOL_RESULT_DETAIL_KEY :6, DEFAULT_MISSING_TOOL_RESULT_TEXT :7-8, TOOL_CALL_TYPES :5, createToolCallOccurrenceQueue :56, makeMissingToolResult :147-161 (isError:true :158), isSyntheticMissingToolResult :163, classifyToolUseResultPairing :228-380. KEEP=FALSE on reachability, which the reader itself asked to be verified first: Halbert never replays provider tool_use/tool_result pairs. state_machine.py:2395-2420 _build_messages emits ONLY system/user/assistant rows and folds every other role into the system prompt as defanged text (:2404-2407); tool outcomes return as ctx observations, and ctx.tool_calls is serialised into persisted turn BLOCKS at end_turn (:1284-1300 via _tool_block), not a provider message array. No role=tool message construction exists in state_machine.py, context/assembler.py or model/client.py. The 400-on-unpaired-tool_use failure this module prevents cannot occur. Record as a deliberate no-op; note the mechanism is already described at .handoff/OSS-REVIEW-OPENCLAW-2026-09-07.md:65 and was never packeted.

candidates.title: Process-group-aware graceful kill for the shell-exec tool path (matches what the PTY path already does)

origin_paths.what: killProcessTree: SIGTERM to the process group with a grace period, then SIGKILL; signalPtySessionTree walks every process/group in a forkpty session

candidates.mechanism: On timeout/cancellation, signal the whole process group with SIGTERM, wait a bounded grace period, then escalate to SIGKILL only for what's still alive, with fail-closed logic when group ownership can't be proven.
candidates.why_solid: Halbert's PTY-backed terminal already implements exactly this pattern correctly, but the non-PTY shell-exec tool path does not — an internal architectural inconsistency this pattern would fix.
candidates.halbert_evidence: streaming/pty.py:269 (os.setsid()), :362-432 (SIGTERM-then-grace-then-SIGKILL with WNOHANG reap) already matches kill-tree.ts closely. But tools/executor.py:832 spawns via asyncio.create_subprocess_shell with no start_new_session/process-group flag, and its only kill on timeout is proc.kill() at line 908 (immediate SIGKILL to the direct child only, no grace, no group signal) — grep for create_subprocess|start_new_session|preexec_fn|process_group in executor.py confirms no process-group scoping. A backgrounded/child-spawning command will leave orphans running after timeout.
candidates.task_proposal: Pass start_new_session=True to the create_subprocess_shell call in tools/executor.py, and on timeout/cancellation signal the negative pid (process group) with SIGTERM, wait a bounded grace period, then SIGKILL the group — reusing streaming/pty.py's existing grace/escalate helper rather than duplicating it.
candidates.prerequisites: streaming/pty.py's SIGTERM/grace/SIGKILL helper can likely be factored out and reused.
candidates.risks: start_new_session changes signal-delivery semantics for code relying on shared process group; flag for test-suite verification by the implementer.

verdict.notes: ORIGIN CONFIRMED: kill-tree.ts (325 lines; the cited 1-120 excludes the Windows half at :260-325) -- contract comment :16-23 ('Unix: send SIGTERM to process group first, wait grace period, then SIGKILL'; group kill only when the PID is a verified group leader), killProcessTree :31-63, signalProcessTree :65, signalPtySessionTree :87, signalUnixTarget :240, taskkill /T and /F /T :263-323. HALBERT STATE CONFIRMED partial, and the gap is WORSE than written. tools/executor.py:832-837 create_subprocess_shell takes no start_new_session/preexec_fn (neither token appears in the file), and the only cancellation kill is proc.kill() at :908 inside 'except BaseException' -- immediate SIGKILL to the direct child, no grace, no group. CORRECTION to 'the PTY path already does this correctly': streaming/pty.py calls os.setsid() at :269 but signals self._pid, NOT the group -- os.kill(self._pid, SIGTERM) :362 and os.kill(self._pid, SIGKILL) :432. Neither path does a group signal; pty.py only has the grace-then-escalate half (:360-372, :425-436 with WNOHANG reaping). That makes the fix cheaper and broader: pty.py is already a session leader so os.killpg(os.getpgid(pid), sig) is a one-line correctness fix there, and executor.py needs start_new_session plus the group signal. High: the steward orphans grandchildren on every shell timeout today.

candidates.title: Idempotency key + retry window on the dashboard's message-submission endpoint

origin_paths.what: SESSION_CREATE_IDEMPOTENCY_RETENTION_MS / SESSION_CREATE_RETRY_WINDOW_MS + optional idempotencyKey param

candidates.mechanism: A client-supplied idempotency key plus a server-side retention window: a retried request within the window carrying the same key is recognized as a resubmission and adopted rather than re-executed.
candidates.why_solid: Halbert's single continuous conversation with no conversation list means a duplicated turn is a visible duplicate inline in the one thread the user reads — double-submission on reconnect is directly user-visible in exactly this architecture.
candidates.halbert_evidence: dashboard/routes/agent.py:1629 POST /message (send_message) takes no idempotency key; grep for idempotenc across halbert_core finds it used only in scheduler/run_receipts.py, nowhere in the dashboard message path. A reconnect/retry resubmitting the same POST (see C8) has no protection against appending the same turn twice.
candidates.task_proposal: Add an optional client-generated idempotency_key to SendMessageRequest; have send_message short-circuit on a repeat key within a retention window, mirroring the openclaw constants.
candidates.prerequisites: Pairs naturally with C8.
candidates.risks: Needs a bounded key store with its own eviction.

verdict.notes: ORIGIN CONFIRMED: sessions-create.ts SESSION_CREATE_RETRY_WINDOW_MS :13, SESSION_CREATE_IDEMPOTENCY_RETENTION_MS :14, idempotencyKey :19 on SessionsCreateParamsSchema :17. HALBERT STATE CONFIRMED absent: routes/agent.py:1629-1631 POST /message takes no idempotency field; the only 'idempoten' hits are run_receipts.py:15,:200, execute_code.py:512, state_machine.py:799,:1015, conversation_sqlite.py:1791, mcp/server.py:502. KEEP=FALSE because the premise does not exist and the pairing with C8 is wrong. (a) No automatic resubmit of POST /message exists: hooks/useAgentStream.ts has no retry logic (its only 'retry' mentions, :1085 and :1103, say retry policy lives on the backend), and useBeingEvents is a separate SSE feed that never re-posts. (b) A second message during a live turn is DESIGNED: the route docstring at agent.py:1632-1639 says it queues on the turn lock, and AgentChat.tsx:894 deliberately sends while isStreaming. An idempotency key would guard a client behaviour Halbert does not have, against a server that already treats a resubmission as a legitimate distinct turn.

candidates.title: Stop-and-surface reconnect policy for the dashboard's WebSocket, instead of retrying forever on unrecoverable auth failures

origin_paths.what: shouldPauseGatewayReconnect: taxonomy of NON_RECOVERABLE_AUTH_ERRORS that pauses reconnect instead of retrying

candidates.mechanism: Distinguishes transient connectivity failures worth an exponential-backoff retry from structurally unrecoverable ones (bad credentials, version mismatch) by matching the connection error's code, stopping auto-reconnect on the latter so the client can surface a real error state.
candidates.why_solid: A single-user local dashboard reconnecting blindly on an unrecoverable auth failure gives the user no signal anything is wrong — it just looks disconnected forever while quietly retrying.
candidates.halbert_evidence: dashboard/frontend/src/hooks/useBeingEvents.ts:161-197 reconnects unconditionally on a fixed 3-second timer regardless of why the prior connection closed — no distinction between a transient blip and an auth rejection from dashboard/auth.py's TOKEN_ENV check.
candidates.task_proposal: Have the WS close/error handler inspect the close code/reason for an auth-rejection signal and, on that signal, stop the reconnect timer and surface a visible reauthenticate state instead of retrying.
candidates.prerequisites: dashboard/auth.py needs to close the WS with a distinguishable code/reason for auth failures if it doesn't already.
candidates.risks: Low; mostly a UX correctness fix.

verdict.notes: ORIGIN CONFIRMED: gateway-client/src/reconnect-policy.ts (54 lines) NON_RECOVERABLE_AUTH_ERRORS :7-21, shouldPauseGatewayReconnect :23-54 with deliberate non-pause carve-outs for PAIRING_REQUIRED+wait_then_retry :34-39 and a pending device-token retry :40-45. HALBERT STATE holds (absent) but the CITATION IS WRONG and the proposal as written is not implementable. hooks/useBeingEvents.ts:183-190 is an EventSource (SSE), not a WebSocket: es.onerror carries no status code or close reason, so 'inspect the close code/reason' cannot be done there. The real instance is hooks/useDashboardTurnReflection.ts:48 new WebSocket(wsUrl('/ws')) whose socket.onclose = () => { retry = setTimeout(connect, RECONNECT_MS) } at :79-83 ignores the close event entirely -- and the server DOES send a distinguishable code: dashboard/auth.py:439-440 await websocket.close(code=1008, reason='unauthenticated'). hooks/useTerminalSessions.ts:309-318 does not auto-reconnect at all. Keep at low priority but retarget the task to useDashboardTurnReflection.ts + the 1008 close code.

OC13-packages.summary: 18-package unit, too large for exhaustive file-by-file coverage in one pass; effort weighted toward the FOCUS areas called out (SSRF/net-policy, tool-call repair for local models, retry, terminal core) plus targeted sampling of the rest — 47 files read in depth or substantial part. Strongest findings: (1) Halbert declares an egress.web_fetch capability but has zero SSRF/private-IP guard anywhere for actual outbound fetches — net-policy's IP classifier is a near-direct port target; (2) tool-call-repair's plain-text/bracket/XML-ish grammar has no Halbert equivalent, and the Ollama path only reads the structured tool_calls field, silently dropping any pseudo-tool-call a weaker local model emits; (3) Halbert's PTY terminal already does graceful process-group kill correctly, but the separate shell-exec tool path does not — an internal inconsistency; (4) no idempotency on the dashboard's message endpoint, and the frontend's WS reconnect retries forever even on unrecoverable auth failures. One clear anti-pattern found and flagged not-to-port: model-catalog-core hardcodes vendor model-id rename tables, conflicting with the founder's never-name-models directive. retry/ was checked and found at parity with Halbert's existing retry/rate-limiter code, so no candidate was raised there.

missed_by_reader.title: Approval bound to the reviewed state: a sha256 of the file the action will mutate, plus a baseHash optimistic-concurrency guard on security-policy writes
missed_by_reader.lines: 184-190 (ExecApprovalsSetParamsSchema: file + optional baseHash), 202-220 (ExecApprovalsNodeSetParamsSchema: the native-policy write REQUIRES baseHash via the oneOf at :212-218), 108-112 (baseHashRequired constraint), 246-272 (ExecApprovalRequestParamsSchema.systemRunPlan carrying policySnapshot :260 and mutableFileOperand {argvIndex, path, sha256} :261-269)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Two halves of one idea, both missed. (1) A pending approval does not merely name the command -- it snapshots the policy it was asked under (policySnapshot) and, when the command mutates a file, the argv index, path and sha256 of that file AS REVIEWED, so redemption can refuse an approval whose operand changed between review and execution (approval-time-to-use TOCTOU). (2) Every write to the exec-approval policy itself carries the hash of the snapshot the editor read, mandatory for the node-native variant, so a concurrent edit is rejected rather than silently clobbered.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert's staged-change surface is the diff proposal and it has neither half. dashboard/routes/agent.py:2172-2179 _apply_target pulls (file_path, new_content) straight from the stored diff, and :2190-2203 _write_file opens the path 'w' and writes new_content wholesale; the current text is read at :2181-2189/:2196 ONLY to build provenance digests for record_file_change (:2209-2219), never to check that the file still matches what the owner reviewed. Two concurrent sessions (this repo runs them) or the owner's own editor silently lose a write. Proposal: (a) stamp a base_sha256 of the target file when a diff proposal is created (state_machine.py:4056-4060 pending_diffs), and have apply_diff refuse with a typed 'the file changed since you reviewed this' when the digest no longer matches, offering re-review rather than overwriting; (b) apply the same base-hash guard to writes of the consent/permission config the lattice reads. Frame as a strengthening of an already-lifted area: consent/copy.py:376-379 and consent/store.py:118,:152 already pin text_shown_sha256, so the COPY the owner saw is hashed while the OBJECT the approval acts on is not.

missed_by_reader.title: A hard byte cap enforced while reading an HTTP response body, plus strict Content-Length parsing
missed_by_reader.lines: 51-83 (readByteStreamWithLimit: running total against maxBytes, throw the caller's overflow error and destroy/cancel the upstream at :74-77), 28-49 (destroyReadableOnOverflow, with the comment that otherwise large media streams keep buffering after the caller already failed); plus packages/media-core/src/content-length.ts:1-18 (parseMediaContentLength rejects repeated or non-canonical lengths such as '05, 5' and non-safe integers)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: The cap is enforced on the stream as chunks arrive rather than by trusting a declared Content-Length, and the producer is torn down at the moment of overflow. The header parser is separately strict: repeated Content-Length values must be byte-identical after trimming, because inconsistent framing is an ambiguity/smuggling signal and numeric comparison would wrongly accept '05, 5'.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Every outbound HTTP read in Halbert is unbounded; only a timeout guards it. tools/web_search.py:109 'html = await resp.text()' and :196 'data = await resp.json()' against a user-configured SearXNG (:176) or DuckDuckGo; config/dynamic_prefixes.py:102-105 'resp.read().decode(...)' on a fetched prefix database; web/search.py:273,:321,:428; agents/peer_conversation_store.py:203; model/client.py:1009 and the model call paths. A multi-GB or slow-loris body from a misconfigured or hostile endpoint is an OOM of the process that IS the host steward. Proposal: one shared read_body_capped(resp, max_bytes) helper (aiohttp resp.content.iter_chunked / requests(stream=True).iter_content) that accumulates against a per-call cap, aborts the connection on overflow and returns a typed 'response too large' error; adopt it at every site above with per-call-site caps. Pairs with the C1 SSRF work -- same egress choke point.

missed_by_reader.title: Model-produced tool arguments validated against the tool's declared JSON schema before dispatch, with coercion that may never invent a null to pass
missed_by_reader.lines: 342-348 (validateToolCall: an unknown tool name is a hard error), 362-403 (validateToolArguments: schema-gated coercion, validator.Check, then a bounded TypeBox Convert retry), 350-360 (introducesNullValue -- a rejected value must never become a nullable placeholder just to pass), 9 (MAX_JSON_COERCE_LENGTH 64 KiB bound on schema-gated JSON coercion), 394-402 (failure returns a per-path error list plus the received arguments, i.e. something the model can act on)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: The declared parameter schema is compiled once per tool (validatorCache :6) and every tool call's arguments are checked against it before execution; limited coercion is allowed (numeric strings, enums, records) but rejected if it would introduce a null the caller did not send, and the failure is a structured, path-addressed message rather than a runtime type error.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert declares full JSON Schemas for its tools (tools/executor.py:71-89 WEB_SEARCH_SCHEMA, :150-174 run_command with required:['command'], ~20 more) and sends them to the provider, but never validates what comes back. model/client.py:440-469 _normalise_tool_calls only json-loads the arguments and guarantees a dict; tools/executor.py:431-438 execute() takes args: Dict[str, Any] and dispatches with handler(args) at :625-631 -- no required-field check, no type check. I verified the consequence with a throwaway snippet against the real module: ToolSafetyFramework().classify('run_command', {'command': ['rm','-rf','/']}) raises AttributeError "'list' object has no attribute 'strip'" (same for dict and int), and that call sits at tools/executor.py:569 OUTSIDE the try block beginning at :624 -- so a wrong-typed argument from a weak local model does not produce a correctable refusal, it throws out of execute() from inside the safety classifier. It fails closed (the tool does not run), so this is resilience/UX rather than a bypass, but it is exactly the failure mode that worsens once C3's plain-text tool-call repair starts synthesising calls from prose. Proposal: add validate_tool_arguments(schema, args) called in execute() before the safety classifier, returning ExecutionResult(success=False, error=<per-field message>); jsonschema is not a current dependency, so a ~60-line required/type/enum checker over the subset the tool schemas actually use keeps the Haloysius dependency discipline.

missed_by_reader.title: Closed wire objects: every protocol payload rejects unknown properties instead of ignoring them

missed_by_reader.title: Declared byte bounds on inbound base64 payloads, validated as canonical base64 before decoding
missed_by_reader.lines: 1-10 (MAX_TERMINAL_UPLOAD_BYTES 16 MiB, TERMINAL_UPLOAD_RETENTION_MS, MAX_TERMINAL_UPLOAD_BASE64_LENGTH as the base64 expansion, MAX_TERMINAL_UPLOAD_NAME_LENGTH 255), 25-31 (terminalUploadDecodedSize), 33-62 (isCanonicalTerminalUploadBase64: length%4, decoded-size cap, alphabet check, and the unused-padding-bits-must-be-zero check at :55-61); consumed as schema bounds at terminal.ts:56-67

missed_by_reader.task_proposal: dashboard/routes/audio.py:198-202 SpeakerEnrollRequest.audio_base64: str and :257-258 SpeakerTestRequest.audio_base64: str declare no max_length, and :215/:267 call base64.b64decode(req.audio_base64) without validate=True -- the whole encoded body is materialised then decoded unbounded. The strict-decode idiom already exists in-tree at ingestion/redaction.py:1419 (validate=True). missed_by_reader.mechanism: A paired device's usable command set is computed from four independent inputs -- built-in platform defaults, plugin-contributed defaults, the commands the device itself advertises at runtime (`node.approvedCommands`), and config allow/deny -- and the dangerous ones are subtracted from the default union at :425-436 with the comment 'Dangerous built-ins that also appear in PLATFORM_DEFAULTS stay declarable at pairing but do not enter the runtime allowlist by default'; only an explicit gateway.nodes.commands.allow re-adds them (:437-442). Three further rules: a plugin's `dangerous` flag governs only the surface that plugin contributes and is explicitly NOT authority to revoke a command core declares (:413-418, with the regression it caused recorded in the comment); the operator deny list is applied last (:451-458) with a narrow declarable-in-pairing-mode exemption; and NODE_WORKER_PRIVATE_COMMANDS are stripped unconditionally at the end (:459-461) so no input path can grant them.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Split 'what a peer says it can do' from 'what this machine lets it do'. Today dashboard/routes/peers.py:222-270 accepts PairRequest.capabilities verbatim from the requesting node, federation/peers_config.py:78-87 defines KNOWN_PEER_CAPABILITIES including 'terminal' (watched terminals / shell execution) and 'sysadmin_tools' (config editing, file management), :384-390 keeps unknown ones with only a warning, and :174-176/:317 route real work to any non-revoked peer whose self-advertised list contains the capability -- so one PIN approval grants every capability the peer asked for, permanently, with no deny list. Add a dangerous tier (terminal, sysadmin_tools, vision at minimum): advertisable and visible at pairing, but excluded from the routed set until the owner allows that capability for that peer explicitly, plus a per-peer deny that is applied last. This lands inside the existing five-axis permission vocabulary rather than beside it.

missed_by_reader.title: View-only observation enforced on the wire by an allowlist re-framer, with the observer forced to shared so it can never evict the human

missed_by_reader.title: PTY output flow control coupled to the viewer socket's send pressure, with a reassert failsafe and an interactive flush window
missed_by_reader.lines: 4-8 (4 MiB high water / 512 KiB low water / 5 s reassert / 1 KiB+100 ms interactive window); 49-63 (push + interactive fast path); 112-154 (reconcile + ensureReassertTimer); src/gateway/terminal/session-limits.ts:1-14
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Instead of dropping output when a viewer falls behind, the controller pauses the PTY itself: reconcile() takes the max bufferedAmount across live recipient sockets and pauses at 4 MiB, resuming only at 512 KiB (:112-129, real hysteresis rather than one threshold). A 5 s interval re-asserts whichever state is currently desired with the comment 'A missed native resume must not wedge the shell' (:131-154) -- i.e. the failsafe is designed around the pause primitive being unreliable. Output is coalesced by default, except that a chunk under 1 KiB arriving within 100 ms of user input is flushed immediately (:59-62), which is what keeps typing feeling instant while `yes` cannot flood the server. session-limits.ts adds the surrounding bounds: 24 concurrent shells, 256 Ki chars of scrollback, 8 detached sessions with a 300 s grace, each with its rationale in one line.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert's fan-out drops instead of pausing and never says so on the live path: streaming/pty.py:32-35 bounds each consumer queue at 1024 x 4 KiB and :204-213 _push_to_all silently discards a chunk on QueueFull ('Never block the reader on one slow consumer'), reasoning that scrollback replays it on re-attach -- but the live viewer receives a seamless, silently corrupted stream (streaming/bounded_output.py does splice an elision marker; the live path does not). There is also no coalescing, so every 4 KiB read becomes its own event. Two small changes: (1) emit an explicit gap marker to a consumer whose queue overflowed, so the tile shows a break instead of a lie; (2) coalesce output with the interactive fast-path rule (flush immediately for a small chunk within ~100 ms of input). Adopt pause/resume only if the drop policy proves wrong -- Halbert's session_manager already carries the per-kind caps and idle TTLs that session-limits.ts encodes.

OC17-gateway-second-pass-B.verify_summary: All 19 origin claims were checked by opening the cited files; every mechanism exists as described, so origin_claim_holds is true throughout, but four candidates carry factual corrections that change their task text and seven have Halbert-state errors. The consequential corrections: C11's approval binding hashes env KEYS AND VALUES (system-run-approval-binding.ts:97-121), not the key set as the reader wrote -- copying the reader's wording would ship a weaker gate; C14's generation hash is consumed server-side to disconnect stale clients on rotation (server-secrets-reload.ts:205-222), not by clients detecting rotation; C1's server-side default for an unclassified method is fail-closed-to-ADMIN rather than a hard deny; C19 and C18 have line ranges drifting 2-13 lines from the code they describe. Halbert-state corrections, all made by grep against live code: C11 and C1 are the two high-priority keeps and both are worse than the reader found -- tools/safety.py:553-559 executes an unregistered tool at MEDIUM with allowed=True, and state_machine.py:3419-3452 applies a human's confirmation to whatever call is last in ctx.tool_calls without re-checking the action_id or args it was granted for. C8 and C18 were called absent but have live partial surfaces (dashboard/routes/peers.py's PIN pairing exchange, which distinguishes four failure modes; mcp/camera_gate.py, whose own header records that the per-source ownership gates are unwritten), which makes both actionable now rather than hypothetical. C10's evidence was strengthened (state_machine.py:484 mints request_id server-side, so a retry queues on the turn lock and runs a second full turn). Three are dropped: C6 (the counter race it fixes cannot occur in Halbert's async handlers -- peers.py:369-384 has no await between increment and compare), C13 (its fail-closed rule already exists at dashboard/auth.py:495-511 guard_bind), and C17 (a 15-counter composite fence with no measured cost on a single-user machine, against the reader's own anti-pattern note). Five missed mechanisms are added from files the reader listed as unread: the method-descriptor registry that makes a missing or duplicate scope a startup error (the structural foundation C1 needs, and the direct answer to the reader's own auditability anti-pattern); the node command policy's dangerous-tier split between what a device may declare at pairing and what it may actually run, which maps onto Halbert's peers granting shell and sysadmin routing on one PIN; the post-approval re-hash of the approved script's bytes and resolved real path; the wire-level view-only RFB filter with its shared-not-exclusive rewrite, for Halbert's watched-shell direction; and the terminal flow-control controller, against which Halbert's silent per-consumer chunk drop reads as a defect.

candidates.title: Sleep/wake-aware suspension lease for the local gateway/agent connection

origin_paths.what: willSleep() requests a short-lived 'prepare for sleep' lease from the gateway (busy vs ready), tracked with a cycleGeneration counter to fence a late prepare-response against an already-completed wake; didWake() refreshes the transport first (sleep usually kills it) then resumes the lease with up to 3 retries at 2s apart, abandoning gracefully if the route/mode changed across the sleep.

candidates.mechanism: A generation-fenced two-phase handshake around OS sleep/wake notifications that lets in-flight work pause cleanly instead of racing a dead connection, with bounded retry and self-expiring leases so a lost resume never wedges the system.
candidates.why_solid: Halbert explicitly identifies as the host machine and is meant to run continuously (one seamless conversation, no session list) — sleep/wake is a real, recurring event on a laptop, and nothing currently reacts to it.
candidates.halbert_evidence: grep -rn 'willSleep|didWake|NSWorkspace|sleep.*notification|wake.*notification' across halbert_core/halbert_core (py/rs/ts/tsx) found nothing related to connection/session lifecycle (only unrelated 'screen lock' privacy mentions in vision_tools.py/screen_capture.py); halbert_core/halbert_core/scheduler has restart_budget.py (crash recovery) but no sleep/wake awareness.
candidates.task_proposal: On macOS (via the Tauri shell or a small native helper), subscribe to NSWorkspace.willSleepNotification/didWakeNotification and forward prepare/resume signals to the agent state machine: pause active generation/tool-call turns gracefully on sleep (or fence a short grace window), then on wake refresh the transport before resuming, with a bounded retry count and a monotonic generation counter so a stale resume from a very short sleep/wake blip cannot race a newer cycle.
candidates.risks: Needs a native bridge from Tauri/Rust to NSWorkspace notifications (or an existing Rust crate); scope carefully to avoid over-engineering for a single-user single-host system — the lease/generation pattern is the valuable part even if simplified.

verdict.notes: ORIGIN CONFIRMED exactly at GatewaySleepCycleController.swift:47-108 - willSleep(mode:) :47-66 bumps cycleGeneration, calls prepare(requestID), and on .ready(suspensionID) releases the lease immediately if the generation already moved (the late-prepare fence, with the comment about not fencing the gateway until its two-minute expiry); .busy is logged and skipped; didWake(mode:) :68-91 nils the suspension, bumps the generation again, calls refresh() FIRST ('after real sleep the transport is usually dead'), then resumes only if the route is unchanged; resumeWithRetries :93-108 loops Self.resumeAttempts with a generation guard on every attempt. HALBERT CONFIRMED absent: my grep for willSleep|didWake|NSWorkspace|caffeinate|IOPMAssertion|sleep_wake over halbert_core/halbert_core (py/rs/ts/tsx) found NSWorkspace only in vision/screen_capture.py:202-203 (frontmostApplication) and tools/vision_tools.py:562, plus caffeinate strings inside rag/scrapers/macos_support.py corpus text - nothing subscribes to a sleep or wake notification. RISK NOTE CORRECTED: the reader says this 'needs a native bridge from Tauri/Rust to NSWorkspace (or an existing Rust crate)'. openclaw has already done that port and it sits in this unit's unread area - apps/linux/src-tauri/src/gateway_sleep.rs (592 lines, same shape: RESUME_ATTEMPTS=3 and RESUME_RETRY_DELAY=2s at :6-7, CycleState{suspension, generation} at :26-30) with gateway_sleep_logind.rs / gateway_sleep_logind_listener.rs for the Linux D-Bus side. On macOS the cheaper path is PyObjC in the sidecar (AppKit already imported at screen_capture.py:202), no Rust required.

candidates.title: Ollama garbled-output detection: retry-or-switch instead of returning degenerate text

origin_paths.what: isLikelyGarbledVisibleText scores accumulated visible text by letter/digit ratio, symbol ratio, and max single-character frequency, but only fires when the model id matches a known-flaky-model regex (isKnownOllamaGarbledVisibleTextModel), throwing a clear 'returned non-linguistic garbled visible text; retry or switch models' error instead of delivering garbage.

candidates.mechanism: A cheap character-frequency/symbol-ratio heuristic that classifies degenerate local-model output (repeated symbol loops, corrupted-quantization gibberish) and converts it into an explicit, actionable error rather than silently returning it to the user or the agent loop.
candidates.why_solid: Local quantized models degenerating into symbol loops is a known, real failure mode; nothing in Halbert's LLM client or error taxonomy currently catches it.
candidates.halbert_evidence: grep -rn 'garbled|repetition|degenerate.*output|repeat_penalty' halbert_core/halbert_core --include=*.py found only unrelated wake_on_lan.py payload-repetition comments and a docstring mention in conversation/summarization.py; llm_client.py's chat()/stream() (halbert_core/halbert_core/agents/llm_client.py:108-250) has no output-quality check at all — only HTTP-status and tool-schema-retry handling.
candidates.task_proposal: Add a lightweight garbled-output classifier (ported from the same heuristic: compact-text letter/digit ratio < ~0.08, symbol ratio > ~0.6, dominant-character or long-symbol-run check) to the local (Ollama) client's response path, scoped to fire only for local/self-hosted responses (never cloud), and surface a distinct retryable error the agent loop can act on (retry once, or suggest switching connection slots) rather than feeding garbage into the conversation.
candidates.constraint_conflicts: Must not hardcode specific vendor model names as the trigger list (OpenClaw scopes it to a regex of known-flaky model ids) — Halbert should scope it generically (e.g. always-on for any local/self-hosted provider) rather than naming models, consistent with 'never bake or recommend model names.'
candidates.risks: False positives on legitimately symbol-heavy output (code, JSON, math) — the origin mitigates this by only enabling the check for models known to have this failure mode; Halbert would need an equivalent scoping (e.g. only check non-code-looking completions, or make the threshold conservative).

verdict.notes: ORIGIN CONFIRMED at both cited ranges (this one the reader got right). extensions/ollama/src/stream.runtime.ts:80-82 defines GARBLED_VISIBLE_TEXT_MODEL_RE = /\b(?:glm|kimi)\b/i, GARBLED_VISIBLE_TEXT_MIN_CHARS = 80, GARBLED_VISIBLE_TEXT_SYMBOL_RE; :131-134 countMatches, :136-144 maxCharacterFrequency, :137-139 isKnownOllamaGarbledVisibleTextModel, :141-165 isLikelyGarbledVisibleText with the exact thresholds quoted (letterOrDigitRatio < 0.08 && symbolRatio > 0.6 && (dominantCharacterRatio > 0.22 || a 12+ symbol run)); the throw sites are at :1333-1340 and :1345-1349, both raising 'Ollama returned non-linguistic garbled visible text for <id>; retry or switch models'. HALBERT CONFIRMED absent: agents/llm_client.py chat() builds the payload at :129-139 and the only post-response handling is the tool-schema retry on HTTP 400/404/422/501 (:144-155) - no output-quality check anywhere. CONSTRAINT: the origin's trigger IS a hardcoded model-family regex (glm|kimi), which the founder rule forbids; the degeneration is clean - the numeric heuristic is model-independent and at these thresholds (under 8% letters/digits over 80+ non-space chars) will not fire on code or JSON, so 'always on for local/self-hosted responses' is safe scoping. Keep at medium: real failure mode, cheap, but nothing is broken today.

candidates.title: Set Ollama's keep_alive so the continuous-conversation design controls model residency

candidates.title: Launch-at-login for Halbert's own app, with the idempotent-reinstall guard

candidates.title: Verify identity of whatever holds the dashboard's expected port before silently hopping to a fallback

origin_paths.what: sweep() reaps orphaned tunnels first, then checks whether the process bound to the gateway's port is the expected one (via managedGatewayPID from LaunchAgentManager, cross-checked against the actual listener) before treating the port as legitimately taken.

candidates.mechanism: Before accepting 'port busy, use a different one' as the answer, confirm whether the occupant is actually a live/expected instance of the app itself (vs. a stale crashed process or something else) and reap it if it's an orphan.
candidates.why_solid: Halbert's dashboard picks an arbitrary free port in a range and moves on with no check of who's already listening on the default one, which on a single-user host is mostly a UX confusion risk (silently landing on a different port after a crash) rather than a security one.
candidates.halbert_evidence: halbert_core/halbert_core/dashboard/__main__.py:48-57 find_available_port() just scans a range and binds the first free one; no check of what currently occupies the default/expected port, and no reaping of orphaned prior Halbert processes.
candidates.task_proposal: Before falling back to a scanned port, check whether the process currently bound to the configured default port is a stale/orphaned Halbert dashboard process (e.g. via psutil cmdline match) and, if so, reap it and reclaim the expected port rather than silently moving; log clearly when the fallback is a genuinely different process.
candidates.constraint_conflicts: Given single-user single-host scope, the full code-signature verification in PortGuardian.swift (csops-based cdhash check) is likely overkill — a lighter psutil-based process-identity check is more proportionate.

candidates.title: Local-provider SSRF bypass in is_safe_url does not re-validate the resolved IP

origin_paths.what: buildOllamaBaseUrlSsrFPolicy scopes every guarded fetch to a hostnameAllowlist of exactly the configured host, and every Ollama request (tags, ps, show, chat) is routed through fetchWithSsrFGuard with that per-request policy, re-checked on every call — not a one-time check at config-save time.

candidates.mechanism: A per-request SSRF guard bound to the exact configured hostname, applied uniformly to every outbound call to that provider, rather than a single upfront validation whose result is then trusted for all future requests.
candidates.why_solid: Halbert's own is_safe_url has a documented unconditional bypass for local providers that never re-checks the resolved IP, unlike its own cloud-provider branch two lines below which does resolve and check ip.is_private/is_loopback/etc.
candidates.halbert_evidence: halbert_core/halbert_core/dashboard/routes/llm.py:110-113 — `if provider in ("ollama", "lm-studio", "apple-foundation"): return True` unconditionally, before any hostname/IP resolution; the private/reserved-IP check at lines 116-127 only runs for the non-local-provider branch, so a user-editable 'ollama' provider URL pointing anywhere (not just loopback) bypasses the SSRF check entirely except for the two hardcoded metadata IPs at lines 108-109.
candidates.task_proposal: Strengthen is_safe_url so the local-provider branch still resolves the hostname and rejects anything that isn't loopback/an explicitly-allowed private host, rather than returning True unconditionally for the three local provider ids — matching the discipline the cloud-provider branch already has, and matching the origin's per-request hostname-scoped guard pattern.
candidates.constraint_conflicts: Single-user single-host lowers the practical severity (this URL is user-configured, not attacker-controlled, in the normal threat model), but 'deterministic policy' and defense-in-depth both favor closing an unconditional bypass that a mistaken paste (e.g. an internal admin URL) could exploit.
candidates.risks: Must not break legitimate local network use cases (e.g. Ollama running on another machine on the LAN, which the code comment 'Local providers need loopback access' seems to assume never happens) — check whether that's an intended supported configuration before tightening.

verdict.notes: ORIGIN CONFIRMED at extensions/ollama/src/provider-models.ts:62-82 - buildOllamaBaseUrlSsrFPolicy rejects non-http(s) schemes, blocks OLLAMA_ALWAYS_BLOCKED_HOSTNAMES (metadata.google.internal, :61), and returns {hostnameAllowlist: [parsed.hostname], allowPrivateNetwork: true}. The 're-checked on every call' claim is CONFIRMED independently: every guarded fetch rebuilds the policy at the call site - provider-models.ts:218 and :502, node-inference.ts:118, setup-pull.ts:76. Note for the founder: the origin DOES allow private-network destinations (allowPrivateNetwork: true); its guarantee is 'this request can only reach the exact host you configured', not 'only loopback'. HALBERT_STATE FIELD IS WRONG: the reader wrote halbert_state='present' while its own evidence describes a gap and its summary treats it as a gap. Corrected to 'partial'. Verified at dashboard/routes/llm.py:99-129: :108-110 blocks the two metadata hostnames, :112-113 `if provider in ("ollama", "lm-studio", "apple-foundation"): return True` returns before any resolution, and the getaddrinfo + ip.is_private/is_loopback/is_link_local/is_reserved check at :116-127 (with an _ALLOWED_LOCAL_PORTS loopback exception) runs only for the cloud branch. anti_patterns.evidence: extensions/copilot-proxy/index.ts:9-18 — DEFAULT_MODEL_IDS lists specific dated model versions (gpt-5-mini, claude-opus-4.6/4.7, claude-sonnet-4.6, gemini-3-flash) baked directly into plugin source.

missed_by_reader.title: Staged commands are written into a live shell with no gate and no control-character escaping - an embedded newline executes
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Before a command is rendered in an approval surface, every scalar whose Unicode general category is control, format, lineSeparator or paragraphSeparator is replaced with a literal \u{XXXX} escape, as is every space separator that is not U+0020 and four invisible fillers (U+115F, U+1160, U+3164, U+FFA0). OC20-extensions-memory-knowledge-automat.summary: This unit is unusually rich and only partially covered in the time available. memory-core, memory-lancedb, and active-memory (the three directories the assignment explicitly flagged) were read in real depth and yielded the strongest candidates: concrete, narrow, well-isolated mechanisms (contamination guards against self-referential promotion loops, PID-liveness-aware lock stealing, per-phase circuit breakers, prompt-injection screening at the memory-recall injection point, multilingual future-vs-retrospective recall-intent disambiguation, standing intents as a distinct capability from fact-durability promotion) that go beyond what the master OSS-review doc already cites about the promotion-ranking algorithm itself. memory-wiki and
