Revisit only if a skill- or MCP-declared redaction-pattern surface is ever specified.

candidates.title: Proactive pattern-based secret redaction (beyond the existing known-value echo guard)

origin_paths.what: word-boundary key-keyword matching (STRONG vs weak keyword classes), _looks_like_opaque_credential heuristic for ambiguous token/key values, _redact_assignments/_redact_url_credentials/_redact_phone, redact_sensitive_text top-level policy, redact_terminal_output's env-dump-command-aware code_file gate

candidates.mechanism: Independent of any known-secret list, this scans arbitrary text for KEY=VALUE-shaped assignments (env/JSON/YAML style) whose key contains a word-bounded credential keyword ('apiKey', 'API_KEY', not 'keyboard' or 'secretary' — camelCase/acronym-aware boundary detection), and separately flags ambiguous values (a bare 'token'/'key'-named field) as credential-shaped via an entropy-ish heuristic (hex string >=16 chars, base64-ish string >=20 chars, or mixed-case+digit density on strings >=12 chars) so short technical scalars like 'CPU' or 'local' aren't masked merely for sitting next to a suggestive key name. A programmatic-env-lookup exception (`os.getenv('X')` as a VALUE) prevents masking code snippets that merely reference a variable name. Terminal-output redaction is command-aware: the env-assignment pass only runs when the command itself looks like an env dump (`env`, `printenv`, `cat .env`) or reads a `.env`-basename file, so ordinary source/config dumps aren't false-positive-masked.
candidates.why_solid: Halbert's redaction (already lifted per the master plan) is purely reactive: SecretVariantRegistry only redacts a value it has already been TOLD is a secret (loaded from config/known credentials). It has no mechanism at all for catching a secret the system has never seen before — a freshly pasted API key, a generated token in a command's stdout, credentials embedded in a URL, a phone number in log output. Given Halbert's ongoing security-hardening posture (186 confirmed findings, active remediation branch) and its terminal-watching design ('user shells stay but are WATCHED by the AI'), a proactive pattern-based layer is a materially different and complementary defense the echo-guard alone cannot provide.

candidates.title: Thread-scoped stdout/stderr silencing proxy (per-thread, not process-global)

origin_paths.what: thread_scoped_silence(): installs a single idempotent per-thread routing proxy as sys.stdout/sys.stderr; only the calling thread's writes route to a sink, every other thread's writes pass through unaffected

candidates.mechanism: Python's contextlib.redirect_stdout reassigns the PROCESS-GLOBAL sys.stdout, so a background worker thread silencing its own noisy library output also silences every other concurrently-running thread's stdout — including, in a multi-threaded host, the gateway/event-loop thread or another worker entirely. This installs one routing proxy object as sys.stdout (once, idempotently, never uninstalled to avoid a race with other threads mid-write) that checks a per-thread-id silence counter and routes to either a shared /dev/null sink or the real passthrough stream accordingly.
candidates.why_solid: Halbert runs a scheduler/heartbeat daemon, a terminal-watching subsystem, background review/consolidation tasks, and MCP server processes — all plausible sources of concurrent threads where one thread wanting quiet output (e.g. a noisy library call inside a scheduled task) must not silence the terminal channel or another live thread's diagnostic output.
candidates.halbert_evidence: grep -rln 'redirect_stdout\|thread_scoped_silence' halbert_core/halbert_core found nothing — if Halbert's scheduler or background tasks use contextlib.redirect_stdout anywhere, it would carry exactly this cross-thread silencing bug; if they don't suppress subprocess/library output at all today, this is a straightforward defensive addition before the need arises.
candidates.task_proposal: Grep Halbert's scheduler/ and background-task code for any use of contextlib.redirect_stdout or similar process-global stream reassignment; if found, replace with a thread-scoped proxy of this shape. If not currently used, adopt this pattern proactively as the standard way any future background worker silences its own noisy output.
candidates.prerequisites: None.
candidates.risks: Low — this is a narrow, self-contained utility with no security surface.

verdict.notes: ORIGIN CONFIRMED: agent/thread_scoped_output.py:1-8 (the process-global redirect_stdout problem stated exactly), :20-26 (per-attribute install registry, one process-lifetime sink, shared routing state), :29-35 _RoutingState, :38-58 _ThreadRoutingStream (_target picks sink vs passthrough by threading.get_ident(); silence/unsilence depth-counted under a lock). READER'S CAVEAT REMOVED — the bug is live in Halbert. tools/execute_code.py:447 assigns the PROCESS-GLOBAL sys.stdout = capture from inside a worker thread ('halbert-script', started :458), restoring at :455 and defensively at :514. While a script runs, every other thread — FastAPI dashboard, scheduler/heartbeat, a concurrent turn — has its stdout routed into THIS script's capture buffer and spill file, and that buffer is returned to the model as the script's output. Two consequences: unrelated output can leak into a tool result the model reads, and two concurrent runs can capture each other's 'original' so stdout is never restored. 217 module-level print() sites exist (mostly __main__ blocks, which bounds but does not remove the exposure); logging handlers bind their stream at construction and are unaffected. Replace the global assignment with a thread-scoped routing proxy. Effort S.

HM02-agent-context-prompt-family.summary: This is an unusually rich unit: Hermes's context/prompt-family is a mature, heavily-incident-driven (many #NNNNN issue references) compaction and prompt-assembly system built over a long time, and it maps onto several genuine, well-evidenced gaps in Halbert rather than duplicating anything already lifted. The strongest finding is structural: Halbert's own code documents its context-compaction trigger (ContextWatermark.should_compact) as having 'NO PRODUCTION CALLER' and its actual compaction path (build_conversation_window) as a hard character-budget trim with no LLM summarization at all, while conversation/summarization.py's compress_conversation_history is a static, non-incremental, non-resume-safe extractive summary. Hermes's micro-compaction (rolling per-exchange summary with a crash-safe cursor, defrag, and DB-consistent archival) and its ContextEngine lifecycle ABC are close to a direct fix for that exact, self-documented gap (C1, C2), and the deterministic per-tool-type summarizer (C3) extends the founder's own 'template, not model, where a template suffices' instinct into the compaction domain. Several security-adjacent findings stood out as concretely actionable given Halbert's active hardening posture: no scan for prompt injection in loaded context docs (C5), no expiry on a stale dangerous-confirmation phrase surviving in a session with NO natural boundary to reset it (C10, arguably MORE load-bearing for Halbert than for Hermes given the one-continuous-conversation design), and a purely-reactive echo-guard redaction system with no proactive pattern-based layer at all (C13) plus no ReDoS-safety net for any future pattern-registration surface (C12). Two findings connect directly to the founder's stated 'hidden topic threads, recall by relevance, no conversation list' continuity direction: side-question forking (C7) is close to a working implementation of 'answer without disturbing the main thread', and thread titling (C8) revealed that Halbert's SQLite schema already has the exact title/title_source provenance ladder this generator would populate — the plumbing exists, the generator does not. A streaming-safe think-block scrubber (C11) is a precise fix for a documented unsafe pattern (batch regex over a complete string) that Halbert's own utils/reasoning.py currently uses. Given the unit's sheer size (context_compressor.py alone is 281KB/~4900 lines and conversation_compression.py is 219KB), full coverage was not attempted for those two files or for prompt_builder.py; grep-driven triage plus targeted reads of the most-cited/most-documented sections were used instead, and the unread_areas list names exactly what was skipped for follow-up.

missed_by_reader.title: Malformed tool-call argument JSON repair ladder (local-model shaped) instead of silently substituting an empty object
missed_by_reader.mechanism: A five-pass repair ladder for tool_call arguments before dispatch. Pass 0 re-parses with json.loads(strict=False), which accepts literal control chars inside strings — the comment names this 'the most common local-model case' — and re-serialises to wire-valid JSON. Passes 1-3 strip trailing commas, close unclosed braces/brackets by count, then trim excess closers in a bounded 50-step loop. Pass 4 escapes 0x00-0x1F inside JSON string values as \uXXXX with a hand-written string-state scanner (_escape_invalid_chars_in_json_strings, :98-114) for llama.cpp-style output mixing control chars with other malformations. Only then does it return '{}', logging the ORIGINAL arguments at WARNING with a deliberately generous 100000-char bound (:118-119) because 'the WARNING log is the last surviving copy of content that can hold real user data (a truncated write_file)'. Every repair logs at WARNING with a before/after excerpt, so silent degradation never happens.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Add a repair ladder in front of Halbert's two tool-call argument decode sites, both of which fail silently today. (1) halbert_core/model/client.py:456-462 (_normalise_tool_calls): a JSONDecodeError logs one WARNING and sets args = {} — so a local model emitting a truncated or control-char-laced blob gets its tool run with NO arguments (a write with no path, a command with no command) and neither the model nor the user is told. (2) halbert_core/agents/llm_client.py:258-267 does not decode at all — it passes func.get('arguments', {}) straight through, so an OpenAI-compatible provider's JSON STRING reaches a downstream expecting a dict. Port the strict=False pass, the bounded structural repair and the control-char escaper; on unrepairable input surface an explicit typed error observation to the model ('arguments were unparseable, reissue the call') instead of executing with {}. Squarely aimed at Halbert's local-first posture, and both sites are on the hot path of every tool-using turn.

missed_by_reader.title: Untrusted-tool-result delimiter wrapping with delimiter neutralization, for external content entering the turn
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Tool results whose content is attacker-controllable — _UNTRUSTED_TOOL_NAMES = {web_extract, web_search} plus the prefixes browser_ and mcp_ (:404-414) — are wrapped before reaching the model in an <untrusted_tool_result source="name"> block carrying an explicit instruction that the content is DATA and that only the user, outside the block, can issue instructions (:484-504). Before wrapping, every occurrence of the delimiter token inside the content is rewritten to a non-matching form (_neutralize_delimiters, :478-481, case-insensitive at :409-410) so poisoned content cannot close the trust boundary early; there is deliberately no 'already wrapped' fast path because that check would be attacker-forgeable (:488-490). Alongside it, _tool_output_risk_metadata (:456-475) runs scan_for_threats(scope='context') as an internal-only advisory classification that never blocks or redacts, and _maybe_append_elision_notice (:449-453) appends an incompleteness notice when an upstream service elided the result.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Wrap external-origin tool results in an untrusted-data delimiter block before they become an observation. In Halbert every tool result — MCP client responses, web_search, browser/fetch output — is rendered by agents/state_machine.py:153-163 _format_tool_observation into a bare 'Executed <call>:\n<text>' string with no trust marking; grep for 'untrusted' shows the concept applied only to discovery text (discovery/schema.py:41), user input (integrations/modality_wiring.py:375) and system-position rows (prompts/agent_prompts.py:1241-1270 defang_system_text). Halbert already owns the right primitive — defang_system_text's fixpoint tag-collapse is exactly the delimiter neutralization needed — so the task is to classify external-origin tools (mcp/ client, tools/web_search.py) and route their results through a wrap+neutralize step in _format_tool_observation. This matters more in Halbert than in Hermes because those results do not stay in the turn: they feed ctx observations, which feed the assistant row, which feeds build_receipt, which is indexed into receipts_fts and re-injected by recall — so a poisoned web page can reach durable memory and re-enter a later prompt.

missed_by_reader.title: Absorption cursor so a per-turn summary is folded incrementally instead of rebuilt from the whole thread
missed_by_reader.mechanism: The transferable, model-free half of micro-compaction: a persistent cursor marking the first message not yet absorbed (_resolve_compact_cursor, :38-59), recovered on a cold start by scanning for the last summary marker rather than by re-processing the transcript, with the recovered marker flagged so a later pass merges instead of replacing; an exchange finder that walks exactly one complete assistant+tool turn bounded by user rows (_find_one_exchange, :61-88); and _next_exchange (:283-292), which computes the compressible window once and returns None when the cursor has caught up, so a turn with nothing new to absorb costs nothing. The summarizer call is the part Halbert should NOT take; the cursor and the one-exchange-per-turn discipline are the part it should.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Make Halbert's per-turn receipt refresh incremental. Today agents/threads.py:1044-1049 _refresh_receipt calls store.list_messages(thread_id) with NO limit and hands every row to build_receipt on EVERY end_turn (threads.py:470), and agents/receipt.py:196-206 states plainly that 'messages is scanned in full' and that a recency window inside build_receipt would be wrong because it would silently drop earlier Commands/Files-written entries. threads.py:645-647 already flags the cost ('the sweep is up to 200 closes, each an unbounded list_messages plus a full build_receipt, which is no better a thing to hold a turn behind'). Under the one-continuous-conversation design a subject thread can run very long, so this is O(thread length) SQLite load + JSON decode + full scan on the turn-finalisation path. Add a per-thread absorption cursor plus accumulated Commands/Files/entities sets so end_turn folds only rows added since the last refresh, recovering the cursor from the stored receipt on a cold start exactly as _resolve_compact_cursor does. Fully deterministic — no model — so it is founder-aligned in a way C1 is not.

missed_by_reader.title: Timeout-bounded read for any file loaded into a prompt, so a stalled mount cannot wedge a turn
missed_by_reader.mechanism: _read_text_with_timeout (:51-77) performs path.read_text on a daemon thread and takes the result off a queue with a timeout (5s default, config-overridable at :43-48). On timeout it logs a WARNING and returns None so the caller skips that file, leaving the orphaned reader thread to finish on its own; real read errors are re-raised on the caller thread so existing per-site try/except handling is unchanged. Its companion _truncate_content (:1412-1428) does head+tail truncation with a middle marker naming the path the agent can read_file to recover the full content, and pushes a user-visible warning into a contextvar that build_system_prompt drains into chat (system_prompt.py:671-673) — the comment notes the previous silent tail-chop cut a real AGENTS.md 'for months unnoticed'.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Bound every disk read that feeds a Halbert prompt. Three sites read with no timeout: skills/parser.py:619 (read_bytes for SKILL.md — the live third-party path), skills/sidecar.py, and prompts/loader.py:196 (read_text for prompt components). Halbert is the host machine: a skill directory or prompt component on a stalled NFS/SMB mount, a sleeping external disk or a hung FUSE filesystem blocks the reading thread indefinitely, and for the skills catalog that is on the path of assembling a turn. Wrap these in a timeout-bounded read with a config-overridable default, skipping the file with a WARNING on timeout. Halbert's byte-cap-and-refuse policy for oversize skill files (parser.py:619-623) is a reasonable divergence from Hermes's head+tail truncation and should stay; the timeout is the missing half.

missed_by_reader.title: One scoped threat-pattern library applied at several boundaries, with an invisible-unicode and homograph check
missed_by_reader.mechanism: A single pattern library with three cumulative scopes — 'all' (classic injection, hidden HTML comments/divs, 'do not tell the user'), 'context' (role hijack, C2/promptware vocabulary, anti-forensic instructions, agent-env-var unset), 'strict' (aggressive checks only where a block is resolvable) — shared by three call sites at different trust boundaries: context files (agent/prompt_builder.py:89, scope='context'), memory writes and the memory snapshot load (tools/memory_tool_store.py:24-28 and :116-120, scope='strict', where a hit is replaced by a [BLOCKED: ...] placeholder in the SNAPSHOT only so the user can still see and delete the poisoned entry), and tool results (agent/tool_dispatch_helpers.py:472, advisory). Two properties matter more than the pattern list: the invisible-codepoint check runs on RAW content BEFORE normalisation because NFKC would strip those codepoints (:120-121, INVISIBLE_CHARS at :91-93 covering zero-width and bidi-override characters), and NFKC folding then defeats full-width homograph bypass (:122-124, with an honest note that cross-script confusables need a TR#39 table). MAX_SCAN_CHARS 65536 bounds worst-case runtime (:16-17), and the header rule is that patterns must anchor on unambiguous attack behaviour, not bossy English, because 'you must' is common in legitimate AGENTS.md.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: If C5 lands, build it as ONE scoped library rather than a one-off scanner for skill files, and include the invisible-unicode check — Halbert has no invisible-codepoint or homograph check anywhere in the prompt path (grep for the zero-width/bidi codepoints and for unicodedata.normalize returns nothing there), while its defanging (prompts/agent_prompts.py:1241-1270) neutralises only its own control tags. Then reuse the library at Halbert's own second boundary: the receipt/recall path. Receipts are built from command stdout and log lines and are re-injected into the prompt (agents/state_machine.py:88-125), and continuity/promotion.py promotes recalled material into durable memory — so bidi overrides or zero-width padding in a tool result can ride into a durable, re-injected artefact. Keep the scoping discipline explicit: the strict SSH-backdoor/persistence/exfil patterns are too aggressive for ordinary host documents, which is why the origin separates the scopes.

missed_by_reader.title: A deterministic tool-result prune with its own cheap trigger, separate from the compaction decision
missed_by_reader.mechanism: prune_tool_results_only is a first-class hook on the engine ABC, distinct from should_compress/compress: it 'deterministically trim[s] old tool-result payloads without an LLM call' and the contract says it 'runs on a low, cost-oriented trigger independent of should_compress, so large-window engines reclaim re-sent tool output long before full compaction'. It returns (messages, n_pruned) and the default is a no-op so older engines stay safe. The separation is the point: the expensive summarisation decision and the free deterministic reclaim sit on different triggers, and the free one fires far more often.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Pair this with C3. Halbert's deterministic reclaim is currently a single fixed cap applied once per observation (agents/state_machine.py:153-163, _TOOL_RESULT_CHARS = 2000 at :46) plus a watermark micro_compact that is documented as a no-op on today's data (context/assembler.py:1353-1358). Give the deterministic pass its own cheap re-trigger over the accumulated ctx.observations list as a turn's tool loop grows, so a long multi-tool turn re-prunes the oldest observations to their per-tool-type one-liners (C3) before the assembler's budget starts dropping content wholesale — rather than only capping each result once at arrival. Costs no model tokens and needs no compaction decision.

OC23-control-ui.summary: OC23-control-ui is an enormous unit; I covered it by depth-first sampling the FOCUS areas (approvals, session checkpoints, chat outbox/tool-cards, diagnostics, cron, memory consolidation, device stats, logs, keyboard shortcuts, MCP-widget security, redaction) rather than breadth-first skimming. Grep of the two prior review docs and the master plan for this directory found nothing — no wave has touched ui/src's control-UI layer yet, so every finding is 'new' or a constraint conflict, none 'already-lifted'. The two standout large gaps are a fully-formed generic JSON-Schema config-form generator (C9, vs. Halbert's 960-line hand-built Settings.tsx) and a complete Automations/cron UI (C13, absent despite Halbert's mature scheduler backend). The richest small-detail harvest was the exec-approval card family (C1-C6): command-span highlighting, countdown+urgency, keyboard shortcuts, stale-resolution handling, an exhaustive scope taxonomy, and a poll/mutation race-reconciliation algorithm — all layered onto a Halbert Approvals.tsx that today is a bare 5-second poll loop with none of these. Two structural findings shaped anti-patterns: OpenClaw's entire sessions-list UI is built around the multi-session-list model Halbert's founder has explicitly ruled out, and its multi-viewer presence system has no second user to serve on a single-user product — both called out rather than proposed, though the underlying checkpoint reversibility-tiering mechanism (C7) is still worth lifting once reframed away from a session list.

missed_by_reader.title: Approval surface forces LTR so a command cannot visually reorder itself (bidi/trojan-source defence)
missed_by_reader.lines: approval-presentation.ts:9,26,33,46; approval.css:197-201,271-273; text-direction.ts:7-47
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Everywhere else in the control UI, text direction is DETECTED per message: text-direction.ts:17-18 tests explicit bidi controls (U+061C, 200F, 202B, 202E, 2067 -> rtl; 200E, 202A, 202D, 2066 -> ltr) before the first-strong-character scan at :30-46. On the approval surface that autodetection is deliberately switched off: approval-presentation.ts hard-codes dir="ltr" on the command summary (:26), the command <pre> (:33), the plugin detail <pre> (:46) and wraps every metadata value in <bdi dir="ltr"> (:9), while approval.css:197-201 and :271-273 set unicode-bidi: plaintext on those same classes. The effect is that a command carrying RTL-override characters cannot present the approver with a different visual ordering than the bytes that will execute — the classic trojan-source spoof against a human authorising a shell line.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: In components/agent/ConfirmationDialog.tsx, render confirmation.tool and confirmation.description inside an explicitly dir="ltr" container with unicode-bidi: plaintext (and the same for any command text added by C1), and wrap metadata values in <bdi dir="ltr">. Today the description goes through renderDescription -> dangerouslySetInnerHTML (ConfirmationDialog.tsx:52-57, 88-95) with no direction attribute anywhere in the file and no stripping of U+202E-class controls, so a model- or filesystem-supplied command can reorder what the founder reads on the one screen where they authorise a privileged action. Consider also rejecting or visibly marking bidi control characters in the approval payload server-side.

missed_by_reader.title: Write-only secret store: the secret variant structurally has no value field, plus per-secret allowed-hosts egress binding
missed_by_reader.mechanism: SecretStoreEntrySchema (secrets.ts:60-64) is a discriminated union of two closed objects: the 'secret' variant (:46-51, commented 'Secret metadata never structurally carries the stored value') has name/scope/timestamps/allowedHosts and NO value property at all, while the 'env' variant (:53-58) does carry value because env entries are intentionally visible. The list RPC returns only that union (:69-72), so the browser cannot receive a secret value even by accident — the guarantee is in the schema, not in a handler remembering to blank a field. Separately, a secret carries allowedHosts (:41-44, max 128 unique hostnames) which the UI collects as a whitespace/comma list at secrets-store/index.ts:118-128 — the credential is bound at rest to the hosts it may be sent to.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Two pieces. (1) Structural: Halbert already implements write-only secrets by convention — dashboard/routes/llm.py:148-169 _redact_api_keys blanks api_key to "" and adds key_set, with _carry_forward_api_keys re-attaching on PUT, and dashboard/routes/mcp.py:141-159 rejects a literal auth.token in favour of token_env. Both are per-route hand discipline over a payload shape that still HAS the field; convert them to response models where the redacted variant does not declare the secret field, so a future handler cannot fill it. (2) New: Halbert has no per-credential egress binding — grep for allowed_hosts across halbert_core finds only dashboard/auth.py:265-430 (inbound Host/Origin checks). Add an allowed-hosts list to each stored credential and enforce it at the egress choke point, which is a deterministic, LLM-free complement to the Tier-2 posture in config/sensitivity.py:87-140.

missed_by_reader.title: Attention dismissals keyed to a content signature, pruned on recurrence, with non-dismissible severities
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Dismissing (snoozing) a sidebar attention chip stores not the chip's id but a SIGNATURE of the condition's content: resolveUpdateAttentionDismissal (:105-122) signs [version, gatewayBootId] so a restart or a new version re-arms the nag, and resolveScopeUpgradeDismissal (:92-103) signs [phase, ...sorted scopes] so 'manual repair' and 'actionable upgrade' are distinct incidents. isSidebarAttentionDismissed (:128-133) is a pure signature membership test, so a condition that clears and later recurs with different content surfaces again by construction. pruneDismissals (:134-177) drops stored signatures whose chip is no longer active, but only when the current response is AUTHORITATIVE for that kind (an all-agent cron inventory may re-arm cron entries; a selected-agent response may only re-arm its own auth warning) so a partial refresh cannot wrongly resurrect a snooze. isUpdateAttentionForced (:125-127) makes warn/danger tones non-dismissible. dismissSidebarAttention (:74-90) does read-merge-write against storage rather than writing a caller-held snapshot, because another tab may have dismissed a different chip meanwhile. The whole thing is deliberately per-device client state (:1-3: 'dismissing a nag on one device should not acknowledge it everywhere').
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert's snooze is finding-id keyed and purely time-based: dashboard/routes/being.py:158-174 POSTs days, findings/store.py:323-336 sets status SNOOZED with snoozed_until = now + N days. That means a finding whose underlying condition materially worsens (severity escalates, blast radius grows) stays silent for the rest of the window. Add a content signature to the snooze record (e.g. severity + the fields that define the finding's current state) and re-arm the chip when the signature changes, and make critical severities non-snoozable the way isUpdateAttentionForced does — both are deterministic checks, no model involved. Keep the server-side store (single user, single host, so the per-device argument does not apply).

missed_by_reader.title: Typed refresh policy: visibility, TTL, interruption and coalescing decide fetch vs defer vs skip
missed_by_reader.mechanism: decideUsageRefresh (:13-35) takes a reason ('focus' | 'manual' | 'poll' | 'reconnect'), whether the document is visible AND focused, whether a disconnect interrupted in-flight work, and the age of the last payload, and returns 'fetch' | 'defer' | 'skip': manual always fetches; an invisible page always defers (the request is remembered, not fired); an interrupted load refetches even inside the TTL because a disconnect invalidated it; otherwise a payload younger than a 5-minute TTL is skipped. requestAndWait (:119-134) coalesces — a request arriving while a load is in flight sets pendingAutomaticRefresh instead of stacking a second fetch, and flushPending (:136-143) replays it once. applyLoadState (:86-96) refuses to start the TTL clock when the payload came back incomplete, so focus/reconnect can still recover.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert's dashboard polls with bare timers that run regardless of whether anyone is looking: grep finds 20+ setInterval sites outside tests, including Dashboard.tsx:61 (2s system metrics), Layout.tsx:244 (5s pending approvals) and :482 (2s status), Approvals.tsx:35 (5s), VitalsModule.tsx:56, AcousticAuraIndicator.tsx:66, NodeFleetCockpit.tsx:104, useDiscoveredPeers.ts:74 — and exactly one visibility check exists anywhere in the frontend (StandbyController.tsx:146, unrelated). A Tauri window left open all day therefore keeps the host busy answering polls nobody reads, on the machine the app claims to be. Add one small usePolling(reason, ttl) hook implementing this decision table (defer while document.hidden, TTL skip, refetch-on-reconnect, coalesce in-flight) and migrate the top-level page polls onto it.

missed_by_reader.title: Config diff preview: sensitive paths redacted by ancestor-prefix inheritance, behind an explicit reveal, with bounded diff computation
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Before a config save, the page shows a structural diff of what will change. isSensitiveDiffPath (:216-228) walks every ANCESTOR prefix of a changed path and treats the leaf as sensitive if any prefix is marked sensitive by the server's shared isSensitiveConfigPath, by a UI hint on that prefix, or by a hint whose key matches that prefix — so marking a subtree sensitive redacts everything under it, and a new nested key inherits the protection instead of leaking by default. renderRawDiffValue (:231-242) additionally scans the VALUE (countSensitiveConfigValues) and substitutes redactedPlaceholder() unless the user has explicitly toggled rawRevealed. The diff itself is bounded against pathological config: MAX_CONFIG_DIFF_DEPTH 64, MAX_CONFIG_DIFF_NODES 20_000, MAX_CONFIG_DIFF_CHANGES 1_000, MAX_CONFIG_DIFF_ARRAY_COMPARE_ITEMS 2_000, MAX_RAW_DIFF_CHARS 200_000 (:13-17), and computeRawDiff caches by (original, current) but deliberately skips caching an empty diff while the lazy JSON5 parser is still warming (:170-181) so a transient parse failure is not pinned.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert has the classifier but never applies it to the editor surface: config/sensitivity.py:87-140 classify_sensitivity returns Tier 0/1/2 per (key, value, file) and even uses redact_text as a value detector, yet components/ConfigEditor.tsx loads and renders whole host config files into Monaco (and into a Monaco DiffEditor at :600-605 for AI-proposed changes) with no tier awareness — grep for sensitiv/redact in dashboard/routes/editor.py returns nothing. At minimum, apply classify_sensitivity to the AI-PROPOSED diff path so Tier-2 values render as a placeholder with an explicit reveal toggle rather than appearing in a change preview the founder is being asked to approve, and carry the ancestor-prefix inheritance rule when the config surface becomes structured.

missed_by_reader.title: Per-request expiry timers and per-source failure isolation in the approval refresh
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Two details inside a file the reader did read but did not surface. (1) Each queued approval gets its own prune timer: scheduleApprovalExpiryPrune (:432-452) sets a timeout for expiresAtMs - now + 500ms which removes the entry from the queue and fires execApprovalChanged, with a generation check (:437-440) so a superseded timer for the same id is a no-op and clearApprovalExpiryTimer (:423-430) cancelling on every reschedule; refreshPendingApprovalQueue re-syncs the timer set to the refreshed queue at :529-537. Expiry is therefore enforced client-side even if nothing else fires. (2) The refresh fans out over three sources with Promise.allSettled (:503-507) and, per source, falls back to the CURRENT queue entries of that kind on rejection (:508-518) rather than treating one failed list call as 'no approvals of that kind' — a partial failure cannot silently empty the queue.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: The expiry half maps onto a real Halbert bug: approval/engine.py:317-332 get_pending_requests selects on status == 'pending' and never compares expires_at (set at engine.py:155-158) to now, and ApprovalStatus.EXPIRED (engine.py:28) is never assigned anywhere, so a timed-out approval remains pending indefinitely and can still be approved. Fix server-side (mark and exclude expired requests on read, or on a scheduler sweep) rather than only in the UI. The per-source isolation half applies to Approvals.tsx:41-51 loadAll, which Promise.all's approvals and history together — one failing call currently blanks both via the shared catch.

missed_by_reader.title: Client-minted idempotency key plus expected-leaf token on the chat send RPC
missed_by_reader.mechanism: chat.send carries three server-checked tokens the client mints: idempotencyKey: params.runId (:53) so a retried or duplicated send is recognised as the same turn rather than creating a second one; expectedLeafEntryId (:50-52) an optimistic-concurrency token naming the conversation leaf the client believed it was appending to, whose mismatch surfaces as a typed 'active-leaf-changed' error (isActiveLeafChangedError, :75-90) rather than a silent fork; and __controlUiReconnectResume (:34-35,42) marking a send that follows a reconnect into the same session so the server can distinguish resume from a fresh turn. The same runId flows back through message identity (lib/chat/history-message-identity.ts:38 matches identity.idempotencyKey against runId or `${runId}:user`) so the server's echo of the user turn can be reconciled with the local one.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert's send has neither token: dashboard/routes/agent.py:39-51 SendMessageRequest declares only message + optional session_id (with a docstring explaining there is deliberately no client-chosen conversation id), and grep for idempotenc/expected_leaf across halbert_core finds hits only in scheduler/run_receipts.py. Halbert already has the server-side half of the leaf invariant — agents/conversation_sqlite.py:734 idx_one_open_leaf, :1656 get_or_open_thread, :1899 move_leaf — so an expected-leaf token is a natural fit and would turn a racing second sender into a typed refusal instead of a silent append. Add (a) a client-minted idempotency key on POST /api/agent/message, deduplicated at the turn writer, so a retried POST after a dropped response cannot produce two turns, and (b) an optional expected-leaf id checked inside the same transaction as move_leaf. This is the candidate C22 was reaching for; C22's cited mechanism was the display-fencing key, not this.

OC23-control-ui.verify_summary: Verified all 23 candidates against the origin at the cited lines. Origin citations were accurate for 22 of 23 — line ranges landed on the right code, occasionally a few lines short of the function that completes the mechanism (C5 stops before clearResolvedExecApprovalPrompt, which is what makes the merge work). One origin claim fails on mechanism rather than location: C22's chatOutboxDeliveryKey fences the DISPLAY of a delivered queued turn (its own comment says so; both call sites confirm), not duplicate sends — the real send-side idempotency is chat.send's client-minted idempotencyKey plus expectedLeafEntryId, which I have surfaced as a missed item instead. Two further drops: C7 (the confirm-severity half already exists in Halbert's two dialogs, the operator.write-vs-admin half does not degenerate to one user, and the compaction-checkpoint feature it hangs off does not exist) and C11 (proposes a UI over a command-lane executor Halbert simply does not have; its justification cites a nonexistent 'master plan packet 99'). Four Halbert-state corrections, all in the direction of making work cheaper or better-targeted: C2 is partial not absent (expires_at already exists in approval/engine.py but is never enforced and never serialised — and get_pending_requests ignoring it is a live 'pending forever' bug); C16 is partial (AgentChat.tsx already has the 100px auto-follow, only the log tail page is missing); C1's attachment point is ConfirmationDialog.tsx, which does render a model-supplied command, not Approvals.tsx, which renders none; C14's origin is a ChatGPT-import review view reached via wiki.importInsights, not the consolidation pipeline the reader described. Priority moves: C15 up to high (a stale reading shown as a live red bar contradicts the founder's grounding rule, and the fix is the cheapest item in the set); C20 up to high because security/result_redaction.py's own docstring states internal executor results are deliberately NOT routed through the redaction core while Timeline.tsx renders them raw — which is exactly parked founder decision 05-C in the master plan; C9 and C14 down (both need backend work the reader treated as free); C5 down (Halbert's UI never consumes the approval websocket broadcast, so the race is one tick wide). Seven missed mechanisms, drawn from files absent from key_files_read: the approval surface's forced-LTR bidi lock, the schema-enforced write-only secret store with per-secret allowed-hosts egress binding, signature-keyed attention dismissals with authoritative-refresh pruning, the visibility/TTL/interruption refresh policy (Halbert has 20+ unconditional setInterval polls and one visibility check in the entire frontend), the sensitive-path-inheriting config diff preview, the per-approval expiry timers plus per-source failure isolation, and the chat.send idempotency/expected-leaf tokens.

missed_by_reader.mechanism: Staleness is remembered ACROSS attempts on the agent, not just within one. Each stale kill bumps a counter; a success clears it; and _check_stale_giveup is consulted BEFORE the next request is issued, so an unresponsive provider costs a bounded number of full stale-timeout waits and then raises a message telling the user to switch backends — instead of an indefinite stall of stale-timeout x forever. missed_by_reader.title: The read-back leg of truncate-and-spill: Halbert's read_file has no offset/limit and refuses >1MB, so its own spill pointer is a dead instruction

missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert emits the pointer but cannot honour it. execute_code.py:318-330 tells the model 'full output saved to {spill_path} — read(offset={len(head)}) continues from where this cuts off (read_file(path=...), or in a script: halbert_tools.read_file(path=...))', but the registered read_file (tools/executor.py:180-200) accepts ONLY path and encoding — no offset, no limit — and _read_file (971-1004) hard-raises ValueError('File too large') above 1 MB before returning the whole file at once. anti_patterns.title: approval_smart.py: an auxiliary LLM decides APPROVE/DENY/ESCALATE for a flagged command
anti_patterns.evidence: tools/approval_smart.py:70-115 (_smart_approve calls an auxiliary LLM with temperature=0 asking it to classify command risk; verdict feeds directly into tools/approval.py's _smart_gate, which can auto-approve or auto-deny a real dangerous-command execution based on that LLM's one-word answer).
anti_patterns.why_not: Directly violates Halbert's founder constraint: deterministic policy — no LLM in any security/permission decision. Even with the injection-hygiene mitigations Hermes applies (comment-stripping, XML-delimited untrusted block), the verdict of whether a dangerous command runs must never turn on a second model's judgment; Halbert should keep such decisions in the deterministic detector (C1/C4) instead.

anti_patterns.title: tirith_security.py: silently auto-downloads and runs an external network-fetched binary as part of the security path
anti_patterns.evidence: tools/tirith_security.py:1-30 (a missing tirith binary is downloaded from GitHub releases to $HERMES_HOME/bin/tirith in a background thread, SHA-256-verified and optionally cosign-verified, then run as a subprocess for every command scan).
anti_patterns.why_not: Contrary to Halbert's minimal-dependency, local-first design (the Haloysius Subtractive Contract keeps even ML stacks lazy-optional) and to a single-host assistant's threat model: pulling and executing a network-fetched binary as part of the SECURITY path is itself a supply-chain attack surface (a compromised release, a DNS hijack of the download, or a delayed/failed update leaving stale verification) that a local, single-user host steward should not introduce. The equivalent content-level threat detection Hermes achieves this way is better achieved deterministically in-process, as its own threat_patterns.py (C4) already demonstrates without any external binary.

anti_patterns.title: Reverting-scheduled 'PLUGIN-COMPAT' backward-compat shims kept alive in shipped modules
anti_patterns.evidence: tools/path_security.py:19-38 and tools/slash_confirm.py:92-121 (both carry a '---- BEGIN PLUGIN-COMPAT (revert-scheduled...) ----' block: a lazy __getattr__/wrapper preserving names external plugin authors imported before an internal refactor, enforced only by a CI script that fails if internal code uses it).
anti_patterns.why_not: Halbert's own directive is explicit: no migrations or back-compat shims for old data or code — there are no users yet, so a clean rename/move costs nothing and a temporary-but-shipped compatibility shim (with its own CI-enforcement machinery) is exactly the kind of permanent-feeling scaffolding for a temporary problem that Halbert should skip entirely by doing the refactor cleanly instead.

HM06-tools-approval-guards.summary: This is a very rich unit: Hermes's tools/approval* family is a mature, deterministic, extensively-tested defense-in-depth system for shell-command execution, far exceeding Halbert's current live command gate. The single highest-value finding is that Halbert's ACTUAL PRODUCTION command-safety gate (halbert_core/halbert_core/tools/safety.py's ToolSafetyFramework, wired into tools/executor.py) is a naive, unanchored regex classifier with no shell-parsing, no quote-awareness, and no obfuscation resistance — a near-total downgrade from Hermes's approval_detection.py engine, and Halbert additionally carries a second, unwired, even-thinner copy of the same idea (prompts/safety.py) as dead scaffolding. Beyond that core gap, this unit surfaces several genuinely absent security primitives Halbert has no equivalent of at all: SSRF/DNS-rebinding protection for its multiple outbound-fetch tools, a self-repo-mutation guard (relevant given Halbert's own worktree-based self-development), ANSI/Unicode-tag-smuggling stripping for terminal and tool output reaching the model, schema-guided small-model tool-argument coercion (directly relevant to Halbert's local-Ollama-model routing), and a structured mid-turn clarify tool. Two flagged anti-patterns matter for Halbert's founder constraints specifically: approval_smart.py puts an LLM in the security-decision loop (a direct violation of Halbert's deterministic-policy directive) and tirith_security.py silently downloads and executes a network-fetched binary as part of the security path (contrary to Halbert's minimal-dependency, local-first ethos) — both should be avoided even though their underlying goals are worth achieving deterministically instead, as Hermes's own threat_patterns.py already demonstrates.

candidates.title: Watch-pattern notification rate limiting: per-session strikes + global circuit breaker

origin_paths.what: WATCH_MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS/WATCH_STRIKE_LIMIT/WATCH_LIFETIME_MAX_HITS/WATCH_GLOBAL_MAX_PER_WINDOW/WATCH_GLOBAL_COOLDOWN_SECONDS constants with rationale comments

candidates.mechanism: A background process can register substring watch_patterns to interrupt the agent when matched (e.g. a build log's 'BUILD FAILED'). Without limits a noisy/looping match would inject a full agent turn every time it fires. Per-session: one match per cooldown window; a match landing inside the cooldown is a 'strike' (not a drop-count), and enough consecutive strike windows or a lifetime hit cap permanently disables watching for that session and demotes it to a single on-exit notification, with one explanatory event so the agent knows why it went quiet. Global: an independent sliding-window breaker caps total watch_match deliveries across every session concurrently, so many well-behaved siblings can't collectively flood the same agent.
candidates.why_solid: This is a genuinely hard problem (autonomous background work interrupting an LLM turn) solved with pure deterministic counters and windows — no LLM judgment anywhere in the safety path, exactly the founder's 'deterministic policy' constraint. It generalizes past terminal watch patterns to any Halbert notification source that can recur (log-tail alerts, sensor thresholds, scheduler run failures).

candidates.title: PID-reuse-safe process termination with kernel start-time verification

origin_paths.what: _is_host_pid_alive/_safe_host_start_time/_host_pid_is_ours: a stored PID is only trusted if it is alive AND its kernel start-time ticks still match what was recorded at spawn

_terminate_host_pid(): refuses to touch a PID whose start-time no longer matches ('PID was recycled onto a stranger'); otherwise psutil-snapshots the whole process tree, SIGTERMs children before parent, waits daemon_term_grace_seconds, then SIGKILLs survivors (re-probed individually, not via psutil.wait_procs's gone/alive partition, which the comment says mis-partitions across zombie transitions)

candidates.mechanism: The kernel recycles PIDs; a checkpointed or long-held PID number can later belong to an unrelated process. Every place this registry acts on a stored PID (adopt after restart, kill) first re-validates it against the kernel process-start-time captured at spawn (host_start_time), refusing to touch anything that doesn't match — with a documented real incident (a browser tree-killed) motivating the guard. Kill itself snapshots the tree, SIGTERMs children-before-parent, and only escalates to SIGKILL after a configurable grace period, re-probing liveness directly rather than trusting a batch API's partition.
candidates.why_solid: This is a small, self-contained, high-confidence correctness fix: any process registry that persists PIDs across a restart (which C3 will need for crash recovery) is vulnerable to this exact bug class the moment it's built, and the fix is cheap (~150 lines, cross-platform via psutil).

HM12-gateway-rooms-platforms-hooks.summary: Very large unit (~30 substantive files, 20k+ lines across gateway/platforms + gateway/relay + hosted_room*). I read the platform-contract core in base.py (media-delivery guard, MEDIA: tag pipeline, SendResult taxonomy, BasePlatformAdapter contract), the ADDING_A_PLATFORM.md checklist, one full concrete adapter (bluebubbles.py, directly actionable for a macOS iMessage channel), the webhook adapter's security primitives (signature verification, rate limiting, dedup, self-elevation guard), the idempotency-key store and digest-sealed room-grant renewal, the relay handshake/auth/transport contracts, the lifecycle hook system, and the browser-control broker. Strongest candidates: (1) a deterministic local-file-delivery allow/deny guard (C1) — Halbert has no equivalent and it's exactly the LLM-independent security gate its own directives call for; (2) a client-submitted-turn idempotency-key store (C7), strengthening the missing half of an already-lifted sibling (scheduler occurrence idempotency); (3) a concrete BlueBubbles/iMessage channel build (C6), directly implied by the assignment's own framing; (4) a local lifecycle hook system (C12), a cheap extensibility point Halbert entirely lacks. The multi-install hosted-rooms machinery (distributed authority epochs, replica takeover, cross-gateway execution grants) is real and sophisticated but explicitly NOT something to lift given single-user/single-host — flagged as anti-patterns; the one piece that degenerates (digest-sealed execution-policy snapshots) is captured separately as C8. Biggest coverage gaps: relay/adapter.py + ws_transport.py (~3000 lines, the actual production relay wire implementation) and the bulk of api_server.py (~4000 lines, the OpenAI-compatible HTTP surface) were only skimmed at docstring/signature level — a follow-up pass there would likely surface additional streaming/session-recovery patterns.

missed_by_reader.title: Turn-owned process ownership + baseline-diff reap of processes an abandoned turn left running, epoch-gated
missed_by_reader.mechanism: When a turn starts, _publish_turn_process_ownership (:582-593) claims a monotonic epoch for the task_id and snapshots the process registry's running ids as a BASELINE. If the client disconnects mid-turn, _reap_disconnected_agent_processes (:544-572) fires a daemon thread that kills exactly the processes that appeared after the baseline -- gated on _epoch_still_current (:561-568) so a stale reaper can never kill a NEWER run that reused the task_id (a missing epoch entry means our own clear pruned it, so the reap proceeds). _clear_turn_process_ownership (:595-608) drops ownership the moment the turn ends, so work the turn deliberately left running in the background survives a later disconnect or cancel. It exists because this surface runs its own agent lifecycle and never passes through the shared TurnRunner, so it needed its own trigger for the same reap.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert kills only its own DIRECT child, and only on the tool call's own timeout/cancel: tools/executor.py:902-909 (`pumps.cancel(); if proc.returncode is None: proc.kill()`), same shape at tools/applescript_tools.py:90-100. A grandchild the command backgrounded (a nohup'd helper, a daemonising script, anything execute_code spawns and detaches) outlives the turn with nothing tracking it -- grep for process_registry/reap across halbert_core returns nothing of this kind. Add a per-turn process baseline: snapshot the machine's own child-process set at turn start (bound to the existing continuity/provenance.current_turn ContextVar) and, on turn end or /stop, reap only the delta, epoch-gated so a later turn's processes are never touched. Squarely the machine-is-the-project identity: the steward should not leave strays on its own host, and can then honestly report what it left running.

missed_by_reader.title: A single shutdown budget apportioned across teardown steps, with every await individually bounded
missed_by_reader.mechanism: One env-configurable total budget (_env_disconnect_budget_s, :64-73, default 5s, the same var and default as the runner's own adapter-disconnect timeout) is APPORTIONED across teardown: each of the three sequential teardown awaits is individually capped at _TEARDOWN_AWAIT_TIMEOUT_S (:37-41) 'so a wedged peer cannot stall adapter.disconnect past the runner's default 5s budget', and the in-flight drain grace is clamped at disconnect time to the REMAINING budget (:55-62: min(drain_grace, budget - 3*teardown - 0.5)). The comment at :45-48 names the failure prevented: blowing the budget cancels teardown mid-drain and leaves callers blocked on the full outbound timeout. Related on the same surface: api_server.py:1169-1184 interrupt_active_runs(reason) and :1186-1203 the draining state, so shutdown refuses new work and actively interrupts in-flight runs rather than waiting on them.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert's dashboard/app.py:1623-1700+ shutdown_event is a long sequential list of unbounded awaits, each wrapped in try/except but none with a timeout: stop_thread_tick_heartbeat, stop_mcp_health_monitor (which cancels in-flight reconnects and reaps stdio subprocesses), _config_watcher.stop, _scheduler_executor.stop, ingestion stop, `await get_terminal_manager().shutdown()`, `await _ha_event_stream.stop()`, the Frigate MQTT subscriber, the Wyoming voice agent. Any one wedging hangs shutdown forever -- on a host steward that is a machine that will not restart cleanly, which is exactly what the already-lifted scheduler restart-budget work assumes. Give shutdown_event one total budget, wrap each step in asyncio.wait_for against the remaining slice, log the step that blew it, and interrupt (not await) any in-flight turn.

candidates.title: Shared parent-death supervisor process for stdio MCP children

origin_paths.what: Standalone stdlib-only supervisor process spawned once per Hermes process (start_new_session=True), told 'register <pgid>'/'unregister <pgid>' over a line-based stdin pipe. Detects Hermes death as EOF on that pipe (exact, instant, free) and SIGTERM→grace(3s)→SIGKILL killpg-sweeps every still-registered process group. Replaces a prior per-server watchdog (~10MB resident per server) with one shared ~15MB process. Line length capped at 256 chars to bound memory against a runaway writer.

_spawn_death_supervisor / _update_death_supervisor / _prune_dead_supervised_pgids: registers/unregisters pgids, respawns and replays coverage if the supervisor dies, releases it when nothing is left to reap.

candidates.mechanism: One long-lived helper process outlives the parent even on SIGKILL/OOM/crash (macOS has no PR_SET_PDEATHSIG); it learns which process groups to reap via a pipe whose write end only the parent holds, so parent death is EOF, not polling. Reaps by process group (stdio children spawned with start_new_session=True so killpg reaches descendants like npx's forked node child).
candidates.why_solid: Directly addresses a real, unowned failure mode: a stdio MCP server (or any subprocess Halbert spawns and expects to own) reparents to init and runs forever if Halbert crashes hard. Read the full mechanism and its residual-risk section (pgid reuse) end to end; the code is self-contained, POSIX-only, no third-party deps.
candidates.halbert_evidence: grep -rn 'death_supervisor|PR_SET_PDEATHSIG|killpg' halbert_core/halbert_core --include=*.py found nothing under mcp/. halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp/client.py's StdioTransport.close() (lines 309-336) only calls proc.stdin.close()/proc.wait()/proc.kill() on the direct child — no process-group tracking (no start_new_session), no orphan sweep, and nothing survives a SIGKILL of the Halbert process itself.
candidates.task_proposal: Add a standalone tools/mcp_death_supervisor.py (or halbert_core equivalent) to halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp/: spawn stdio MCP children with start_new_session=True, spawn the shared supervisor once per Halbert process (its own pgid, POSIX-only), and register/unregister each server's pgid with it in StdioTransport.connect()/close(). Given Halbert is single-host and often runs as a background dashboard service, this closes a real orphan-process leak on crash/OOM-kill.

candidates.title: MCP image/audio/embedded-resource content-block caching to media/document cache instead of raw JSON dump

origin_paths.what: _cache_mcp_image_block / _cache_mcp_audio_block: base64-decode with a SIZE CAP applied on the b64 string BEFORE decoding (never doubles memory) and again on decoded bytes, then write through gateway.platforms.base.cache_image_from_bytes/cache_audio_from_bytes and return a 'MEDIA:<path>' tag consumed by messaging adapters that render images natively; fail-open (returns a bracketed notice, never raises) if the gateway module is unavailable.

_render_mcp_resource_block: embedded text passes through; embedded blob is decoded (size-capped) into a document cache with a path marker and a 'read it with read_file' pointer; a resource_link (not yet fetched) renders as a pointer at the server's own read_resource tool rather than fetching it inline.

candidates.mechanism: Rather than either silently dropping non-text MCP content blocks or forwarding raw base64 into the model's context (bloating tokens, unreadable), each media/resource kind is decoded (size-capped both pre- and post-decode), written to Hermes' existing media/document cache, and replaced with a compact reference tag the model and downstream UI already know how to render.
candidates.why_solid: Read the full content.py caching pipeline including the two-stage size cap (base64-length pre-check, then decoded-byte-count post-check) and the fail-open gateway-import guard.
candidates.halbert_evidence: halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp/bridge.py's format_tool_result only special-cases dict results with a 'content' key by joining TEXT items (join_text_content); any non-text content (images, embedded resources) falls through to a raw json.dumps() of the whole result dict — no caching, no MEDIA-tag convention, no size cap on the decoded bytes.
candidates.task_proposal: If/when Halbert's dashboard/chat surfaces gain an image/media rendering convention (check for one under dashboard/frontend first), port the two-stage-capped base64 decode + cache-and-reference-tag pattern into halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp/bridge.py's format_tool_result for ImageContent/AudioContent/EmbeddedResource blocks, so a screenshot- or document-returning MCP tool (e.g. a browser-automation or file-reading server) doesn't dump raw base64 into the model's context.
candidates.constraint_conflicts: Depends on Halbert's dashboard having (or gaining) an equivalent media-cache/reference-tag convention; if none exists this is a prerequisite, not a drop-in port.
candidates.risks: Needs its own size-cap constants and a real cache backend; a half-done port that caches but never renders would just move the bloat rather than fixing it.

candidates.title: content vs structuredContent alternation with reserved _meta key stripping

origin_paths.what: _capped_structured_content / _render_call_tool_result: content and structuredContent are treated as ALTERNATIVES never both forwarded (a spec-following server already renders its data into content, so duplicating structuredContent doubles token cost for no information gain); structuredContent only fills in when content rendered effectively empty. Server-level _meta is surfaced too, but PROTOCOL-RESERVED keys (a 'modelcontextprotocol' or 'mcp' label followed by ≥1 more label) are stripped first — vendor-namespaced keys like com.example.mcp/... pass through.
_is_reserved_mcp_meta_key / _strip_reserved_meta_keys implement the exact reserved-prefix rule, ported from a specific upstream fix (kimi-code#2600).

candidates.mechanism: A precise reading of the MCP spec's dual content/structuredContent emission SHOULD-behavior, applied as a deterministic dedup rule rather than a heuristic richness comparison (the code explicitly notes no size/semantic heuristic is reliable, so it doesn't attempt one).
candidates.why_solid: Read both the dedup logic and the reserved-key-prefix regex rule end to end, including the explicit rationale for NOT attempting a richness heuristic.
candidates.halbert_evidence: grep -n 'structuredContent|structured_content|isError|is_error' halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp/client.py shows only isError handling; there is no structuredContent handling anywhere in Halbert's mcp/ package, and no _meta stripping logic.
candidates.task_proposal: When Halbert's format_tool_result is next touched, add structuredContent-vs-content dedup and reserved-_meta-key stripping so a spec-compliant MCP server that emits both content and structuredContent (or namespaces vendor metadata under _meta) doesn't have its content doubled or its protocol plumbing leaked into the model-facing payload.

candidates.title: Persistent tool-schema cache enabling lazy MCP server startup (no stdio spawn at idle boot)

origin_paths.what: Per-server JSON cache (0o600, atomic write) keyed by server name + a sha256 fingerprint of the connection-defining config (command/args/url/transport/tools include-exclude filters). get_cached_entry respects an optional server-advertised ttl_ms (SEP-2549 tools/list hint) so a stale manifest expires; write-through skips a rewrite when byte-identical to avoid needless disk churn.

_resolve_server_lazy / _ensure_lazy_server_connected / _register_lazy_from_cache: register a server's tools into the agent snapshot straight from the cached manifest WITHOUT spawning the stdio child; the real subprocess only launches on first actual tool CALL (or cache miss/fingerprint mismatch).

candidates.mechanism: Startup cost for a stdio MCP server (10-60s per Hermes's own comment) is decoupled from tool-list visibility: the agent can see and offer a server's tools from disk the instant the process boots, and only pays the real connect cost lazily, at first use.
candidates.why_solid: Read the full cache module and the lazy-registration call sites' docstrings describing the exact idle-dashboard-startup problem this solves.
candidates.halbert_evidence: grep -rln 'schema_cache|lazy.*start|fingerprint' halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp found nothing; halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp/bridge.py's discover_and_register always performs a live connect+list_tools for every configured server (no disk-cached-manifest fast path).
candidates.task_proposal: Add a fingerprinted, TTL-aware on-disk tool-schema cache under halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp/ so Halbert's dashboard boot (and any CLI-only session) can register MCP tools without cold-spawning every configured stdio server; real connection happens lazily on first actual tools/call. Directly reduces dashboard startup latency, which matters for a locally-run, frequently-restarted host-steward app.

candidates.title: Rapid-drop reconnect budget gated on demonstrated session health ('session_proven')

origin_paths.what: _session_proven flag on MCPServerTask: a freshly (re)established session is UNPROVEN until it survives a full keepalive interval OR serves one successful tool call; only a PROVEN session clears the reconnect-retry budget. Comment: 'a transport that flaps right after the handshake keeps getting charged and still reaches the park instead of hot-cycling respawns forever.'

_mark_session_proven: called from both the keepalive-success path and the tool-call-success path; resets _reconnect_retries, clears the one-time permanent-failure grace and the was_parked/teardown_race bookkeeping.

candidates.mechanism: A naive reconnect-retry counter that resets on 'session established' is exploitable by a server that handshakes successfully and then immediately drops — it looks healthy at the instant of reset and the budget never actually charges. Requiring a REAL health signal (one full keepalive cycle or a real tool call) before clearing the budget closes that gap.
candidates.why_solid: Read the full state machine including the specific hot-cycling failure mode it is designed to prevent, cross-referenced against the referenced upstream issue number.
candidates.halbert_evidence: halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp/health.py's _probe_succeeded (health.py:395-407) resets record.reconnect_attempts=0 immediately upon ANY successful ping/probe response — there is no intermediate 'proven' gate requiring the connection to survive an interval or serve a real call before the budget resets, so a server that answers one ping and then drops repeatedly would reset its backoff on every cycle.
candidates.task_proposal: In halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp/health.py's ServerHealth/MCPHealthMonitor, add a 'proven' bit that only clears reconnect_attempts after the connection survives a full probe interval past the initial handshake (or serves a real tool call), rather than resetting on the handshake/first-ping success alone — closing the hot-cycling gap for a flapping MCP server.

candidates.title: Fail-fast on a dead stdio child by racing the RPC against a liveness watcher

origin_paths.what: _call_tool_racing_stdio_death: pre-call check (a dead child must not hold a call slot for the FULL timeout) plus a mid-call race between the actual session.call_tool coroutine and _watch_stdio_children (polls psutil.pid_exists every 0.25s) via asyncio.wait(FIRST_COMPLETED) — whichever finishes first wins; a dead-child win cancels the RPC and raises _StdioChildExited, which the handler layer turns into a bounded respawn-and-retry-once instead of the caller waiting out the full tool_timeout on a transport nobody will ever answer.

candidates.mechanism: Distinguishes 'the server is slow' from 'the server's process is provably gone' using OS-level PID liveness, so a dead child fails a call in ~0.25s instead of the full configured timeout (which can be tens of seconds).
candidates.why_solid: Read the full racing implementation including the psutil-based liveness poll and the pre-call fast-path check.
candidates.halbert_evidence: halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp/client.py has no PID-liveness tracking or watcher; a call to a server whose stdio child died would only fail when the request's own timeout elapses or the reader task observes stdout EOF, whichever the transport's read loop notices first — no fast-fail race is implemented.
candidates.task_proposal: Track the stdio child's PID in StdioTransport and, in call/request, race the RPC against a lightweight psutil.pid_exists poll so a dead subprocess fails fast (sub-second) instead of waiting out the full per-call timeout — most valuable for Halbert's terminal/execute_code-adjacent flows where a hung tool call blocks a turn.

candidates.title: Cross-process advisory file lock around MCP discovery

origin_paths.what: _acquire_discovery_lock_with_retry: a lock loser waits (bounded retries × delay) for the holder then discovers itself locally; unavailable locking or an expired wait runs UNGUARDED (fail-soft, never blocks discovery entirely). Comment cites issue #62771: without it, gateway + CLI + TUI processes running concurrently would all spawn the same stdio servers, destabilizing the healthy ones.

candidates.mechanism: An advisory (not mandatory) file lock so multiple OS processes belonging to the same Hermes installation don't independently spawn duplicate copies of the same stdio MCP server.
candidates.why_solid: Read the acquire-with-retry function and its docstring referencing the specific restart-storm issue it fixes.
candidates.halbert_evidence: grep -rn 'flock|fcntl|filelock|FileLock' halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp found nothing; discover_and_register is called from three separate call sites (mcp/bridge.py, mcp/health.py, dashboard/routes/agent.py) with no cross-process coordination beyond in-process locks.
candidates.task_proposal: If Halbert's CLI, terminal channel, and dashboard backend can ever run as separate OS processes against the same mcp_config (worth confirming against Halbert's actual process topology first, since the 'one continuous conversation' design may keep everything in one process), add a bounded-retry advisory file lock around MCP server discovery/spawn to prevent duplicate stdio children.
candidates.constraint_conflicts: Only relevant if Halbert genuinely has multiple OS processes touching the same MCP config concurrently; verify process topology before prioritizing — may be moot if the dashboard backend is the sole owner.

candidates.title: Dashboard-mediated OAuth callback bridge for future MCP OAuth support

origin_paths.what: DashboardOAuthFlow: moves the two human/browser OAuth callbacks (authorization redirect + token exchange completion) from a local loopback-port listener into the already-authenticated desktop dashboard session, while the SDK still owns discovery, dynamic client registration, PKCE, state validation and the token exchange itself.

Central per-process OAuth state manager: cross-process token reload via mtime-based disk watch (tokens refreshed by a separate CLI invocation are picked up without restart), 401-deduplication (N concurrent 401s on the same access_token trigger exactly one recovery), reconnect signalling that MCPServerTask consumes.

candidates.mechanism: Rather than opening an ephemeral local HTTP listener to catch an OAuth provider's browser redirect (a real footgun on a shared/remote host, and awkward for a Tauri app), the dashboard's own already-open, already-authenticated session receives the callback and correlates it to a pending flow by a server-minted flow id.
candidates.why_solid: Read the module purpose/docstring and cross-referenced against the manager's mtime-based cross-process token-reload mechanism, which is a genuinely reusable detail independent of whether Halbert adopts the full dashboard-callback approach.
candidates.halbert_evidence: grep -rln 'oauth|OAuth' halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp found nothing at all; halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp/config.py has only a static resolve_token() (literal token or a named env var, config.py:180-200) — no OAuth flow, no dynamic client registration, no browser-callback handling of any kind exists for MCP servers today.
candidates.task_proposal: When/if Halbert needs to connect to a remote MCP server that requires OAuth (increasingly common for hosted MCP servers), route the browser-redirect callback through the Tauri dashboard's own session (avoiding a loopback port) rather than a standalone local listener, and use mtime-based token-file watching so a token refreshed by one Halbert entry point (CLI) is picked up by a long-running one (dashboard) without restart.
candidates.constraint_conflicts: Large feature (full OAuth client: PKCE, dynamic client registration, token storage) — only worth building when a specific remote MCP server actually requires it; not a standalone task today.

candidates.title: MCP sampling support (server-initiated LLM completion requests), trust-gated

origin_paths.what: SamplingHandler converts an MCP server's sampling/createMessage request (its own SamplingMessage objects, including tool-use/tool-result blocks) into OpenAI-shape chat messages so the CLIENT's configured model can answer it, then converts the reply back to the MCP result shape.

candidates.mechanism: MCP's sampling capability lets a connected server ask the CLIENT (not a server-side model) to run an LLM completion — useful for servers that need a bit of language understanding without shipping their own model/API key.
candidates.why_solid: Read the message-conversion functions (tool_use_id dual-spelling handling, content-part construction for text/image blocks) confirming this is a real, implemented protocol feature, not a stub.
candidates.halbert_evidence: grep -rn 'sampling|elicit|createMessage' halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp --include=*.py returned nothing — Halbert's MCP client implements no server-initiated request handling of any kind.
candidates.task_proposal: If a specific MCP server Halbert wants to use depends on sampling (uncommon but real), implement a client-side sampling/createMessage handler routed through Halbert's own model slot selection — gated the same way write-capable tools are (trust tier + consent), since a malicious server asking Halbert's own LLM to generate arbitrary content is itself a vector worth treating deliberately, not silently.
candidates.constraint_conflicts: Must never let sampling select or reveal a model name to the requesting server (founder rule: never bake/recommend model names on any surface) — the response content only, never provider/model identity, may cross this boundary.

candidates.title: Hidden-whitespace warning on MCP config values (tokens/URLs/headers)

origin_paths.what: _warn_hidden_whitespace flags leading/trailing whitespace in url, headers.*, and other config string values — a pasted bearer token with a trailing newline, or a URL with a leading space, otherwise surfaces as an opaque auth/connect failure. The secret VALUE itself is never logged, only the field path (e.g. 'headers.Authorization'), and the warning is deduplicated per (server, field).

candidates.mechanism: A tiny, cheap sanity check specifically for the class of config-entry bug that is invisible in a text editor (trailing/leading whitespace from copy-paste) and produces a confusing downstream symptom (401, connection refused) with no clue pointing back at the real cause.
candidates.why_solid: Read the test file directly (source module wasn't separately re-read but the test pins the exact behavior: which fields are checked, dedup, and the no-secret-in-log guarantee).
candidates.halbert_evidence: grep -n 'hidden.*whitespace|trailing.*newline' halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp/config.py found nothing; existing .strip() calls in config.py silently normalize name/transport/command/url fields with no warning, and MCPAuthConfig.resolve_token() (config.py:180-200) returns the token value as-is with no whitespace check at all.
candidates.task_proposal: Add a small hidden-whitespace check in halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp/config.py's MCP server entry loading (url, headers.*, auth.token) that logs a warning naming the field (never the value) when a string carries hidden leading/trailing whitespace — a cheap fix that turns an opaque auth failure into a one-line diagnosis.

candidates.title: MCP tool-description prompt-injection scanning (warn-only heuristic)

origin_paths.what: _MCP_INJECTION_PATTERNS: ten regex heuristics (ignore-previous-instructions, identity-override, system-prompt injection, role-tag injection, concealment instructions, network-command-in-description, base64-decode/eval/exec references, dangerous-module-import references) scanned against every tool description at registration; matches log a WARNING (server name, tool name, matched reasons, truncated description) but NEVER block registration — explicitly to avoid false-positive breakage of legitimate servers.

candidates.mechanism: An MCP tool's description text is attacker-controlled content that flows directly into the model's context (it's part of the tool schema the model sees on every turn); a server that has been compromised, or a malicious server, can embed prompt-injection payloads there. This is a detection/audit-trail control, not a blocking one.
candidates.why_solid: Read all ten patterns and the surrounding warn-only rationale.
candidates.halbert_evidence: grep -rln 'injection|prompt.*override' halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp --include=*.py found nothing (echo_guard.py, the one hit under security/, addresses a different problem — output echo-back, not inbound tool-description content).
candidates.task_proposal: Add a warn-only prompt-injection heuristic scan over MCP tool descriptions at registration time in halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp/registry.py or bridge.py, logging (never blocking) a match so a compromised or malicious MCP server's injection attempt leaves an audit trail instead of passing silently into every turn's context.

candidates.title: Agent-initiated MCP server install/enable/authorize proposal tool

origin_paths.what: setup_mcp_tool: an agent-callable TOOL (not a human-driven CLI/dashboard action) that asks the desktop GUI to show an inline install/enable/authorize card for a named MCP server, round-tripping through the gateway's blocking-prompt bridge; explicit distinct outcomes for 'unanswered' (renderer never responded — do not retry immediately) vs an explicit decline vs approval. Only enabled in the desktop_ui toolset for desktop-sourced sessions; elsewhere the agent is told to fall back to a terminal command.

anti_patterns.title: Server-side MCP approval-respond tool with no enforcement path (in-memory dict pop)
anti_patterns.evidence: mcp_serve.py:264-340 (EventBridge.respond_to_approval): pops an approval id from an in-memory _pending_approvals dict and enqueues an 'approval_resolved' event — there is no gateway IPC connecting this decision back to whatever originally asked for approval; the docstring itself says 'best-effort without gateway IPC'. This is the exact anti-pattern the prior OSS-REVIEW-HERMES-2026-09-07.md synthesis (line 88) already flagged: 'the approval-respond tool pops an in-memory dict with no enforcement path — do not copy'. Verified directly against the source in this pass.
anti_patterns.why_not: An MCP tool that LOOKS like it enforces an approval decision but has no wired enforcement path is worse than no tool at all — it gives external MCP clients (and any model reasoning about the tool's existence) false confidence that calling it actually gates something. Halbert's own MCP server (halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp/server.py, 18 tools) must never add an approval/consent tool whose backing store isn't actually consulted by the thing it claims to gate — every consent surface should route through the existing consent ledger, never a parallel in-memory structure.

anti_patterns.title: Vendor-hosted managed tool gateway passthrough (Nous-specific)

Not applicable and should not be adapted even in spirit.

HM09-tools-mcp.summary: HM09-tools-mcp is an exceptionally rich unit: Hermes's MCP client (tools/mcp_tool*.py, 22 files, ~7,300 lines) is a mature, incident-hardened subsystem covering discovery, a persistent tool-schema cache for lazy startup, a per-server circuit breaker + trust-tier/readOnlyHint approval gate, a shared parent-death supervisor process for orphan reaping, dual-gate config security scanning with a real post-incident IOC blocklist, an OSV malware preflight before spawning third-party packages, size-capped content rendering (text/image/audio/resource) with MEDIA-tag caching, and a rapid-drop reconnect budget gated on demonstrated health. Cross-checking each mechanism against Halbert's existing halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp/ (client.py 1120 lines, health.py 663, config.py 955, server.py 1879/18 tools, bridge.py, response.py) and tools/mcp_safety.py found Halbert has solid foundations (stdio+HTTP transports, pagination, per-server exponential reconnect backoff, ping-fallback keepalive, in-flight-call teardown failure, a config-driven risk classifier with fail-closed server-absence handling, and a redaction choke point on the SERVER side) but is missing nearly all of the client-side hardening layer Hermes has: no filtered stdio subprocess environment (the single highest-priority finding — Halbert forwards the ENTIRE parent os.environ to third-party MCP server subprocesses today), no config security scanner, no death supervisor / orphan reaping, no MCP-specific circuit breaker, no result size cap, no lazy-startup schema cache, no trust-tier/readOnlyHint approval gating, and no OAuth, sampling, or elicitation support at all (protocol features simply unimplemented). 18 concrete candidates were written up, ranked with the environment-leak fix (C4), the config security scanner (C5), and the death supervisor (C1) as the highest-priority, most self-contained wins; several protocol-feature and larger-scope items (OAuth, sampling, cross-process locking) are flagged lower-priority/scope-dependent pending founder direction on whether Halbert needs those specific server shapes. One anti-pattern (the server-side in-memory approval-respond tool with no enforcement path) was independently re-confirmed from source, matching the prior OSS-REVIEW-HERMES synthesis's existing flag.
