candidates.mechanism: A generic OIDC relying-party skeleton that: always layers PKCE regardless of client confidentiality, excludes symmetric-key JWT algorithms by design (not just by config), pins the OIDC discovery document's advertised issuer against the configured one to catch a wrong/malicious discovery response, and carefully distinguishes 'the identity provider is down' from 'this bearer isn't ours' so the two failure modes don't collapse into the same misleading error.
candidates.why_solid: If Halbert's dashboard is ever reachable beyond localhost (LAN access from another device), it will need SOME auth story; this skeleton's hardening choices (algorithm allowlist, issuer-pin, PKCE-always, distinct JWKS-down-vs-foreign-token errors) are worth having on file even though the full multi-provider OAuth abstraction is overkill for single-user single-host.
candidates.halbert_evidence: grep -rn 'dashboard_auth\|oauth\|OIDC' halbert_core/halbert_core/dashboard --include=*.py found nothing — Halbert's dashboard currently has no remote-auth surface at all.
candidates.task_proposal: If/when Halbert's dashboard needs to authenticate a session from a second device (not just localhost), build a minimal single-provider auth skeleton using the hardening choices at plugins/dashboard_auth/self_hosted/__init__.py: PKCE-always, HS256 excluded, issuer-pinned discovery, and a JWKS-down vs foreign-token error distinction.
candidates.constraint_conflicts: Halbert is single-user single-host; a full OAuth/OIDC flow is plausibly overkill unless remote-device access is an actual near-term requirement — flag to founder before building rather than assume.

verdict.notes: Origin verified and it is good code: plugins/dashboard_auth/self_hosted/__init__.py:1-8 (PKCE S256 always, client_secret layered on top and 'never replacing it'), :45-48 _ALLOWED_ID_TOKEN_ALGS with the stated reason HS256 is excluded, :58-60 _require_https_or_loopback, :211-215 the discovery issuer pin rejecting a document advertising a different issuer with only a trailing-slash tolerance, :233-236 verify with iss/aud pinned; _shared.py:192-229 verify_jwt distinguishing ProviderError (unreachable JWKS, 503) from InvalidCodeError (foreign/opaque bearer, try next provider) with #94558 cited. But the reader's central Halbert claim is FALSE. dashboard/auth.py (512 lines) is a 'one door' boundary: :22-33 three credentials in order (Bearer for peers/CLI/MCP, X-Halbert-Token for the cross-origin Tauri webview, halbert_session cookie after redeeming an HMAC ticket), :64-70 a deliberately tiny PUBLIC_PATHS set policed by tests/test_route_auth_census.py, plus a Host allowlist middleware, and dashboard/app.py:1042-1053 wires it so a route added tomorrow with no auth dependency is protected by omission; its docstring at :5-9 explicitly rejects loopback as an authorization boundary. The stated need (a second device) is already met without an external identity provider, and adding an OIDC relying party would introduce a separate identity authority to a single-user single-host machine that identifies as the host - the one multi-tenant assumption here that does not degenerate cleanly. Not a lift; record the four hardening choices as review criteria if remote auth is ever revisited.

candidates.title: Silence expected liveness-probe error tracebacks without hiding real errors

origin_paths.what: _BENIGN_PROBE_METHODS = {ping, health, healthcheck}; _BenignProbeMethodFilter: the JSON-RPC router correctly answers -32601 method_not_found for these (clients treat that as 'agent alive'), but a background dispatcher task ALSO logs a full traceback per probe — the filter suppresses ONLY that specific (method_not_found, benign-method) combination, every other background-task error (including method_not_found for a non-probe method) stays visible

candidates.mechanism: A narrowly-scoped logging.Filter that inspects both the log record's message AND its actual exception payload (not just a string match) before suppressing — so a liveness-probe client polling an unsupported diagnostic method every few seconds doesn't spam the log with tracebacks for entirely expected, harmless behavior, while a genuine unknown-method error (a real bug) still surfaces.
candidates.why_solid: Small, immediately-applicable logging-hygiene detail: any Halbert surface that gets periodically polled (MCP server health checks, the scheduler's own heartbeat, the dashboard's status poll) likely has or will have this exact noise problem; the fix pattern (match on the SPECIFIC exception's structured data, not a blanket method-name string) avoids accidentally hiding a real error with the same name.
candidates.halbert_evidence: grep -rn 'BenignProbe\|method_not_found' halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp --include=*.py found nothing; unverified whether Halbert's MCP server currently logs tracebacks for expected liveness/health probe calls.
candidates.task_proposal: Check halbert_core/halbert_core/mcp/server.py and mcp/health.py for whether liveness/health-probe calls generate log-level tracebacks from a background dispatch path; if so, add a narrowly-scoped logging filter that inspects the actual exception payload (not a message substring) to suppress only that specific benign case, per acp_adapter/entry.py:31-53.

verdict.notes: Origin verified at acp_adapter/entry.py:31-56: _BENIGN_PROBE_METHODS = {ping, health, healthcheck}, and _BenignProbeMethodFilter.filter suppresses only a record whose message is exactly 'Background task failed' AND whose exc_info holds an acp RequestError with code -32601 AND whose data['method'] is one of the three - inspecting the structured exception payload, not a message substring, exactly as described. But the problem does not exist in Halbert, so there is nothing to port: mcp/server.py:1286-1287 answers ping directly ('return None if is_notification else self._success(req_id, {})'), :1289-1291 returns a -32601 error RESPONSE for any other unknown method rather than raising, and the only traceback path is the catch-all at :1294 on a genuine handler exception - exactly the case that should stay visible. mcp/health.py:1-48 shows the reverse direction too: Halbert's own monitor treats a JSON-RPC error answer to ping as HEALTHY. HM17-plugins-acp-providers.summary: HM17 covers a rich, largely NEW-to-Halbert area: Hermes has a mature plugin architecture (directory-based loader with careful sys.modules/relative-import handling, per-plugin storage/singleton utilities, a declared-capability+consent-hash registry, and a deprecated-import compat layer) plus a full Agent Client Protocol (ACP) adapter (permission bridging, edit-approval, session provenance, model catalog) that Halbert has none of today (confirmed absent via grep across halbert_core for plugin/ACP/capability-consent/disk-cleanup/achievement terms). The two strongest, most concrete lifts are the disk-cleanup ephemeral-file lifecycle plugin (C2 — a direct fit for Halbert's host-steward role, and a genuine gap next to the existing read-only DiskUsageScanner) and the security-guidance pattern-matched write-content warnings (C3 — a small, literally-attributable, immediately-composable addition next to Halbert's existing write_guard/provenance-recording _write_file). The declared-capability consent-hash registry (C1) is the best fit for Halbert's MCP third-party-server trust surface, which today has only risk-level classification (mcp/config.py) and no consent/re-consent tracking. Several ACP mechanisms (permission-ladder collapsing, ContextVar-scoped approval, conservative auto-approve-with-sensitive-override, additive bounded-walk provenance) are small, well-evidenced, low-risk hardening patterns rather than 'adopt ACP wholesale' proposals — ACP itself (editor integration) is plausibly out of scope for a host-steward vision and is reported as mechanism-only. Two features (gamified achievements, self-hosted dashboard OAuth) are flagged as plausible-but-optional and explicitly gated on founder confirmation given constraint tension (model-branding in the achievement catalog; whether Halbert's dashboard is truly staying localhost-only). Anti-patterns are dominated by one real constraint collision: Hermes's entire model-providers/ catalog and picker UX directly violates the 'never name/recommend models' directive and must not be copied as a user-facing surface, though the underlying per-provider-plugin ABC shape is fine as internal plumbing.

missed_by_reader.title: Tool-surface refresh is gated to a turn boundary (and to pre-first-turn) for prompt-cache and mid-turn-swap safety
missed_by_reader.lines: 444-496 (_schedule_mcp_late_refresh), with 405-441 (_register_session_mcp_servers) for the eager path
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Background MCP discovery that lands AFTER the agent was built is not allowed to mutate the agent's tool list whenever it finishes. The refresh runs on its own thread, waits up to 30s off the critical path, then refuses in four separate ways before touching anything: the session object must still be the same in-memory one (a get_session() would restore from DB and build a different agent, so it reads self.session_manager._sessions directly); it takes the session's runtime_lock, which prompt() flips is_running under before dispatching, explicitly 'to close the window where a refresh would swap tools= mid-turn'; it bails if is_running; and it bails if _user_turn_count or _api_call_count is greater than zero. The docstring states the reason in the code, not in a doc: 'Cache safety: only pre-first-turn (nothing cached yet); afterwards the snapshot stays frozen and late servers land via the between-turns prologue refresh.' A change to the advertised tool schemas is a change to the cached prompt prefix, so it may only happen at a turn boundary.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert has the refresh but not the boundary. halbert_core/mcp/health.py:359-372 piggybacks a full re-bridge onto the health sweep: when the mcp_config.yml identity changes, or after any server recovers, it sets _needs_refresh and then awaits bridge.discover_and_register(self._tool_executor, self._client) directly from the tick. That monitor is an asyncio task on the SAME loop as the agent (mcp/health.py:22-25 says so deliberately, for the client's per-loop lock rule), so it runs at any await point inside a live turn. mcp/bridge.py:49-60 confirms the refresh is diff-based and DROPS tools whose server the current config no longer names. Consequences to fix: (1) the tool list handed to the model can change between two API calls of one turn, churning the cached stable prefix the skills-catalog work was built to protect; (2) a tool can be deregistered after the model has already emitted a call for it, turning a config edit into a mid-turn unknown-tool failure. Task: give ToolExecutor (or the state machine) a turn-in-flight signal, have the health monitor defer a pending re-bridge to the next turn boundary instead of applying it inline, and pin it with a test that runs a sweep while a turn holds the loop and asserts the registered tool set is byte-identical until the turn ends. Cite acp_adapter/server.py:444-496 as the reference shape (guard on live object identity, the runtime lock, and the turn counters).

missed_by_reader.title: Per-entity cooldown on EVERY watched entity, plus an ignore list and a closed-by-default filter warning, on the Home Assistant event ingress
missed_by_reader.lines: 79-87 (watch_domains / watch_entities / ignore_entities / watch_all / cooldown_seconds default 30, _last_event_time), 108-114 (the explicit warning when no filter is configured), 216-243 (_passes_filters closed by default, then the per-entity cooldown applied before anything downstream sees the event)

Every entity that passes the filter is then subject to one uniform per-entity cooldown (self._last_event_time[entity_id], default 30s) applied BEFORE the event is rendered or forwarded, and a separate ignore_entities denylist beats the allowlist. missed_by_reader.title: Markdown fences sized to the content, so a preview containing backticks cannot break out of its code block on the approval dialog

missed_by_reader.title: Mid-session model-switch warning: the next turn will preflight-compress because the new window is smaller
missed_by_reader.mechanism: A guard that runs AFTER a successful model switch and, before the user sends anything, tells them what the switch just did to their conversation. It resolves the incoming model's real context length (resolve_display_context_length, honouring custom-provider declarations -- the comment at 70-71 records the bug where the hardcoded catalog said 131072 for a provider that declared 1M), estimates the live session's token count from the compressor's own protect_first_n/protect_last_n accounting or its last_prompt_tokens (22-47), computes the new auto-compress threshold as max(new_ctx * threshold_percent, MINIMUM_CONTEXT_LENGTH) (18-19), and only then appends a warning: 'Context window shrinks (old -> new). Session is ~N tokens; <model> allows M (auto-compress at ~T). Your next message will run preflight compression before the model replies' (104-112). It stays silent when the estimate is unavailable, when compression is disabled, and when compression has already proven ineffective twice (_ineffective_compression_count >= 2 at 101-102) -- so it warns about a consequence, never nags.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert has the sharper half of this already and none of the user-facing half. model/client.py:731-751 computes num_ctx per call and, when the prompt exceeds it, logs 'Prompt for {model} is ~{prompt_tokens} tokens but num_ctx={num_ctx}; Ollama will truncate the head of the prompt' -- to the LOG, at call time, after the operator has already sent the message. In a product whose whole design is one continuous conversation with hidden topic threads, repointing the chat slot to a smaller-window model is exactly the action that silently costs conversation head. Add a deterministic post-save check on the endpoint/model save path (dashboard endpoint-save route + packages/model-picker save flow) that compares the outgoing slot's effective window against the incoming one using the existing architecture_context_length()/_MODEL_MAX_CACHE machinery, estimates the live thread's token count, and returns a plain statement of consequence for the picker to render. No LLM, no new probe -- it reuses numbers Halbert already computes. Suppress it when the numbers are unknown rather than guessing.

missed_by_reader.title: Route-keyed, fail-closed invalidation of a cached context-length verdict when the endpoint changes
missed_by_reader.mechanism: normalize_route_base_url (9-44) canonicalizes ONLY provably-equivalent URL components -- lowercase scheme and host, IPv6 zone-id preserved, default ports 80/443 dropped but any other port kept, one trailing slash removed unless a query delimiter was present, userinfo preserved, and any control character or unparseable URL returns the raw string untouched rather than a guess. should_clear_context_pin (47-59) then answers 'does this configured context_length pin still describe the route that is actually in force?' and its docstring states the posture: 'Fail-closed: any error during route comparison returns True (drop the pin) so a stale window never silently inflates the compression threshold.' should_clear_context_pin_async (62-67) runs it off the event loop because the resolution chain, though cache-only, can still do cold-start disk I/O.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert's equivalent cache is keyed by MODEL NAME ALONE and is monotonic. model/client.py:909-912 (remember_model_context_limit) writes _MODEL_MAX_CACHE[model] = limit only when the new limit is larger, and the surrounding comment argues the case: understating a window truncates, so a producer may only ever raise it. That is correct reasoning for one route and wrong across routes -- the same model name served by a local daemon at one window and by a saved remote OpenAI-compatible endpoint advertising a much larger one collapses into a single process-lifetime maximum, and the larger value wins permanently for both. Change the cache key from model to (provider, normalized_base_url, model), reusing a normalize_route_base_url-equivalent so http://localhost:11434 and http://localhost:11434/ do not become two entries, and keep the monotonic-raise rule WITHIN a key. This is a small, self-contained fix to a module Halbert already reasons about carefully; it needs no new probe and no config.

missed_by_reader.title: Credential headers are stripped when a model-endpoint request redirects cross-origin
missed_by_reader.mechanism: SafeCredentialRedirectHandler (41-61) subclasses urllib's redirect handler, lets urllib settle status/method semantics first, then compares url_origin(new) against the origin the request started at and, on any mismatch, strips every header not in a tiny allowlist (_CROSS_ORIGIN_SAFE_HEADERS = {'accept','user-agent'} at 20). The comment at 19-20 gives the reason an allowlist is used rather than a denylist of known credential header names: 'custom provider headers routinely carry credentials under arbitrary names'. _CrossOriginRequestSanitizer (64-80) is a second handler pinned with handler_order = float('inf') so that an installed cookie/auth/instrumentation processor running after the redirect handler cannot re-add a secret to the sanitized Request. url_origin (25-32) deliberately lets a malformed port raise ValueError -- 'let that fail the request closed instead of collapsing it to a default'.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert calls operator-configured model endpoints with a bearer credential and follows redirects with library defaults: model/client.py:526-528 builds headers['Authorization'] = f'Bearer {api_key}' and posts at 534/575/668 via requests, with no session, no allow_redirects=False and no redirect policy anywhere in halbert_core (grep for allow_redirects finds only rag/ingestion.py:254 and federation/connectivity.py:127). requests happens to strip the literal 'Authorization' header on a cross-HOST redirect, which covers today's shape by luck rather than by design -- it does not strip a same-host scheme downgrade in every version, and it strips nothing if C14's per-endpoint extraHeaders ever lands. Route every credentialed model call through one shared requests.Session configured with the endpoint's origin, and either set allow_redirects=False for model API calls (a model endpoint that redirects is a misconfiguration worth surfacing, not following) or add an explicit origin check that drops all non-allowlisted headers. Make this a prerequisite of C14 rather than a follow-up.

missed_by_reader.title: LM Studio loaded-state and real runtime context come from /api/v1/models loaded_instances, not the OpenAI-compat /v1/models list
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Hermes reads LM Studio through its own REST API (_lmstudio_server_root 360-365, _lmstudio_fetch_raw_models 373), whose per-model entry carries max_context_length and a loaded_instances array. _lmstudio_loaded_context (471-483) walks loaded_instances[*].config.context_length and returns the first positive value -- the window the model is ACTUALLY loaded with, as opposed to what it could hold. ensure_lmstudio_model_loaded (484-520+) uses that to make load-on-demand safe: 'Existing loaded-instance context is authoritative. Cold loads omit context_length unless the caller supplied an explicit override; the returned context comes from LM Studio's echoed or refreshed state', it rejects an explicit target above max_context_length (517-518) rather than silently clamping, and it returns a typed LMStudioLoadResult distinguishing 'not loaded', 'load attempted' and 'rejected'.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert's loaded-model check for OpenAI-compatible providers is wrong for LM Studio, which the model picker lists as a supported provider. model/client.py:1466-1474: for provider == 'openai' it GETs f'{endpoint}/v1/models' and maps every entry to a name, and is_model_loaded (1487-1497) then reports True for anything in that list. LM Studio's /v1/models enumerates AVAILABLE models, not loaded ones, so is_model_loaded() is effectively 'is this model installed' for every LM Studio endpoint -- and any surface that says 'the model is loaded' on the strength of it is stating something Halbert did not measure, which is squarely against the grounded-in-measured-data posture. Two things: (1) probe LM Studio's native /api/v1/models and read loaded_instances for the loaded verdict, falling back to 'unknown' rather than True when the endpoint does not answer it; (2) feed loaded_instances[*].config.context_length into the context-length ladder as a stronger signal than a listing (it is the loaded window, exactly the distinction client.py:915-935's remember_listing_context_length docstring says a listing cannot make). That request also currently sends no Authorization header, so a credentialed OpenAI-compatible endpoint 401s silently into an empty list.

missed_by_reader.mechanism: _directory_links (11-13) collects every symlinked component along the path, parents first. _ensure_directory (15-41) then checks each link resolves to a real directory BEFORE any mkdir, with the comment stating the whole point: 'Never materialize a missing mount's target on the underlying disk' (22). If a link's target is unavailable it raises HomeInitializationError -- a distinct exception type from an invalid-YAML error (7-8) -- carrying the link chain and an explicit promise: 'Hermes has not replaced the link or created its missing target' (39). It also declines to chmod through a link: 'The operator owns permissions beyond a link' (30-32).
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert has symlink awareness where it writes single files (config/being_config.py:861 resolves a symlinked config path before writing; persona/store.py:113,157 handles a symlinked being.yml and an atomic tmp_link) but nothing equivalent for DIRECTORY creation, and grep finds no mkdir(parents=True) guard in utils/paths.py or model/config_locator.py. This is not hypothetical for this product: Halbert identifies as the host and this very repo lives on an external volume (/Volumes/4TB-BAD). If a config or data home is a symlink into an unmounted external disk, a plain mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) creates an empty stub on the internal disk, the assistant starts with a blank memory/config and reports itself healthy, and the real data reappears as a divergent tree the next time the volume mounts. Add a pre-flight in the path helper that walks link components, refuses to create through an unavailable one, and raises a typed error naming the link chain -- explicitly without deleting or replacing anything, which also satisfies the 'leave old data unread, never delete' directive.

missed_by_reader.title: Provider credentials are scrubbed from the environment of any shell command the agent or user runs
missed_by_reader.mechanism: _bang_env (89-99) does not hand os.environ to the child. Its docstring states the threat model plainly: 'The CLI process holds every provider API key; a user-typed command may still run a third-party script, so reuse the sanitizer quick_commands and the local terminal backend use' -- it calls tools.environments.local.build_subprocess_env(), annotated as '== _sanitize_subprocess_env(os.environ.copy())', and only falls back to a raw copy when the tools package is unimportable. The sanitized mapping is then passed explicitly as env= at the Popen site (120). The same sanitizer is shared with the agent's own terminal path, so the human shortcut and the model's tool calls get the identical environment, not two policies.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert passes the parent environment straight through. tools/system_tools.py:157-162 calls subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout) with no env= argument, so the child inherits os.environ from a process that holds saved-endpoint credentials; grep across halbert_core/tools and halbert_core/streaming finds no os.environ.copy(), no env= and no sanitizer anywhere. Every subprocess Halbert spawns -- system_tools.py, accelerator_tools.py, gpu_tools.py, schedule_cron.py, and anything reached through execute_code's RPC host -- therefore exports whatever the parent holds to arbitrary local tooling. Add one build_subprocess_env() in halbert_core/tools/ that strips credential-shaped names (reuse C13's _CREDENTIAL_SUFFIXES-style suffix list, plus the concrete names models.yml loads into the environment) and make it the only way a subprocess environment is constructed, with a test asserting no spawn site passes the bare environment. This is Tier-2 secrets posture applied at the process boundary rather than only at the response choke point, it is deterministic, and it is independent of whether C17's bang-shell affordance is ever built.

origin_paths.what: extract_user_instruction_from_skill_message strips the injected skill-scaffolding markers off a slash-command-expanded message so memory/telemetry providers store what the user actually asked, not the full injected skill body; the docstring notes the markers 'MUST stay byte-identical to the builders'

candidates.mechanism: When a user's short slash-command invocation gets expanded into a large message embedding an entire skill body before it reaches the model, a paired extraction function (using stable, byte-identical marker strings) recovers just the human's original instruction so anything downstream that records 'what the user said' (memory writes, transcripts, telemetry) doesn't capture the injected scaffolding instead.

candidates.task_proposal: If/when Halbert adds an explicit slash-invoked skill message that embeds full skill content into the conversation, ship a paired extraction function (with byte-stable markers) from day one so memory writes and turn-event telemetry record the user's actual instruction, not the injected skill body.

Dropped: Halbert's slash channel resolves /<name> to a skill (intake/pipeline.py:32-65) and the text is composed into the system prompt (skills/composer.py:119), never scaffolded into the user's message — there is no injected body for memory to mistake for the user's words.

anti_patterns.title: Inline `!`cmd`` shell expansion during SKILL.md preprocessing
anti_patterns.evidence: agent/skill_preprocessing.py:1-2,44,80-89 — !`command` snippets embedded in a SKILL.md are executed via subprocess.run(['bash','-c', command]) and their stdout is spliced into the model-facing message; the docstring itself names this 'prompt-to-RCE' territory (matches the already-recorded OSS-REVIEW-HERMES anti-pattern #4). Off by default (skills_cfg.get('inline_shell', False)) but present and enable-able.
anti_patterns.why_not: Any untrusted or externally-sourced skill (hub-installed, org-shared, or one an LLM curator wrote) that reaches this preprocessing path with inline_shell on gets arbitrary shell execution merely by being loaded/viewed — a content-injection-to-code-execution path with no gate of its own beyond the single config flag. Halbert's own directive is deterministic policy everywhere; this feature has none. Do not add an equivalent to Halbert's skill preprocessing, template-variable substitution only.

anti_patterns.title: Cross-account/cross-device 'org sync' as a git-like push/pull/merge system gated by a cloud admin JWT claim
anti_patterns.evidence: tools/skills_sync_client.py:1-9,29-31 — resolve_identity() decodes an unverified JWT to check a 'tool_gateway_admin' claim before any sync operation is even attempted; the whole subsystem (content-addressed object push, ref CAS, three-way merge) exists to synchronize skills across a Nous account's devices/org.
anti_patterns.why_not: This entire feature assumes a cloud account and multi-device/org identity model that directly conflicts with Halbert's standing constraints: single-user single-host, no cloud account system, and 'Halbert identifies as the host machine' (identity is per-machine, not fused across a user's fleet via a remote service). The underlying git-like sync primitives (push objects, CAS a ref, three-way merge) are reusable ideas in the abstract, but the feature as built should not be lifted wholesale — any future Halbert cross-machine sync would need its own design starting from the single-user constraint, not this org/account-gated shape.

anti_patterns.title: Hand-maintained 'PLUGIN-COMPAT' re-export shims scattered across every decomposed module
anti_patterns.evidence: tools/skills_hub.py:281-330, tools/skills_guard.py:639-647, tools/skillevaluator_scan.py:143-150 — each carries a 'BEGIN/END PLUGIN-COMPAT (revert-scheduled; see COMPAT_MANIFEST.md)' block re-exporting names external plugins used before a module was split up, enforced only by a CI script (scripts/check_compat_pointers.py) that fails if internal code imports from the shim.
anti_patterns.why_not: This is organizational debt from a large module-decomposition migration under an external-plugin-API compatibility promise Halbert does not have (Halbert has no third-party plugin ecosystem depending on its internal module layout). Copying the pattern would be solving a problem Halbert doesn't have; if Halbert ever splits a large module, a clean import-path change (with call sites updated) is preferable to a permanent compatibility shim with its own CI enforcement machinery.

HM10-tools-skills-second-pass.summary: This is a rich, previously-untouched unit: Halbert has SK-1/SK-2 (skill format/parser/provenance-sidecar/catalog/telemetry-vocabulary — the READ side of skills) but literally nothing on the WRITE/install/curate side this unit covers — no skill install tool, no hub/trust concept, no content scanner, no delete/edit tool, no mutation ledger, no lifecycle store, no readiness status, and no dashboard skills UI. Hermes's tools/skills_hub_*.py + skills_guard.py + skill_manager_*.py + skill_ledger.py + skill_usage.py family is a mature, incident-hardened reference implementation for almost that entire missing surface, each mechanism carrying a specific cited bug (#75983 category-bucket wipe, #67140 ownership-guard race, #29912 fail-open consolidation delete, #48974 project-skill injection, Kilo Code #11227 rmtree-to-cwd) rather than generic caution. The single most actionable finding is C16: Halbert's own loader.py already discovered and partially patched (daemon-only) the exact project-local-skill-injection risk Hermes defends against with a full trust-gate+scan+quarantine system — the CLI/test code path is still open. C12 (skill lifecycle store) and C15 (generic write-approval gate) are the next-most-actionable: both are direct continuations of work Halbert has already designed for (telemetry.py's unemitted lifecycle events; the standing 'commands are staged, never executed' directive currently implemented only for the terminal). Two anti-patterns are worth flagging explicitly: inline shell expansion in skill preprocessing (prompt-to-RCE, matches the already-recorded OpenClaw/Hermes review finding) and the cloud-account-gated cross-device org-sync system, which structurally conflicts with Halbert's single-user-single-host identity model and should not be lifted as a whole feature even though its underlying push/pull/merge primitives are individually reusable ideas.

missed_by_reader.lines: 1-24 (the three pipeline properties that drive the design, incl. 'Reads are chunked, not message-framed... A CSI escape, a UTF-8 code point, and a long blank-line run can each straddle a frame boundary, so all three need trailing-state buffering to survive reassembly'), 26-47 (BLANK_LINE_BURST, ERASE_LINE, ERASE_CHAR, PARTIAL_ESC, TRAILING_NEWLINES), 65-120 (class PtyResumeSanitizer: #pending holds a trailing partial escape or newline run across frames; endEraseSuppression() bounds erase-stripping to the replay window; the drain comment notes that emitting a buffered partial escape 'would leave xterm's parser in an "in-escape" state that swallows subsequent output after reconnect')
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Hermes's PTY bridge forwards each os.read(fd, 65536) as its own WebSocket frame, so nothing guarantees a frame ends on a token boundary. The sanitizer holds back a trailing incomplete CSI sequence and a trailing newline run until the next frame arrives, applies filters only to the safely-completed prefix, and drops (never emits) a buffered partial escape at end of stream. Separately it bounds erase-code suppression to a short post-connect window because ESC[K/ESC[X are pathological only during replay and legitimate afterwards. Halbert has the identical pipeline shape and none of the buffering: dashboard/routes/websocket.py:104-108 does `chunk.decode('utf-8', errors='replace')` on each chunk independently inside pump_stdout, so a multi-byte code point split across a read boundary is permanently corrupted into replacement characters before it ever reaches the client — a live bug on any non-ASCII terminal output large enough to be split, not merely a replay concern. HM13-state-root-files.summary: Rich unit with many independently-liftable storage-layer safety mechanisms beyond what earlier OpenClaw waves covered. Strongest concrete gaps: Halbert has NO conversation export/import/backup path (C5); its test-isolation guard against writing to the real audit ledger is env-only, missing the process-ancestry backstop Hermes added after a documented production incident (C7); the dashboard/scheduler have no startup-deadlock watchdog, only a different parent-liveness one (C9); Halbert has zero timezone concept despite a scheduler/heartbeat/morning-brief workstream needing 'every morning at 7' to mean the founder's local time (C11); four+ independent SqliteConversationStore instantiation sites share no connection/fd budget, the precondition for an EMFILE-class bug (C6); and no VACUUM/auto-maintenance exists anywhere on a store that only grows (C8). Two user-facing feature candidates: edit-a-message-and-regenerate (C4) and conversation portability (C5). Anti-patterns are clearly bounded: visible session-list UX, multi-profile/multi-backend gateway routing, and Windows shims should not be lifted wholesale, though their underlying techniques generalize cleanly to Halbert's single-user, hidden-thread architecture.

missed_by_reader.title: PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL RETURNS the resulting mode — a silent refusal leaves the store in rollback-journal mode and nothing notices
missed_by_reader.lines: 173-235 (apply_wal_with_fallback + _enable_wal), 22-28 (_WAL_INCOMPAT_MARKERS), 52-75 (_on_disk_journal_mode)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Hermes treats the ROW returned by `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` as the only truth about the mode in force: hermes_state_wal.py:232-235 says it outright — 'PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL RETURNS the resulting mode: macOS NFS, SMB/CIFS and the AgentFS overlay refuse WITHOUT raising. Trust the row, not the absence of an exception.' Around it sit three rules an exception-only approach cannot express: (1) _WAL_INCOMPAT_MARKERS at :27 enumerates the filesystems that DO raise ('locking protocol' on NFS/SMB/some FUSE/WSL1, 'not authorized' on some FUSE, 'disk i/o error' where ZFS corrupts -shm under concurrent COW+mmap bursts) so the fallback is a classified decision, not a bare except; (2) a hard never-live-downgrade invariant (:184-187, again at :204-210) — if the on-disk header reports WAL, or cannot be read, the mode is left alone, because other processes may hold uncheckpointed commits a downgrade would destroy; (3) _on_disk_journal_mode (:52-75) is a read-only probe that retries a transient 'disk i/o error' up to four times and returns None (fail-closed, 'refuse to downgrade') when undeterminable. One function serves every database the process opens, taking a db_label so the ERROR logs once per process per file rather than once per connection.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert enables WAL in two places and reads the result in neither. agents/conversation_sqlite.py:546-548 is `try: cur.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL") except Exception as e: logger.warning(...)` — its own comment (:540-545) accepts running 'in the connection's default rollback-journal mode' on failure, but a silent refusal is invisible: the warning never fires and the store believes it has WAL. continuity/state_store.py:311-312 is worse — a bare `conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")` with no try, no row read, while the ledger's durability story (secure_delete + _checkpoint_or_raise at :682-693) assumes WAL is on. missed_by_reader.title: Refcounted shared-store registry with generation-aware retirement — the real lift behind the read-pool candidate
missed_by_reader.lines: 1-29 (module contract), 47-64 (_TeardownBarrier), 184-215 (acquire)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: hermes_state_registry.py:1-8 names the failure this module prevents, and it is not descriptor exhaustion: 'Each bare SessionDB() mints its own writer connection, lock, close-time WAL checkpoint and token writer thread, and one connection's close-time checkpoint can race another's growth (lost/reordered-page-write corruption).' The contract at :9-28 is the liftable part: acquire(path) hands back the CURRENT generation and bumps a refcount; close() on a shared instance RELEASES a reference rather than tearing the connection down, so legacy call sites cannot leak or double-close; release() is object-keyed (id(db)) so an inode replacement cannot strand a still-owned generation; on inode change (snapshot restore, recovery swap) the old generation is RETIRED — never lent again — but stays alive until its holders release (implementation at :198-208); all teardown runs OUTSIDE the registry lock so one file's checkpoint cannot stall acquisition for every other; and _TeardownBarrier (:47-64) COUNTS admitted-but-unfinished closes per path and is lifted only by the last to settle, because 'Signalling on the first lets close_all() return and acquire() publish a replacement while an older handle is still inside PRAGMA wal_checkpoint/sidecar unlink.'
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert mints conversation stores ad hoc: agents/threads.py:1235-1265 _create_conversation_store() constructs a fresh SqliteConversationStore(_cs._DEFAULT_DB) on both fallback paths with no memoisation; dashboard/routes/guest.py:647 constructs another; dashboard/routes/conversations.py:73 caches a module-level singleton (a third independent connection to the same file). agents/conversation_sqlite.py:469-483 gives each its own sqlite3.connect + threading.Lock, and close() at :3206-3212 just conn.close()s. Task (the small version worth doing): give conversation_sqlite.py a module-level acquire(path)/release(store) returning one refcounted shared store per resolved path, and route threads.py:1256/1265, guest.py:647 and conversations.py:73 through it, so there is exactly one writer connection and one lock per database file in the process. This supersedes candidate C6 — the fd budget solves a problem Halbert does not have; this solves the one it does.

missed_by_reader.title: close() cancels every POSIX advisory lock on a file — never open/read/close a live SQLite database, pread from a cached fd instead
missed_by_reader.lines: 33-42 (rationale comment + fd caches), 45-77 (_pread_db_header), 152-166 (_connect_tracked_db), 168-196 (is_zeroed_state_db's live-connection gate)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: hermes_state_dbfile.py:33-38 states the hazard precisely: 'A bare open()/read()/close() there is the howtocorrupt §2.2 bug: close() cancels every POSIX advisory lock this process holds on the file, dropping the writer's WAL-mode DMS shared lock so another process can treat this writer as dead and rerun WAL-index recovery underneath it.' The fix is three-part and each part is non-obvious: (1) _pread_db_header (:45-77) preads from a per-path fd cached for the life of the process, since OPENING never cancels locks — only closing does; (2) when the path is re-pointed at a new inode the stale fd is RETIRED into a list that is 'intentionally never closed' (:41), because closing it would cancel the live connection's locks; (3) _connect_tracked_db (:152-166) registers every open fd so byte-level probes of a live file are REFUSED, and the only tolerated fallback is the tracking helper being absent — 'a silent untracked retry would disable the guard for that connection.' is_zeroed_state_db (:168-196) consumes that registry: it returns False once a connection is live and takes force=True only for offline files. Windows is explicitly exempted (:47-52) because advisory-lock cancellation is POSIX-only.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert has no raw byte probe of a live database today (the read_bytes() hits are crypto/storage.py:177, skills/sidecar.py:66, skills/parser.py:618 — none a SQLite file), so there is no bug to fix. This is a RULE to record before the work that would introduce it: any corruption check, zeroed-file detection, backup, fingerprinting (candidate C14 proposes exactly a size+partial-hash fingerprint of a damaged file) or 'how big is the DB' report must never open()/read()/close() a database this process holds open — use PRAGMA page_count*page_size over the existing connection for size (see C8), and a cached-fd pread for header bytes. Task: write it as a one-paragraph invariant in the store-hardening section of the design doc and as a comment at the top of agents/conversation_sqlite.py and continuity/state_store.py, so the next person adding a health check does not reach for Path.read_bytes(). Cheap, and it prevents a corruption class that is essentially undiagnosable after the fact.

missed_by_reader.title: Title sanitisation against invisible/bidi/object-replacement code points and lone surrogates — Halbert fences brackets but not glyphs
missed_by_reader.lines: 17-21 (_TITLE_CONTROL_RE / _TITLE_INVISIBLE_RE), 33-45 (sanitize_title), 26-32 (_title_rank)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: sanitize_title (hermes_state_titles.py:33-45) runs three passes before a title is stored: _sanitize_surrogates strips lone surrogates 'sqlite3 cannot bind' — i.e. a title that would otherwise raise on INSERT; _TITLE_CONTROL_RE (:18) strips ASCII controls while deliberately KEEPING \t\n\r for the whitespace collapse that follows; _TITLE_INVISIBLE_RE (:19) strips zero-width (U+200B-200F), the bidi override block (U+2028-202E), isolates (U+2060-2069), BOM, object-replacement (U+FFFC) and interlinear annotation (U+FFF9-FFFB). Whitespace then collapses, empty normalises to None, and over MAX_TITLE_LENGTH raises ValueError rather than truncating. Separately _title_rank (:26-32) encodes a provenance rule worth noting: a NULL title_source from before provenance existed ranks as USER, because it is indistinguishable from a manual /title of that era — so an auto-titler can never silently overwrite it.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert's title defence is real but aimed at a different threat. agents/threads.py:105-170 _fence() neutralises the bracketed-system-row delimiters — substituting [ and ] with fullwidth lookalikes (deliberately substituting, not deleting, because deleting a bracket silently rewrites a shell command quoted out of a receipt), collapsing </continuity> tags to a fixpoint, flattening whitespace and capping at PREV_TITLE_MAX=120. That is prompt-injection hardening. It does nothing about zero-width or bidi-override characters, and grep for 'surrogate' over halbert_core/halbert_core returns nothing. Two consequences: (a) a thread title containing U+202E renders reversed in the dashboard's node-list rail and in any spoken surface, a display-integrity problem for an assistant whose titles are model-generated from user text (threads.py:605 new_thread(title, ...) takes the model's own argument); (b) a lone surrogate in a title raises on the sqlite3 bind rather than being cleaned. Task: extend _fence (or add a sibling sanitize_title used by new_thread and the title-refinement path) with the two character-class regexes plus surrogate stripping, leaving the existing bracket substitution unchanged. Small, deterministic, no new surface.

candidates.title: Process (pid, create_time) incarnation identity to avoid PID-reuse bugs when reaping/relaunching

origin_paths.what: REAPABLE_PURPOSES frozenset explicitly excludes interactive processes (chat/REPLs) from anything a reaper is allowed to kill — only serve/dashboard/gateway/mcp-helper purposes qualify

SpawnTag dataclass + build_spawn_tag(): a colon-delimited env-var value (version:install_id:purpose:spawner_pid:spawner_create_time) stamped by the spawner into a child's env, letting any later reaper positively identify lineage instead of guessing from PPID or cmdline text matching

candidates.mechanism: Because OS PIDs get reused, any long-lived reaper/supervisor logic that identifies a process by bare PID is subject to a (rare but real) false-positive: killing or relaunching an unrelated process that happens to have inherited the same PID number. HM14-cli-ops-lifecycle.summary: This is an unusually large unit (74 named files, several 1000+ lines) covering Hermes's full operational-hygiene surface. I read ~33 files substantively (doctor/*, macos_tcc_anchor, update_lock/receipt/contract/abort_recovery, process_identity, resource_limits, context_switch_guard, prompt_stash, terminal_notify/breadcrumbs, input_sanitize, archive_safe, timeouts, urllib_security, stderr_timestamp, sqlite_util/runtime, diagnostics_upload, lifecycle, relaunch, gitlock, security_audit_startup, security_advisories, service_manager, checkpoints, mem_trim, install_identity, desktop_update_verify, session_lost_and_found) and skimmed the rest by docstring, then cross-checked every mechanism against Halbert's actual code (not just its design docs). The standout finding: Halbert's own permission-lattice design docs already NAME the exact macOS TCC signing-identity problem Hermes solves (os_grant.py explicitly cites the cdhash-vs-identifier-pinned DR issue as an unwired gap), and Halbert's tauri.conf.json currently ships the vulnerable signingIdentity:null configuration — this is the single highest-confidence, most concretely-evidenced candidate in the set (C2). Close behind: Halbert has genuinely NO diagnostic CLI (`halbert doctor`), NO backup/export command for its own irreplaceable single-conversation SQLite state, and NO awareness of SQLite's documented WAL-reset bug despite heavy reliance on SQLite across four+ independently-reimplemented stores (C1, C4, C5) — these are the next-highest-value, cheapest-to-lift items given the founder's 'no migrations, no back-compat shims, never delete old data' directive makes a working backup/recovery path unusually important. Everything Hermes-fleet/multi-service/multi-install-method-shaped (the ~7500-line self-update core, active-session concurrency leases) was deliberately NOT proposed for direct lift given Halbert's single-user/single-host/one-continuous-conversation constraints; those are called out explicitly in anti_patterns rather than silently dropped.

missed_by_reader.title: A bare open() on a live SQLite file cancels that process's advisory locks — and Halbert raw-copies a live chroma.sqlite3 today
missed_by_reader.mechanism: POSIX advisory locks are released process-wide when close() is called on ANY file descriptor for that file, so a plain open(db_path,'rb')/close() inside a process that also holds SQLite connections silently drops every lock SQLite holds from that process — a VACUUM's EXCLUSIVE lock, an in-flight BEGIN IMMEDIATE's RESERVED lock (docstring 1-6). The module keeps a refcounted registry of live connections per canonical path (22-25), canonicalises the path from PRAGMA database_list rather than trusting the caller's string (44-53), hands out a TrackedConnection whose close() untracks only AFTER the real close succeeds and under the same lock (85-104, with the #75629 note that untracking before a failing close leaves the fd open while the byte-probe guard believes nothing is live), and refuses raw byte reads while any connection is live. connect_tracked (132-140) is the entry point for 'any database that might be byte-probed'.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Two parts. (1) Fix the concrete offender: halbert_core/halbert_core/storage/chromadb_manager.py:862-872 copies every file under the chroma directory with shutil.copy2 — including a live WAL-mode chroma.sqlite3 — and _verify_copy (757-770) accepts the result if source and destination st_size match, which a torn mid-checkpoint copy satisfies. Route .db/.sqlite3 members through an online-backup snapshot (C5's _safe_copy_db) plus PRAGMA integrity_check, and stop treating size equality as verification. (2) Add a small halbert_core.utils.sqlite_live module with the connection-refcount registry and a guarded raw-read helper, and use it before any future code that stats, hashes or byte-reads one of the four WAL stores (continuity/state_store.py, continuity/promotion.py, attunement/store.py, agents/conversation_sqlite.py) from a process that may also hold them open.

missed_by_reader.title: Store-health rows a user can actually see: an FTS write-health probe and a WAL-size warning with a checkpoint fix
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Three things the reader's C1 sketch does not include. (a) FTS corruption is invisible to reads: COUNT(*) succeeds while every write fails through the FTS triggers, so the check drives a deliberately rolled-back write (_db_opens_cleanly) to surface it (189-201, citing #50502), and distinguishes that class from a malformed sqlite_master where even COUNT(*) fails and sqlite_master itself must be repaired (202-208). (b) --fix routes both classes through one repair path that always backs up first and reports strategy and backup name (169-187). (c) Unbounded WAL growth is its own row: >50 MB warns and, with --fix, runs PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE) and reports before/after size; >10 MB is an info line, not a warning (228-246). The stats row opens mode=ro precisely so it is safe against a live database held by another process (212-215).
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert detects FTS degradation reactively and persists it — agents/conversation_sqlite.py:915-923 writes fts_degraded into store_meta and 755-761 reads it back at open — but grep across every .py and .tsx outside that one file returns ZERO readers: the breadcrumb is written for nobody, so a user whose conversation search has silently stopped indexing is never told. Add to the C1 doctor: (1) a row reporting store_meta.fts_degraded and naming rebuild_fts() as the remedy; (2) a proactive rolled-back-write probe so the degraded state is discovered rather than waited for; (3) a WAL-size row per WAL store — only continuity/state_store.py:685 ever checkpoints (TRUNCATE), so conversation.db's -wal is unbounded and unmeasured.

missed_by_reader.title: macOS TCC grants are keyed to the interpreter binary too, not only the .app bundle — and Halbert's venv python is a symlink
missed_by_reader.mechanism: A separate TCC problem from the bundle DR that C2 covers: grants are keyed to the interpreter binary's identity, so a venv bin/python that symlinks into a package-manager store changes identity on every interpreter upgrade and every grant made to it evaporates (docstring 1-10). Hermes replaces the symlink with a signed real-file copy, materialises alias names (python3, python3.N) as real files rather than symlinks because the symlink form crashes (#95541), hardlinks libpython into venv/lib so the existing LC_RPATH resolves, and gates the swap on a real boot of the staged copy (_passes_boot_gate 244-283) so a failed anchor never touches the live venv. ensure_tcc_anchor/tcc_anchor_state (318-368) are no-ops off macOS and for non-managed interpreters and never raise; doctor renders the state at doctor_platform.py:305-317.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert runs in at least two OS identities — the Tauri Halbert.app and the venv interpreter that runs the CLI, scanners and voice paths — and /Volumes/4TB-BAD/Halbert/.venv/bin/python is a symlink to python3, itself a symlink to /Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.10/bin/python3, so any TCC grant earned by the CLI lands on the shared framework interpreter (every project on the machine inherits it) and not on Halbert. Extend the lattice rather than porting the anchor: persona/permission/os_grant.py's OS-grant axis (four states, docstring 9-16) has no notion of WHICH binary holds a grant, so GRANTED read from one identity is not GRANTED in the other. Record the grant-holding identity with the state, and have the C3 FDA doctor row name the identity it measured. The anchor itself is only worth building if Halbert ships a managed interpreter.

missed_by_reader.title: Undo that survives the process: a durable checkpoint store with a status/prune/clear operator surface
missed_by_reader.mechanism: `hermes checkpoints` is the operator surface over a durable on-disk checkpoint store backing /rollback of agent file edits: status reports base path, total/store/legacy byte sizes and a per-project table of workdir, commit count, last touch and live-vs-orphan state (29-59); prune takes retention_days, a max_total_size_mb ceiling and an explicit orphan policy and reports scanned/deleted-orphan/deleted-stale/errors/bytes-reclaimed (100-120); clear and clear-legacy are the escape hatches (137-184). The docstring's first line is the design point: none of it requires the agent to be running (1-4). 'Orphan' means a workdir not currently reachable, and the confirmation text warns that unreachable can mean an unmounted external volume or a down VPN rather than a deleted project (82-84).
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Halbert's equivalent is halbert_core/halbert_core/somatic/checkpoints.py:26-50 — a per-file LIFO stack of byte contents held in a Python dict, bounded at 50, explicitly scoped to 'before SomaticLifecycle executes a proposal's changes' and 'if execution fails and rolls back'. It dies with the process: nothing can undo an edit the machine made yesterday, there is no surface listing what was changed, no retention policy and no disk accounting. For an assistant that edits its own host, decide whether undo is a durable promise or a within-one-action safety net; if durable, persist the checkpoint stack (content-addressed under the Halbert data dir) with retention + size caps and a status/prune surface in the C1 doctor or the dashboard. The founder directive 'leave old data unread, never delete' cuts toward retention-with-a-ceiling rather than aggressive pruning.

missed_by_reader.title: A destructive confirmation must bind to the exact set that was previewed, not to a re-scan at execution time
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Before deleting orphan checkpoint projects, cmd_prune builds the preview, prints exactly what will be deleted, asks for confirmation, then passes an orphan_allowlist of exactly the identities that were displayed into prune_checkpoints — so a project that becomes orphaned only AFTER the preview (a volume unmounting while the prompt waits on input()) cannot be swept up by the later rescan. The comment at 93-96 pins the sharp edge: the allowlist is set unconditionally on every non-force run, because an EMPTY preview must bind an EMPTY allowlist rather than degenerating to 'no restriction'. --force is the only path with no allowlist, and it is the path with no preview.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: This is the general rule behind the founder's 'commands from the UI are staged, never executed' constraint, and is worth auditing Halbert against rather than porting: an approval names a specific set of targets and execution must act on that set, not re-derive it. Concretely — dashboard/routes/terminal.py:423 returns {'ok': True, 'staged': request.command}, and findings/proposals.py carries an approved state with approved_at (32, 52) and an execution_result column (148); check whether the executed action is bound to the proposal's recorded target set or recomputed at execute time, and whether the consent records in consent/store.py (scope field, 153/175/209) pin the scope actually shown to the owner. Any place a preview and an execution can disagree about the target set is a place a user approves one thing and gets another.

candidates.title: Event-loop liveness watchdog + off-loop heartbeat + loop-tick witness socket

origin_paths.what: start_loop_liveness_watchdog (OS-thread probe via call_soon_threadsafe, 3 missed strikes -> faulthandler dump + os._exit); write_loop_heartbeat (pid/monotonic/start_time/mem sample, atomic write, off-loop via asyncio.to_thread so a stalled fsync can't wedge the loop it's supposed to be proving alive); get_loop_tick_socket_path + _tick_socket_handler (PID-suffixed unix socket SERVED ON the loop so an answer proves scheduling, not just file freshness; TCP fallback on non-POSIX); _sweep_stale_tick_sockets (os.kill(pid,0) probe to unlink dead PIDs' sockets); _arm_loop_floor_timer (keeps selector wait bounded); arm_shutdown_watchdog (drain-timeout+grace hard-exit thread, dumps stacks, releases PID file/lock before log-drain before os._exit)

candidates.mechanism: A frozen asyncio loop takes every asyncio-based recovery path down with it. Hermes runs a plain OS thread that pings the loop via call_soon_threadsafe every N seconds; 3 consecutive missed pings dump all thread stacks (faulthandler) and os._exit so the OS supervisor can restart. Separately, a heartbeat FILE is written off-loop (to_thread, awaited so writes never queue) every 30s with pid+monotonic+start_time+a cheap /proc memory sample, for external supervisors to read; because the file write itself moved off-loop, file freshness alone no longer proves the loop is scheduling, so a second witness -- a tiny unix-domain socket bound and served ON the loop -- answers a liveness probe with 1 byte, and only an answer (not a fresh file) is treated as proof of real scheduling. A self-rescheduling 'floor timer' keeps at least one asyncio timer pending so the selector's wait is always bounded. A separate shutdown-only watchdog thread hard-exits if a graceful drain doesn't finish within drain_timeout+60s grace, writing a full faulthandler dump plus process/signal context to a log file first.
candidates.why_solid: This is the concrete implementation the master plan flagged as missing ('Watchdog/daemon: no packet yet -- deliberately... Hermes's startup watchdog is the template when it does', OPENCLAW-LIFT-MASTER-PLAN-2026-09-07.md:67). Halbert's dashboard backend is a long-running asyncio FastAPI process behind a Tauri sidecar; today only a parent-liveness watchdog exists (kills self when the PARENT dies), nothing detects the backend's OWN event loop wedging while the process stays alive and the OS supervisor (launchd) sees a healthy PID.

HM11-gateway-core.summary: Read gateway/AGENTS.md plus 38 of the ~70 assigned files (prioritizing lifecycle/shutdown/delivery/session-safety mechanisms per FOCUS over the largest turn-execution files, which likely overlap the already-merged interrupt algebra). The richest, most novel material was the lifecycle/watchdog cluster (event-loop liveness watchdog + heartbeat + loop-tick witness socket, unclean-exit/OOM sentinel with a post-crash state.db integrity check, multi-check readiness endpoint, code-skew detection, two complementary restart-loop breakers, shutdown-signal forensics) -- all confirmed fully ABSENT in Halbert, which today has only a minimal parent-liveness watchdog and a flat healthy/unhealthy /health endpoint, matching the master plan's explicit note that the watchdog/daemon workstream was deliberately left unpacketed pending Hermes's reference implementation. Also strong: a durable delivery-obligation ledger for the final agent response (genuinely relevant given Halbert's single-continuous-conversation model with no session list to fall back on), a wake-into-conversation pattern for background completions with a load-bearing durable-record-not-new-turn distinction for delegated work (directly relevant to Halbert's permission-gate discipline), and a fully-hardened MEDIA:<path> outbound file-delivery convention with a credential-path denylist that fills a real, currently-total gap (Halbert's dashboard chat has no mechanism at all for the agent handing back a generated file). Several files (mirror.py, channel_directory.py, whatsapp_identity.py, dead_targets.py, rich_sent_store.py, sticker_cache.py, cgroup_cleanup.py, systemd_notify.py, scale_to_zero.py) were confirmed to be multi-platform-messaging or Linux/cloud-specific machinery with no matching problem in Halbert's single-user/single-host/single-conversation/macOS design and were deliberately excluded from candidates or listed as anti-patterns. The entire slash-command surface and most of the stream_consumer_*.py family were not reached given the file-count budget and are flagged as the top follow-up areas.

candidates.title: Literal-string SSRF classifier + general-purpose WebFetch tool with one shared choke point

origin_paths.what: isPrivateHost(): blocks loopback/link-local/private/CGNAT/reserved/multicast IPv4+IPv6 ranges, cloud metadata hostnames, *.local, and numeric/hex IP bypass encodings, operating purely on the literal hostname/IP string (deliberately no DNS resolution, to avoid TOCTOU/DNS-rebind).
WebFetchTool.validateInput() calls isPrivateHost() before every fetch.
RemoteTriggerTool posts to an arbitrary endpoint with ZERO SSRF check — same repo, same risk shape, gate not reused.

candidates.mechanism: A dependency-free SSRF classifier that blocks by literal IP/hostname match (not DNS resolution), wired into every tool taking a user/model-supplied URL through one shared choke point.
candidates.why_solid: Halbert has no general-purpose URL-fetch tool at all, and its one SSRF check (dashboard/routes/llm.py) is scoped to LLM provider settings and does live DNS resolution (TOCTOU risk). A literal-string layer closes that gap and fits Halbert's 'one policy pipeline' constraint if built as ONE shared function.

verdict.notes: ORIGIN CONFIRMED, all three paths read. v2/src/permissions/ssrf-check.mjs:18-25 (BLOCKED_HOSTNAMES incl. metadata.google.internal), :35-59 (literal-string only, explicit 'does NOT perform DNS resolution (to avoid TOCTOU races)' at :28-30, plus the numeric/hex bypass rule at :56), :68-88 (IPv4 ranges 0/8,10/8,127/8,100.64/10,169.254/16,172.16/12,192.0.0/24,192.168/16,198.18/15,198.51.100/24,203.0.113/24,>=224), :90-101 (IPv6 ::1, ::, ::ffff: mapped, fe80:, fc/fd, ff). v2/src/tools/web-fetch.mjs:9 imports it, :30-46 validateInput is the single gate. v2/src/tools/remote-trigger.mjs:34-36 validateInput checks only `task`; :50 fetches an arbitrary `endpoint` with no SSRF check -- the per-tool-instead-of-choke-point anti-pattern is real. HALBERT EVIDENCE CORRECTED AND MATERIALLY STRENGTHENED. The reader's framing (DNS-resolution TOCTOU) is true but is the lesser half. The larger, verifiable defect: dashboard/routes/llm.py:98-130 `is_safe_url(url, provider)` early-returns True unconditionally at :110-112 for provider in ('ollama','lm-studio','apple-foundation') BEFORE any resolution, and dashboard/routes/llm.py:505-510 `proxy_models` passes BOTH `req.url` and `req.provider` from the same caller-supplied request body -- so any caller who sets provider='ollama' bypasses the entire SSRF check for any URL. Same shape at llm.py:681 and :739. (compute.py:214-218 is NOT affected: url and provider both come from a stored endpoint record, not the request.) Also confirmed: `egress.web_fetch` is already a declared capability with no consumer -- consent/copy.py:225 and persona/permission/ceiling.py:81 define it, and grep found no tool that requires it; halbert_core/halbert_core/tools has no general URL-fetch tool. SCOPE CORRECTION FOR DISPATCH: the valuable, low-risk half is hardening the existing check -- a deterministic literal-IP/hostname classifier in a shared module (Python `ipaddress` classifies a literal without getaddrinfo) applied BEFORE and INDEPENDENT of the provider string, closing the caller-chosen-provider bypass. Registering a new general WebFetch tool is a capability expansion (a new egress surface on a machine-identity steward) and is a founder product call, not a lift -- do not bundle the two into one packet. If a fetch tool is ever built, the reader's redirect anti-pattern (web-fetch.mjs:59-63 `redirect: 'follow'` after one upfront check) must be honoured: manual redirect with a per-hop re-check.

verdict.notes: ORIGIN CONFIRMED. v2/src/permissions/path-check.mjs:9-33 is SENSITIVE_PATTERNS exactly as described (23 patterns: .env/.env.*, credentials.json|.yaml, .pem, .key, id_rsa|id_ed25519|id_ecdsa|id_dsa, .ssh/config, .netrc, .pgpass, .aws/credentials, .docker/config.json, secrets.json|.yaml, .npmrc, .pypirc, .claude/credentials, service_account*.json, kubeconfig, .kube/config); :66-71 tests each pattern against BOTH `resolved` and `path.basename(resolved)` and returns {safe:false, reason:'Sensitive file'} regardless of the write flag -- reads are blocked too. v2/test/test.mjs:1387-1401 and :1410-1413 confirm .env/credentials.json/server.key/cert.pem rejected while /etc/hostname reads pass. HALBERT EVIDENCE CORRECTED UPWARD -- there is a better citation than the reader's. The gap is not only that executor.py:971-1003 `_read_file` does no pattern check; it is that the PRE-DISPATCH classifier is asymmetric: tools/safety.py:451-458 `_classify_builtin` returns risk_level=SAFE, allowed=True, reason='Read-only operation' for read_file/cat/read_config with no path inspection at all, while tools/safety.py:722-732 `_classify_write` DOES walk SENSITIVE_PATHS (safety.py:326-337, which already includes ~/.ssh/ and ~/.gnupg/ expanded at import). So the machinery, the path set and the choke point (executor.execute -> safety.classify at :569-577) all already exist; only the read branch declines to use them. anti_patterns.title: SSRF protection applied per-tool instead of at one shared choke point
anti_patterns.evidence: web-fetch.mjs calls isPrivateHost(); remote-trigger.mjs posts to an arbitrary endpoint with no SSRF check at all — same repo, same risk shape, inconsistently applied.
anti_patterns.why_not: Validates Halbert's own 'one policy pipeline' constraint by counter-example: any lifted SSRF check must be one shared function every URL-taking tool imports, never a per-tool copy that can be forgotten.

anti_patterns.title: WebFetch validates the initial URL, then follows redirects unchecked
anti_patterns.evidence: web-fetch.mjs: fetch(url,{redirect:'follow'}) — isPrivateHost() checked once against the original URL, but a 3xx can redirect to a private IP and the fetch follows with no re-check.
anti_patterns.why_not: Textbook redirect-based SSRF bypass. Any Halbert WebFetch equivalent must re-validate each redirect hop, never trust a single upfront check with auto-follow enabled.

anti_patterns.title: Plugin loader clones and loads arbitrary git-URL code with only a shell-metacharacter regex as a gate
anti_patterns.evidence: plugins/loader.mjs loadFromGit(): validates repoUrl only against a shell-injection-safety regex, then git-clones and trusts whatever plugin.json (declaring tools/hooks) the URL serves — no signature check, no allowlist, no review step.
anti_patterns.why_not: Directly violates 'no downloading/executing files from untrusted sources' and Halbert's single-user/single-host trust model; skills already use a provenance sidecar specifically to avoid this shape.

anti_patterns.title: npx-delegate subcommands fetch-and-run a published npm package at runtime
anti_patterns.evidence: optimize/commands.mjs delegateToCli(): spawn('npx',['-y',pkg,...]) downloads and executes an arbitrary npm package on demand.
anti_patterns.why_not: Same class of problem as the plugin loader — dynamically fetching and executing remote code at runtime has no place in Halbert's security posture, opt-in framing notwithstanding.

anti_patterns.title: Hook engine's PreToolUse gate fails OPEN by default on hook error/timeout
anti_patterns.evidence: hooks/engine.mjs: catch block returns null (allow) unless the operator explicitly set failOpen:false on that hook.
anti_patterns.why_not: A broken deny-capable hook should never silently become a permission grant; any Halbert hook engine must default fail-closed for deny-capable events — the inverse of the origin's default.

anti_patterns.title: Permission mode literally named 'default' silently allows everything when non-interactive
anti_patterns.evidence: permissions/checker.mjs: in 'default' mode, no readline interface means every tool requiring permission is allowed ('headless mode').
anti_patterns.why_not: A mode named 'default' becoming maximally permissive without a human to prompt is a footgun; any Halbert path that cannot prompt interactively must fail toward the restrictive outcome, not the permissive one.

anti_patterns.title: Provider/router modules hardcode concrete vendor model IDs and USD prices in source
anti_patterns.evidence: optimize/router.mjs DEFAULT_LADDER and core/providers.mjs hardcode specific Anthropic/OpenAI/Google model IDs and prices as source constants.
anti_patterns.why_not: Directly conflicts with Halbert's directive to never bake or recommend model names; any lifted routing/transform mechanism must be re-derived over the user's own connection slots only.

anti_patterns.title: Session 'teleport' (base64 session export to move between machines)
anti_patterns.evidence: core/session.mjs exportForTeleport/importFromTeleport serialize full conversation state to a base64 blob meant for transfer to another machine.
anti_patterns.why_not: Not a fit for Halbert's single-user single-host, machine-identity design; noted only so it is not accidentally proposed, though the strict input-validation technique inside it is a fine generic idiom.

Cannot display binary content.' rather than handing bytes to the model. (2) Directory detection with a redirect rather than an error: :63-66 returns '... is a directory, not a file. Use Bash with ls to list directory contents.' (3) Windowed reads instead of refusal: :44-46 offset/limit parameters, :88-92 slicing with DEFAULT_LIMIT=2000, and :102-105 a footer '[File has N lines total. Showing lines X-Y. OCC02-archive-bundle-and-tracking-pipeli.summary: This is a rich unit with two distinct payloads. First, cli.mjs (the real bundled early Claude Code v0.2.9, 7.6MB) yielded genuine product-behavior fragments not present anywhere in archive/open_claude_code/src or the docs/ tree (both of which are thin clean-room placeholder sketches, not real internals) — the actual system/agent prompts, the Bash tool's banned-network-binary denylist, an LLM-driven command-prefix/injection-detection gate for permanent allow-rules, the malicious-code refusal guard, the doctor/init command definitions, the three-way permission-confirmation UI, and several smaller tool-usage micro-instructions. Cross-checking against Halbert found two verified, live gaps worth prioritizing: Halbert's ToolSafetyFramework has no rule at all for direct network-egress binaries (confirmed by actually running curl/wget/nc through the live classifier — all three came back MEDIUM, and Halbert's own tests document MEDIUM as running unconfirmed), and there is no mechanism anywhere for narrowing or gating a persistent 'always allow' Bash grant against command-injection smuggling. Second, scripts/ + ADR-003 describe a complete, well-designed nightly upstream-tracking pipeline (poll -> hard verification gates -> optional never-blocking AI analysis -> templated release) that Halbert has no equivalent of for tracking its own dependencies or the very OSS repos this review program covers — offered as a process-shape candidate, explicitly excluding its most dangerous piece (auto-update-capabilities.mjs's unsupervised LLM-driven self-patching, flagged as an anti-pattern given its regression-tolerance bug and conflict with Halbert's deterministic-policy rule). Ten candidates returned, ranging from two high-priority live-verified security gaps down to several small prompt-instruction deltas; four anti-patterns recorded, the most important being the origin's use of an LLM inside a security-decision path, which Halbert's founder constraints explicitly forbid reproducing.

missed_by_reader.title: run_command has two execution paths with different redaction, output bounding and audit — and which runs depends on whether a dashboard client is subscribed
missed_by_reader.lines: bytes 7170900-7171400 (Bash tool description steps 3-5: one execution path with its output contract declared to the model — 'If the output exceeds ${Ws} characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you', Ws=30000 at 7170700) and 7182800-7183640 (the single validateInput/execute path every bash call goes through)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: The origin has exactly one shell execution path and declares its output-processing contract in the tool description, so model, gate and user see the same behaviour on every call. Halbert has two paths and they do not agree. tools/executor.py:796-830 tries the PTY pool first: streaming/agent_pool.py:330-331 runs redact() over output_head and output_tail, BoundedOutput caps them (head 20 lines + 4 KiB tail), and executor.py:801-826 writes a terminal_blocks audit row with a `redacted` flag. executor.py:832-903 is the fallback: asyncio.create_subprocess_shell, both pipes drained into unbounded buffers, `return output.strip()` — no redact(), no cap, no audit row. The fallback is taken whenever terminal_pool_wanted() is false, which per streaming/terminal_bridge.py:148-154 requires terminal_stream_wanted(), i.e. 'the current context has a consumer for terminal events' — so a scheduler job, a voice turn, an MCP-originated call or any turn with no subscribed SSE client silently loses credential redaction; also when the pool is at its cap of 3 busy sessions (agent_pool.py:44-60, run_block returns None) or on any exception (executor.py:828-830, 'Pool path failed, falling back to subprocess'). There is no downstream net: security/result_redaction.py:11-15 states in its own docstring that 'Routing internal (executor) results through this core is deliberately NOT done here'. streaming/redact.py:1-40 shows what is lost — password=, -p<token>, Authorization: headers. This is 'redaction at the response choke point' failing open on a condition (is a browser tab watching?) unrelated to security. The pool IS enabled in the dashboard app (dashboard/app.py:198-202), so this is partial coverage, not a dead feature.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Make the two run_command paths agree, with the pool as reference: apply streaming.redact.redact() and a BoundedOutput-equivalent cap to the subprocess fallback's stdout/stderr before they are returned to the model, and write the same terminal_blocks row (owner=agent, redacted flag) so the fallback is auditable. Tests: call _run_command with the terminal event bus having no subscribers and assert (a) a password= / Authorization: token in output comes back redacted, (b) output over the cap is truncated, (c) a terminal_blocks row exists. Separately decide and record whether internal executor results should route through security/result_redaction.redact_result — that module's docstring leaves the question open and this is the case that answers it.

The runtime side is correct: tools/executor.py:415-429 narrows the offered function schemas to persona/guest_tools.is_tool_allowed_for_guest when a guest fronts, and executor.py:463-480 refuses again at execute() ('a model can imitate a call it was not offered'). missed_by_reader.title: Hard steer away from the shell toward the narrow, gated tools — stated as a MUST with the alternatives named
missed_by_reader.lines: bytes 7172150-7172700 (Bash tool 'Usage notes': 'VERY IMPORTANT: You MUST avoid using search commands like `find` and `grep`. Instead use ${Ps}, ${ys}, or ${qa} to search. You MUST avoid read tools like `cat`, `head`, `tail`, and `ls`, and use ${Fd.name} and ${zI.name} to read files.' and immediately after 'When issuing multiple commands, use the ; or && operator to separate them. DO NOT use newlines')
missed_by_reader.mechanism: The shell is the one tool with an unbounded surface, so the origin spends prompt weight pushing every operation that has a purpose-built tool off the shell onto that tool — substitutes named by their interpolated real names, at MUST strength, twice. The newline prohibition is the same instinct: a newline is a chain operator the prefix extractor and the per-sub-command validator cannot see, so the model is told to keep commands in a shape the deterministic gates can parse. This matters more for Halbert than for a coding agent, because Halbert's per-tool machinery is where the guarantees live: continuity/write_guard.check_before_write and continuity/provenance.record_file_change on write_file (executor.py:1023-1080), skills.telemetry.record_skill_read on read_file, the terminal_blocks audit row and redaction on the pool path — every one of which a `cat`, `printf >`, `sed -i` or `grep` through run_command walks past. Halbert says this once, at the weakest severity it defines: config/prompts/v2/tools/run_command.xml:44 '<rule severity="PREFERRED">Prefer specific tools over general shell commands when available</rule>', no alternatives named, sitting under seven CRITICAL/IMPORTANT rules that outrank it.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Raise the steer in config/prompts/v2/tools/run_command.xml from PREFERRED to CRITICAL and name the substitutes explicitly (read_file not cat/head/tail, list_directory not ls, search_files not find/grep, write_file not shell redirection or sed -i), with one line of reason — those tools carry the write guard, the provenance record and the audit row run_command does not. Add the newline rule too ('separate commands with ; or &&, not newlines'), which also keeps commands in the shape safety._shell_segments (safety.py:590-620) parses. The one worth recording as an anti-pattern is that an automated tracking script mutates a checked-out dependency's source file in place, unprompted, as an import side effect, announced only on stderr: exactly the class of unannounced self-modification Halbert answers with a compiled path fence (consent/selfmod.py's GOVERNED_PATHS / assert_not_governed, 'never writable by the agent, at any autonomy level, with no override'). Five halbert_state claims were wrong, four because the reader grepped halbert_core/halbert_core/prompts (assembly code) instead of /Volumes/4TB-BAD/Halbert/config/prompts/ (where prompt text lives, per loader.py:19-26 and routes/agent.py:203-208): the malicious-code deny block (C3) and the no-preamble rules (C8) are already there; Halbert has a scripts/ directory and an eight-job CI whose suite-census meta-gate (ci.yml:9-118) is stronger than ADR-003's gates (C4); consent/selfmod.py is already the protected-path fence (C5); and scheduler/monitor_hash.py already IS the poll-state-diff primitive C6 proposes building, lifted from Hermes and better (four-state decision, hash persisted before the run, source failure never a change).
