anti_patterns.title: cron/AGENTS.md's '3-minute hard interrupt on cron sessions' claim contradicts the actual code
anti_patterns.evidence: cron/AGENTS.md states a 3-minute hard interrupt; cron/scheduler.py:955-965 (_cron_inactivity_seconds parsing HERMES_CRON_TIMEOUT) and cron/scheduler.py:1741-1745 (_run_agent_with_watchdog docstring: 'inactivity (not wall-clock) watchdog: default 600s') show the real default is a 600-second INACTIVITY timeout, not a flat 3-minute wall-clock interrupt.
anti_patterns.why_not: Re-confirms the prior review's general warning about hand-written cron docs with a concrete verified number. Halbert should verify every specific numeric invariant Hermes docs claim against the enforcing code path before adopting it as a Halbert constant — C16 lifts the VERIFIED behavior (inactivity-based, 600s default), not the doc's wrong figure.

anti_patterns.title: Chronos hosted 'scale-to-zero' NAS-webhook cron provider architecture is a multi-tenant cloud pattern, not a fit for a single-host assistant
anti_patterns.evidence: docs/chronos-managed-cron-contract.md:1-30 describes a three-hop JWT/webhook trust model letting a HOSTED gateway stop between fires and be re-armed by an external NAS scheduler; cron/scheduler_provider.py:90-186 defines the full pluggable CronScheduler ABC (two-phase CAS claim, external registry reconciliation) largely in service of this hosted case and a multi-machine fleet model.
anti_patterns.why_not: Halbert is single-user, single-host, always-on and never needs to scale to zero; lifting the JWT/webhook/multi-machine-reconciliation machinery would import real complexity against the founder's single-host constraint with no honest degeneration path. Keep only the narrow signature-detected-capability-negotiation pattern and 'fail closed to the built-in ticker' invariant.

anti_patterns.title: cron/ is 16,970 lines split across ~19 sibling files bound by late-bound bottom-of-file imports, purely to stay under a line-count budget
anti_patterns.evidence: cron/scheduler.py is 3,916 lines, cron/jobs.py 3,164, cron/scheduler_delivery.py 1,714, cron/lifecycle_guard.py 1,023; every split-out sibling (scheduler_preflight.py, scheduler_prompt.py, scheduler_script.py, scheduler_provider.py, scheduler_delivery.py) ends with a late-bound 'from cron import scheduler as _sched' import block explicitly commented as needed to dodge circular imports.
anti_patterns.why_not: Confirms and extends the first review's finding #1: module boundaries follow a linter line-count rule, not a domain seam, producing a circular-import workaround as a side effect. Halbert's scheduler/ should keep growing along real domain seams (a preflight module, an incidents module, a notepad module, each independently useful per C4/C8/C11) rather than mechanically splitting one god-module once it crosses a line-count threshold.

HM16-cron-second-pass.summary: cron/ in Hermes is a rich, ~17k-line subsystem split (over-aggressively, per a repeated anti-pattern finding) across ~19 sibling files. Beyond the durability set Halbert already lifted (catchup, run receipts, monitor-hash, restart budget), this second pass surfaced a genuinely new layer largely absent from Halbert: a consent-gated "propose a scheduled job from a detected pattern" pipeline (blueprint catalog -> suggestion queue -> curated starter catalog, C1-C3) that is the concrete missing bridge from Halbert's existing home/behavior.py pattern-confidence tracker to an actual scheduled job; a durable delivery-handoff queue and delivery-evidence discipline for once Halbert's scheduler can deliver into live channels (C6-C7); a scheduler-specific failure-incident dedup/lifecycle layer that extends (rather than duplicates) the existing findings/store.py (C8); a job-creation-time self-restart-loop guard meaningfully stronger than Halbert's existing general HIGH-risk-command approval gate because it must work unattended (C9); an actual implementation of the preflight checks behind Halbert's already-designed-but-unimplemented blocked_config status (C11); a two-tier prompt-injection scanner keyed to content provenance, needed once skills load into scheduled-job prompts (C12); a verified, concrete correction to the scheduler's job-timeout model — inactivity-based with a 600s default and a claim-heartbeat, versus Halbert's current flat wall-clock join(timeout) (C16); a PID-reuse-safe liveness check that strengthens the already-lifted run-receipts recovery logic (C17); and a single-shared-thread periodic-scheduler pattern directly applicable to the 15 separate hand-rolled polling threads already present across Halbert's codebase (C18). Two clear anti-patterns to avoid: trusting cron/AGENTS.md's specific numeric claims without checking code (its "3-minute hard interrupt" claim is simply wrong, the real value is 600s), and the Chronos hosted-NAS-webhook "scale to zero" cron-provider architecture, which is multi-tenant cloud machinery with no honest single-host degeneration path.

missed_by_reader.title: The fire path re-reads the durable record and refuses to fire a paused/disabled job (Halbert: the dashboard's cancel button does not stop a scheduled job)
missed_by_reader.lines: 477-486 (_has_pause_marker, is_job_runnable), 488-501 (effective_job_state); callers cron/scheduler_provider.py:261 and tools/cronjob_tools.py:180-201 (_claim_for_manual_run distinguishing 'paused/disabled' from 'already being fired')
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Every dispatch path in Hermes re-reads the job record and asks is_job_runnable(job) immediately before firing: bool(job.get('enabled', True)) and not _has_pause_marker(job), with the docstring stating that the pause marker is a deliberate SECOND gate 'so a contradictory half-paused record never fires even before self-heal runs'. effective_job_state then makes enabled=true authoritative for display so a list can never show 'paused' while the job keeps firing. The durable record, not an in-memory copy, is the authority at fire time.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Fix the cancel path in halbert_core/halbert_core/scheduler, then generalize it. Today: SchedulerEngine._load_jobs runs once in __init__ (engine.py:22, 27-40) and self.jobs is never refreshed; AutonomousExecutor holds one long-lived engine whose in-memory dict backs get_job; dashboard/routes/jobs.py:103-110 cancels by constructing its OWN SchedulerEngine and calling engine.cancel_job, which writes state='cancelled' to that job's JSON file but never touches APScheduler and is never seen by the running executor (AutonomousExecutor.cancel_job at executor.py:528-544 is the path that would remove the APScheduler trigger, and the route does not call it). _wrap_task's wrapped() (executor.py:581-620) reads the record only to pull a confidence float and never checks state; Job.is_terminal() (job.py:29-30) has exactly one caller, engine.cancel_job itself (engine.py:91). Net effect: cancelling a job from the dashboard leaves it firing on schedule until the process restarts. Two changes: route cancellation through the live executor (or have the executor re-read the record), and add an is_job_runnable-style re-read check at the top of wrapped() that returns without running when the record is cancelled/terminal/paused.

missed_by_reader.title: Deterministic natural-language schedule parser (no model needed to turn 'every weekday at 8' into a cron expression)
missed_by_reader.lines: 655-677 (_parse_clock_time: 9am / 9:30am / 14:00 / bare 24h hour / noon / midnight), 680-712 (_natural_every_to_cron: weekday keyword or comma/'and' list, optional 'at', then the time), 716-731 (_cron_schedule validating through croniter, _interval_schedule), 733-760 (parse_schedule: 'every X' -> natural cron or interval, bare 5-6 field cron, ISO timestamp -> once)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: A pure-function ladder turns the phrases a person actually says into a validated schedule dict {kind: once|interval|cron}. Every branch is deterministic and every cron expression is validated through croniter before storage, so an unparseable phrase raises at creation time rather than producing a job that silently never fires. No model is involved anywhere in the path.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Add a deterministic schedule parser to halbert_core/halbert_core/scheduler/ (e.g. schedule_parse.py) returning the same three-kind dict and validating cron expressions before storage. Today Halbert has no user-facing schedule input at all: scheduler/executor.py:462-468 takes cron_expr as a dict of APScheduler CronTrigger kwargs supplied by code, and job.py:15 documents Job.schedule as 'cron expression or ISO timestamp' with no parser anywhere. This is the missing piece that lets the one continuous conversation accept 'every weekday at 8' without spending a model call to build a cron string - directly downstream of the standing directive that a template beats a model. Prerequisite for C1/C2 to have anything to fill.

missed_by_reader.title: Two-signal ticker liveness markers: 'alive but failing' is distinguishable from 'firing'
missed_by_reader.lines: 1128-1152 (_write_marker atomic best-effort; record_ticker_heartbeat writing ticker_heartbeat every loop and ticker_last_success only on a clean tick), 1155-1183 (_epoch_file_age, get_ticker_heartbeat_age, get_ticker_success_age - None means 'cannot determine', not 'dead'), 1185-1215 (catch_up_occurrences counter, record_ticker_error / clear_ticker_error / get_ticker_last_error)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Two epoch-stamp files, not one: the loop stamps ticker_heartbeat every iteration and ticker_last_success only when a tick completes without raising, because 'a ticker stuck failing every tick would otherwise keep the plain heartbeat fresh and falsely report healthy'. A third marker persists the last tick error text so another process can show WHY, not just staleness, and a fourth counts catch-up occurrences. All writes are atomic and all failures swallowed so markers can never break a tick. This answers 'are my automations alive and did they run' with no model in the loop.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Add heartbeat/last-success/last-error epoch markers to Halbert's scheduler data dir, written by the executor's tick, and surface their ages in the jobs route and any scheduler health check (pairs directly with C19's doctor). grep -rn heartbeat over halbert_core/halbert_core/scheduler/*.py and dashboard/routes/jobs.py returns nothing - there is currently no way to tell 'the scheduler thread died' from 'nothing was due'. Overlap note: OPENCLAW-LIFT-PACKET-03 addendum item 9 already describes this as the fallback if the founder declines a prompted heartbeat, so this is a parked decision to close rather than a new idea.

missed_by_reader.title: A timed-out script must be killed as a process GROUP, or a surviving grandchild holds the pipes open forever
missed_by_reader.lines: 150-168 (_terminate_cron_script_process: 'hard stop of a cron script and every child it spawned'; taskkill /T /F on Windows), 170-186 (_terminate_process_group: killpg SIGTERM, wait, killpg signal 0 to test for survivors, then killpg SIGKILL - because 'a survivor holds the pipe write ends open and the caller's communicate() would block on EOF forever'), 188-214 (_terminate_cron_script_tree with a tree-kill first and the group path as fallback)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Termination is layered and group-scoped: try a process-tree kill, fall back to the process group, TERM then verify with signal 0 then KILL, and only then reap. The stated failure mode is not the orphan itself but the caller hanging on EOF because a grandchild inherited the pipe write ends.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Give Halbert's subprocess call sites a group-scoped kill. grep -rn 'start_new_session|setsid|killpg|preexec_fn' over halbert_core/halbert_core returns only utils/ollama.py:136, streaming/pty.py:269 and dashboard/__main__.py:90 - no tool path. tools/executor.py:903-910 kills only the direct child on timeout (proc.kill(); await proc.wait()), and tools/system_info.py:43, tools/applescript_tools.py:85 and mcp/client.py:331 do the same. Spawn tool subprocesses with start_new_session=True and kill the group (TERM, verify, KILL) so a shell-out that forks a child cannot survive the timeout or wedge the reader.

missed_by_reader.title: Reentrant in-process lock + cross-process flock around the whole load->modify->save cycle, degrading to in-process-only rather than dying
missed_by_reader.lines: 198-236 (_jobs_lock_file, _acquire_flock with a timeout, _release_flock), 238-291 (_jobs_lock: depth-counted reentrancy, then _jobs_file_lock, then flock on <cron dir>/.jobs.lock; on timeout it logs loudly and proceeds in-process-only because 'a briefly torn cross-process write beats a dead scheduler'), 292-345 (_fire_job_lock: a per-job lock that MAY be held across network delivery, scoped so unrelated jobs keep progressing, and which fails CLOSED when cross-process locking is unavailable)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Two locks with deliberately opposite failure postures: the global store lock fails OPEN (availability wins - a scheduler that cannot take the flock still runs) while the per-job fire fence fails CLOSED (correctness wins - never double-fire). The docstring names the concrete bug the global lock prevents: a `cron pause` from the CLI being clobbered by the gateway's write, leaving the job firing.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Give SchedulerEngine a lock discipline. engine.py:44-63 _persist_job is atomically replaced per job file (good) but there is no lock of any kind and no reload: self.jobs is populated once at __init__ (engine.py:22) and every mutation writes from a possibly-stale copy. Several instances coexist by construction - dashboard/app.py:1249 (the long-lived executor's), dashboard/routes/jobs.py:31 and executor.py:114 each build their own. Add a reload-before-mutate (or a single shared engine) plus a per-job fence around the fire path that fails closed. This is the general form of the cancel bug in the first missed item.

missed_by_reader.title: Cron expresses wall-clock intent: a stored next-run under a different UTC offset must be re-read as wall clock, not as an instant
missed_by_reader.lines: 807-824 (_ensure_aware reading legacy naive values as system-local wall time; _parse_aware), 826-840 (_timezone_offset_mismatch; _stored_wall_clock_is_future with the rule 'Cron expresses wall-clock intent; after a timezone change an old offset can make a future run look due (21:00+10 -> 13:00+02)'), 1006-1030 (_cron_next_run_matches_expr detecting a stored next_run_at that is not an occurrence of the current expr), 1039-1062 (_classify_stale_cron_next_run separating expr_edit - re-anchor without firing - from timezone_migration - fire, because treating it as an edit silently skipped a due occurrence that had never fired)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Two stored-time hazards are separated rather than conflated: a stored next-run that no longer matches the schedule because the expression changed (re-anchor, do not fire) versus one that no longer matches because only the offset representation changed (fire - it is a genuine, never-served occurrence). The discriminator is whether normalization moved the wall clock AND the stored instant's own wall clock is a legal occurrence.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Decide and document Halbert's scheduler timezone posture, then make catch-up honour it. scheduler/catchup.py contains no timezone reasoning at all (grep for tz|timezone|utc|wall returns nothing); AutonomousExecutor defaults timezone='UTC' (executor.py:131, 153) and only dashboard/app.py:1241-1254 resolves the real zone from being config - dashboard/routes/jobs.py:31 and the executor.py:114 docstring example construct with the UTC default, so a cron_expr registered through those reads as UTC. The lift is not the legacy-row migration classifier (the no-migrations directive rules that out - there is no old data) but the invariant underneath it: a wall-clock schedule compared across a DST boundary or a config timezone change must be compared as wall clock, and boot catch-up must not silently skip an occurrence that never fired.

missed_by_reader.title: Job-script confinement: resolve-then-relative_to a single scripts directory, and the shebang is deliberately not honoured
missed_by_reader.lines: 256-292 (_resolve_script_path: eager NUL rejection before Path ops, expanduser inside a try, absolute paths resolved and relative paths joined to the scripts dir, then path.relative_to(scripts_dir_resolved) as a traversal/absolute-injection/symlink-escape guard, then exists/is_file), 296-315 (_script_argv: 'Interpreter by extension - the shebang is deliberately NOT honoured (small, auditable surface)': .sh/.bash -> bash, else sys.executable)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: Two containment rules. A job script must resolve inside one designated directory after full symlink resolution, which closes traversal, absolute-path injection and symlink escape in a single check. And the interpreter is chosen by file extension with the shebang ignored on purpose, so the executed interpreter is a property of the host's policy rather than of the (possibly agent-authored) file's first line.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Apply both rules wherever Halbert executes a file on a schedule. tools/execute_code.py:202 already bans the subprocess module from generated scripts (a stronger stance for its own lane), but tools/schedule_cron.py:16-30 accepts a free-text command and writes it into the OS crontab with no path or interpreter discipline. If Halbert's scheduler gains a script-augmented job (C15), require the script to resolve inside one scripts directory after resolve(), and pick the interpreter by extension rather than by shebang. Note the tension with 'scope by capability boundary, not filesystem path': a scripts allowlist directory is a containment mechanism, not an identity scope, and should be argued as such.

missed_by_reader.title: Owner-only permissions on the job store, and ownership restored after a privileged writer's atomic replace
missed_by_reader.lines: 525-537 (_secure_dir 0700, _secure_file 0600, both suppressing OSError/NotImplementedError for Windows), 538-560 (_preserve_file_ownership: an atomic replace makes the file owned by the writer's euid, so a root CLI write against the unprivileged daemon's store would flip it to root:root 0600 and lock the daemon out - restore the previous uid/gid, warn loudly if that fails)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: The store's confidentiality and its accessibility are treated as two obligations of the same write. os.replace silently transfers ownership to the writer, which is exactly what makes a one-off privileged CLI write permanently lock out the unprivileged process that normally owns the file.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: chmod the scheduler store owner-only on write. grep -rn 'chmod|0o600|0o700' over halbert_core/halbert_core/scheduler/*.py and utils/paths.py returns nothing: engine.py:44-63 writes each job record (which carries the job's task and inputs) and run_receipts writes receipts.json, both at the process umask. Set 0700 on the scheduler data dir and 0600 on the files at creation. The ownership-restore half is a lower-value edge case for a single-user host but is the reason to put the chmod inside the atomic-replace helper rather than once at directory creation.

missed_by_reader.title: The agent-facing scheduling tool is deliberately denied the model/provider/endpoint fields the human surfaces have
missed_by_reader.lines: 996-1002 (_HANDLER_FORWARDED_ARGS with the comment: 'model / provider / base_url are intentionally NOT here: per-job inference pins are user-owned (dashboard, hermes cron create/edit --model, hand-edited jobs) - the agent must not point unattended spend at a different model. Programmatic callers of cronjob() itself retain the parameters.'), 986-995 (check_cronjob_requirements gating the tool to interactive/gateway/exec-ask contexts)
missed_by_reader.mechanism: One tool implementation, two argument surfaces: the human surfaces can pin inference for a job, the model-facing handler cannot, because a scheduled job runs unattended and a model that could re-point its own future runs is an unbounded spend and trust hole. The split lives in the forwarded-argument tuple, not in a runtime check, so it cannot be forgotten.
missed_by_reader.task_proposal: Record this as an invariant to preserve rather than a gap to fill. Halbert has no model-setting tool today (grep -rln 'set_model|switch_model|select_model' over halbert_core/halbert_core/tools returns nothing) and no run-now or create-job route (dashboard/routes/jobs.py exposes list/get/cancel only), so the property currently holds by absence. When C1/C2 add a job-creation path, the model-facing argument list must exclude any inference-slot field - which is also the concrete mechanism behind the standing 'connection slots, not model menus' directive.

HM16-cron-second-pass.verify_summary: All 21 origin claims verified by reading the cited lines; every one holds, with three factual corrections and two mechanism-precision fixes. Corrections: C1 says 18 catalog blueprints, the CATALOG has 16 (blueprint_catalog.py:105-524); C2 describes accept_suggestion as flipping status before create_job, when the flip happens in the CronSchedulerRegistrationError handler after the job is already durable (invariant survives, ordering does not); C7 says an unverified delivery is "never conflated with a confirmed send", when _confirm_adapter_delivery returns True and records the doubt out of band via last_delivery_unverified. One halbert_state corrected: C14 was "unknown" and is "absent" — Halbert's scheduler has no pause concept at all (engine.py:88-97 cancel only, job.py:9-30 has no enabled/paused fields), so an unrunnable job re-fires forever with no auditable reason. Six candidates are re-discoveries rather than discoveries: C4, C5, C8, C11 and C16 are already written into OPENCLAW-LIFT-PACKET-03's addendum (items 6, 6, 5, 3 and 7, each citing the same Hermes file) and C2's suggestion queue is named in OSS-REVIEW-HERMES-2026-09-07.md:69 — all unimplemented, so they are kept, but the founder decision is "finish packet 03's addendum", not "adopt something new". Priorities re-set by value to a single-host steward: C6 medium→low (cross-process claim fencing exists because Hermes's worker lives outside the gateway process; Halbert is one process, and only the degenerate single-process outbox transfers), C17 medium→low (occurrence idempotency already prevents double fires; PID reuse only mismarks "interrupted"), C18 medium→low (the origin's justification is 130 subagents × 2-3 threads; 15 idle threads on one host does not repay a 15-subsystem migration), C11 high→medium (only model-resolvability has a subject — no delivery target, no skill attachment), C2 high→medium (its accept path needs a job-creation API that does not exist), C14 low→medium. C9 is strengthened rather than merely confirmed: the guard's live Halbert surface is tools/schedule_cron.py:16-50, which writes a free-text command into the OS crontab behind only BaseTool._policy_check's per-tool-name decision (tools/base.py:40-59) — a scheduled `launchctl kickstart`/`pkill` against Halbert's own daemon is reachable today. Nothing was dropped for a founder-constraint violation, though three carry conditions: C12 should lift the provenance-tiering and sanitize-don't-block principles, not the strict command-shape blocklist as a security boundary; C13's cleaner answer is not to add per-job endpoint overrides at all; C14 and C19 must drop the origin's emoji. Nine missed mechanisms, all from files absent from key_files_read (cron/jobs.py, unread bodies of scheduler_script.py, cronjob_tools.py, hermes_cli/cron.py). The highest-value one is a live Halbert defect this unit's own comparison should have caught: Hermes re-reads the durable record and calls is_job_runnable before every fire (jobs.py:477-486, scheduler_provider.py:261), while Halbert's dashboard cancel writes state='cancelled' through its own SchedulerEngine instance (routes/jobs.py:103-110) that the running executor never reloads (engine.py:22 loads once) and whose wrapped task never checks state (executor.py:581-620) — so cancelling a scheduled job from the dashboard does not stop it firing. Also missed: a deterministic natural-language schedule parser (jobs.py:655-760), the prerequisite for C1/C2 to have any user input to fill; two-signal ticker liveness markers (jobs.py:1128-1215); process-group termination on script timeout (scheduler_script.py:150-214) against Halbert's direct-child-only kills (tools/executor.py:903-910); the two-posture lock discipline (jobs.py:198-345 — global lock fails open, per-job fire fence fails closed); wall-clock-intent timezone reasoning (jobs.py:807-840, 1006-1062) against a catchup.py with no timezone logic at all; script-path confinement with the shebang deliberately ignored (scheduler_script.py:256-315); 0600/0700 on the job store (jobs.py:525-560), which Halbert writes at the process umask; and the deliberate exclusion of model/provider/base_url from the agent-facing tool (cronjob_tools.py:996-1002), which Halbert satisfies today only by absence and should preserve explicitly.
